models.title: Sunk Cost
models.lead: What you've already spent and can't get back shouldn't decide your next move.
models.when: When the main reason you want to keep going is "I've already paid for it," "I've put in so much time," or "it would be a waste to quit now," pause and think it through.
models.body:
"I paid for it, so I'd better use it." Sound familiar? We sit through a bad movie to the end, force ourselves through a course that isn't working, and keep pushing when we're exhausted because "I've come this far." We often treat what we've already put in as a reason we have to keep going.

In economics, a sunk cost is a cost that has already been incurred, cannot be recovered, and will not change no matter what you choose now. It should be left out when you compare the future costs and benefits of your options.

The trap is that stopping feels like admitting everything before was wasted. But the money you've spent won't come back because you keep suffering, and the hours already gone won't become more worthwhile because you add a few more. What you can still change is what you're willing to put in from here on, and what you'll get in return.

It helps to think in two columns. One holds what you've spent and can't recover. The other holds the costs and benefits that start now. The first column explains why letting go is hard, but when you decide what to do next, the choices you compare all belong in the second.
models.example:
You paid $280 for an online course. A few lessons in, you realize it's pitched well above your current level. Every session leaves you lost and doesn't help with the problem you actually have, yet you still make yourself watch an hour a night: "If I don't finish it, I've thrown that money away."

First, check whether you can get a refund, switch courses, or tackle the material in a different order. If the money really can't come back, separate what you've already paid from tonight's choice. Will another hour of this course actually help you? Would a better-suited beginner's book teach you more? Base the decision on which plan is more useful from here, not on proving that the original purchase wasn't a mistake.
models.extra: You buy a non-refundable movie ticket and, half an hour in, realize you really don't like the film. Whether you stay or leave, the ticket money is gone either way. The better question is about the next ninety minutes: will watching the rest be enjoyable, or would a walk or some rest suit you better? If you still want to see how it ends, staying is fine, as long as the reason is the experience ahead of you.
steps: Sort out what's truly gone and what can still be refunded, transferred, or adjusted, so you don't give up on what can be saved.
Ask yourself: if I were starting fresh today, would I still choose to spend another hour or another dollar on this?
Compare the future costs and benefits of continuing, adjusting, and stopping, then pick your next step instead of repeating "but I've already spent so much."
models.caution: This doesn't mean quitting whenever things get hard. Basic practice can be dull for a while and still be worth continuing, so of course you can stick with it. Cancellation fees, money not yet spent, missed opportunities, and commitments you owe others all belong in the decision too. The point is simply not to let unrecoverable past investment make the call on its own.
models.exercise: Write down one thing you're continuing mainly because you can't bear to waste what you've put in. Make two columns, "already gone" and "still to come," then ask: if I looked only at the second column, what would I choose?

models.title: Heuristic
models.lead: Set a few reliable rules of thumb for small things, so you don't have to think everything through from scratch every time.
models.when: When you face too many small decisions, keep going back and forth, or already have some dependable experience to draw on, give it a try.
models.body:
Glancing at the sky before you head out in the morning, restarting your phone when it acts up, checking the return policy before you buy something: these are all heuristics. The word sounds technical, but the idea is simple: use a handy rule of thumb to help you decide a bit faster. It usually isn't the perfect method, but the time and energy it saves are worth something too.

In cognitive psychology, a heuristic is a rule of thumb or mental shortcut people use to simplify judgments and solve problems. It lowers the cost of thinking but doesn't guarantee the best answer.

Why do we need them? Because there are simply too many things to decide in a day. What to have for lunch or when to reply to a message isn't worth a full analysis every time. Still, experience has a "shelf life" and a limited range: a rule that works well most of the time needs to be swapped out when something unusual comes up.
models.example:
Whenever you're waiting on a reply, you agonize: "Should I nudge them? Will I seem pushy?" Eventually you set a rule for ordinary work emails: if there's no reply after three business days, follow up once, politely, and spell out what you need next.

Now you no longer fret about it every day. But if the other person is handling the venue for tomorrow's event, you can't just wait three days; you agree on a time to confirm in advance. A good rule lets you worry less and still leaves a way out for emergencies.
models.extra: A beginner cook adds salt exactly as the recipe says. With practice, they add a little less first, taste, and then add more. "Start with less, add more later" is a handy rule of thumb: it won't make every dish perfect, but it's much easier to fix than pouring in too much at once.
steps: Pick a small thing you keep agonizing over and set a simple rule for it.
Write down the exceptions too: when shouldn't you follow it, and when do you need to think of something else?
Try it for a week or two and see whether it actually saves you energy or creates more hassle.
models.caution: Catchy rules of thumb aren't always reliable. "Expensive means good" and "If everyone's buying it, it can't be wrong" are shortcuts too, and they can cost you. For high-stakes decisions like buying a home or signing an important contract, don't rely on a one-liner alone.
models.exercise: Find a small thing you've already agonized over three times this week and write one sentence: "Next time this happens, I'll first..." Then add: "But if..., I won't follow it."
models.brief: A map of a shortcut versus a full search: a stick figure looks for fruit among many trees and follows a short trail of footprints to quickly find a basket of fruit; beside it, a longer thin gray search route visits more trees and might find bigger fruit.

models.title: The Law of Non-Contradiction
models.lead: Don't contradict yourself, and first make sure everyone is talking about the same thing.
models.when: When you run into promises, explanations, or rules that don't add up, it helps you ask the right questions.
models.body:
Suppose someone says, "The shop didn't sell a single coffee today," and then turns around and says, "We sold five coffees today." Something feels off. Counted over the same time and in the same way, both statements can't be true. That's the law of non-contradiction in its simplest form.

In classical logic, the law of non-contradiction states that a proposition and its negation cannot both be true at the same time and in the same respect.

It helps us check whether what we say hangs together, and it can uncover conditions hidden inside an argument. But don't rush to say "You're contradicting yourself." Does "today" mean the same day? Could one person be counting only delivery orders as "sold," while the other includes dine-in too? Line up what's being said first, then judge who's right.

The easiest mix-up is between "at the same time" and "one after the other." A door can be closed and then opened later, but it can't be fully open and fully closed at the same moment and in the same sense. Before deciding whether two statements contradict each other, pin down the time and the aspect being discussed.
models.example:
A store advertises "All items can be returned within 7 days, no questions asked." After you buy something, customer service tells you, "This item isn't eligible for no-questions-asked returns." If the item, the timing, and the purchase conditions haven't changed, the two statements don't match.

At that point you can ask them to be specific: is it all items, or all items except certain categories? The issue shifts from blaming each other to a rule that needs clarifying. The point of spotting a contradiction is to get the promise stated clearly so things can move forward.
models.extra: You say "I'm completely busy this weekend," and then a friend finds out you went to a movie. Maybe what you really meant was "I don't want any more social plans." Saying no accurately is usually easier than over-explaining.
steps: Write down the two statements exactly as you heard them, without adding your own interpretation.
Check the time, the subject, and the wording: are both statements really talking about exactly the same conditions?
If they still conflict, ask the other person which one should change, or what condition was left out.
models.caution: "I love being around people, and I also need time alone" isn't a contradiction, since the two can happen at different times. "I used to like it, now I don't" just means a change of mind. Don't strip out the conditions on purpose just to catch someone out.
models.exercise: Find an absolute promise you often make, like "Call me anytime." Can you really keep it? Rewrite it as a version you're both willing and able to keep.
models.brief: Two conflicting statements about the same door at the same moment: in the center, a fully closed door; on each side, a stick figure shows a thought of the door open or closed, with small crosses beneath marking that the two can't both apply to the center door at once.

models.title: First Principles Thinking
models.lead: Get clear on the most basic facts before looking for a solution, instead of rushing to copy others.
models.when: When an old approach keeps getting more complicated, when it feels like you can only do what others do, or when you've already decided you have to buy something to fix a problem, use it to break things down again.
models.body:
Your desk is a mess, and your first instinct might be to buy another organizer. Your studying isn't going anywhere, so you think about signing up for another course. But before adding more, you can take a step back: what am I actually trying to solve? Which conditions truly can't change, and which are just "the way everyone's always done it"?

First principles thinking means starting from the most basic facts or premises in a problem area and building up conclusions or solutions step by step, rather than relying only on analogies to existing practice. In practice, you have to check that those starting points are well supported.

The name sounds grand, but in daily life you can practice it with one simple move: separate facts from habits. For example, "The desk is only three feet wide" is a condition you can measure, but "All my books have to be on the desk" isn't necessarily a real rule. Keep the conditions that truly hold, then recombine your approach. That can be more useful than simply scaling up the old way.

Think of it as "take apart, then rebuild": break a complete solution down to its well-founded basic conditions, then build a new solution up from them. Breaking things down finely isn't the goal in itself. What matters is that the starting points are solid and the rebuilt solution solves the real problem.
models.example:
You want a bigger desk because once your laptop is open, there's no room to write. Before buying one, measure the room and the desktop, then look at what you actually use at the same time each day: a laptop, a notebook, and a pen. Most of the rest is books and odds and ends you're not using right now.

The real goal is "enough usable surface while I work," not necessarily "buy a bigger desk." With the room size unchanged, you could move unused books elsewhere, tidy up the cables, or try a different layout. You might still end up replacing the desk, but this time the decision rests on real measurements and needs, not on people saying bigger is better.
models.extra: When planning a friend's birthday, you don't have to start with "Which restaurant does everyone book?" First pin down the number of people, the budget, how everyone will get there, and the experience your friend really wants: a quiet chat, cooking together, or a lively party. Working back from these needs and constraints, dinner at home, a picnic in the park, or a small restaurant could all be good options, with no need to copy trendy photos.
steps: Write down the goal without mixing in a solution: for example, "be able to write comfortably," not "must buy a bigger desk."
List the well-founded basic conditions, then circle the unproven assumptions, such as "it has to be this way" or "everyone does it like this."
Starting from those conditions, come up with two or three approaches, try the cheapest one first, and use the real results to check your reasoning.
models.caution: First principles thinking doesn't mean ignoring experience and starting from nothing, and asking "why" a few more times won't automatically get you to the truth. What you take as basic facts might be wrong too, so measure and verify them. For small, well-understood things, reliable experience often saves time; you don't need to reason from scratch every time.
models.exercise: Write down a small problem you want to solve in three columns: the real goal, the facts you've confirmed, and the approaches you assume are required. Pick one item from the third column and ask: without it, are there other workable options?
models.brief: A bicycle taken apart layer by layer into basic parts, then rebuilt into a new design for carrying loads.

bodyDiagram.caption: The whole is broken down into basic parts, and a solution is rebuilt from those parts.

models.title: Maslow’s Hammer
models.lead: Just because all you have is a hammer doesn't mean every problem is a nail.
models.when: When you've used the same approach again and again and the problem hasn't budged, or you've just learned a new tool and want to use it everywhere, it's worth pausing.
models.body:
When we first learn a method, we want it to solve everything. Buy a time-management app, and suddenly beating procrastination is all about that app; take a communication course, and every conflict seems solvable by talking. That's what Maslow's hammer warns about: the method you're good at can easily become the only one you can see.

This phenomenon is also called the "law of the instrument" or "law of the hammer": people tend to over-rely on a familiar tool and use it to understand and handle all kinds of different problems.

The real first step is to understand the problem. Someone who's always late might have a poor sense of time, or their schedule might be unreasonable. A room that's always messy might come down to habits, or the storage might just be awkward to use. Different causes naturally call for different tools.
models.example:
You can never get up in the morning, so you buy a louder alarm clock and set more reminders. The alarms multiply, but you're still tired. Thinking it over, you realize you've been going to bed at 2 a.m. and getting up at 7.

At this point, continuing to research "how to wake myself up" is like swinging the hammer over and over. Rather than buying another alarm, you probably need to change your evening routine, cut back on late-night tasks, and leave yourself enough sleep. When you solve the actual problem, the tools stop being busywork.
models.extra: A child who's slow with homework doesn't necessarily just need nagging. Maybe they don't understand the problems, the desk is noisy, or they don't know which subject to do first. Sitting with them once to see what really happens makes it easier to find a fix than slapping on the label "dawdler."
steps: Start by describing what's happening, like "I was late three times this past week," without jumping to a cause.
Try coming up with one explanation each from habits, environment, resources, and rules.
Compare the options, pick the one that best fits the cause and is easy to try, and start with a small adjustment.
models.caution: Having lots of tools isn't the goal either. If you collect eighty models and try to throw all of them at every situation, you'll just complicate things. Reach first for whatever this particular situation actually needs.
models.exercise: Think of something you've tried three times and still haven't solved. Forbid yourself from using your original approach, then write down two completely different directions.
models.brief: A fan diagram of one tool misapplied: a stick figure holding a hammer faces a nail, a screw, a glass, and a knotted rope, and only the nail fits; the lines from the hammer to the other objects are blocked with small brick-red marks.

models.title: Circles of Control and Influence
models.lead: Take the step you can take first, and don't let every worry grab your energy at once.
models.when: When you're waiting on a result, worried about what others think of you, or something makes you more anxious the more you think about it and you don't know where to start, try sorting it this way first.
models.body:
After a job interview, you keep replaying the answers you didn't nail and check your phone every few minutes to see whether they'll hire you. Worrying is normal, but refreshing over and over won't make the result arrive any sooner. The circle of control helps you sort things out: in this situation, what can I do directly, what can I work toward, and what isn't up to me for now?

The circle of control is a thinking tool that organizes a problem by how much control you have, usually dividing things into what you directly control, what you can indirectly influence, and what you currently can't control. It's related to Stephen Covey's ideas of the circle of influence and the circle of concern, and it's used to help direct your attention and actions.

This isn't telling you to "stop thinking about it." It's giving your worry somewhere practical to go. You can't decide who they ultimately pick, but you can review your answers, send any missing materials, keep applying elsewhere, and schedule a little rest. Separating outcomes from actions makes it easier to find your next step instead of just going around in circles in your head.

The three circles represent different ranges of action. The innermost holds what you can do directly, the middle holds what you can discuss, ask for, and influence, and the outer one holds conditions you need to watch and adapt to but can't decide on your own. Putting your energy back into the inner circle doesn't mean ignoring outside problems.
models.example:
You have an important interview coming up. You're worried it might rain, traffic might be bad, and the interviewer might not like you. Thinking about all of it at once, nothing feels certain. Taken apart, it gets clearer: you decide when to leave, whether to check the route ahead of time, and how to prepare your materials; you can influence their judgment through how you present yourself and your work; the weather, the other candidates' performance, and the final number of openings aren't directly up to you.

So you leave extra time for the trip, practice telling two real stories from your experience, and check that your files open. After the interview, if needed, you follow up at the agreed time and carry on with your other plans. The outcome is still uncertain, but you've taken care of the parts you can, and you don't need to keep blaming yourself to prove you took it seriously.
models.extra: A friend hasn't replied to your message. You can't make them answer right away, but you can check whether your question was clear, say when you need a reply, and try another way of reaching them if necessary. If it isn't urgent, you can also agree with yourself to check your phone later. Reaching out and giving each other space are both things you can do; guessing at what they're thinking a hundred times won't necessarily help you understand them better.
steps: Write down each worry and sort it into three groups: "I can decide this directly," "I can discuss or work toward this," and "I can't decide this right now."
Pick one small action from the first group; for the second, work out whom to ask and for what, and don't confuse influence with a guaranteed result.
For the third group, keep the attention and backup plans you need, set a time for checking messages, and get back to what you can move forward now.
models.caution: What's controllable and what isn't can change over time, and it isn't the same as how important something is. Some problems call for asking for help, negotiating, or working toward a solution together; not being able to solve something alone doesn't mean you just have to put up with it. Feelings also don't vanish because someone tells you to "look on the bright side." You can take care of yourself first, then choose the right action.
models.exercise: Write down the thing weighing on you most right now, then complete three sentences: "What I can do now is...", "Who I can ask for help or talk to is...", and "What I can't decide for now is...". Then do one small action from the first sentence that takes under ten minutes.

models.title: Critical Thinking
models.lead: When you hear a claim, don't rush to nod along, and don't rush to argue either.
models.when: When you come across a catchy conclusion, hear very absolute advice, or notice you already badly want to believe something, that's when it's most useful.
models.body:
"Critical thinking" sounds like nitpicking, but it's really more like careful checking: what exactly is this saying? What's it based on? Are there other explanations? You don't have to win the other person over; you're just adding one more check to your own judgment.

More formally, critical thinking is a way of thinking that carefully evaluates information, evidence, and reasoning, and forms or revises judgments based on that evaluation.

This step matters most for views you like. It's easy to let your guard down when something agrees with you: "I've always thought so, so it must be right." The point of practicing is to become willing to change your mind based on new evidence, not just to get better at arguing.
models.example:
You see a video saying "Get up an hour earlier every day, and your life will change." It sounds convincing, and you almost share it right away. Pause and think: what specific change does he mean? Were the people shown already very disciplined? Are there people who got up early and saw no improvement?

You can still try getting up early, but give yourself a more practical question: "If I get up earlier without cutting my sleep, can I get an extra half hour of calm reading?" That way you end up with a life experiment you can check, not a slogan you have to believe.
models.extra: A friend says, "Everyone at your company is hard to get along with." You can start by asking what happened recently. It might be one clash, or there might really be a long-running problem. Separate the experience from the generalization first, then decide how to help.
steps: First restate what the other person means in your own words to check you haven't misunderstood.
Ask three questions: Where's the evidence? Could there be other causes? Whose situation isn't being mentioned?
It's fine to make a provisional decision; just jot down what new information would change your mind.
models.caution: Don't turn careful thinking into endless faultfinding. Life can't wait until every question is settled. Check important things more thoroughly, and try small things first while leaving room to come back and adjust.
models.exercise: Pick a view you recently shared or saved and write one sentence: "I believe it because..." If all you can write is "it sounds reasonable," go find one concrete piece of support.
models.brief: An evidence-screening funnel: wordless message icons pour into a magnifying glass and layered sieves held by a stick figure, pass checks marked by a magnifying glass, a source link, and a reasoning chain, and come out as a lightbulb conclusion backed by evidence; a return arrow loops from new evidence back into the screening, showing revision rather than rejecting all information.

models.title: Black-and-White Thinking
models.lead: Getting one thing wrong doesn't mean you're no good as a person.
models.when: When one slip makes you want to give up on everything, or an argument in a relationship turns into "you always...", use it to slow down.
models.body:
"Either it's perfect or it's pointless." "If you don't back me, you don't care about me." "I broke my diet today, so the whole week is ruined." Thoughts like these, which leave only two extremes, are black-and-white thinking. They let you reach a conclusion fast, but throw away all the useful information in between.

In cognitive psychology, this is usually called "all-or-nothing thinking": seeing a complex situation as two mutually exclusive extremes and ignoring differences of degree and the possibilities in between.

Most of life looks more like this: some parts are good and some still need work; you didn't manage it this time, but you did before. Describing things more specifically isn't just consoling yourself; it leaves room for the next step. You don't have to declare your whole self a winner or a loser before you can deal with one small problem.

Many real-life assessments are more like a scale than two on-off switches. "I didn't do well this time" may just mean one step needs fixing; it doesn't jump straight to "I'm completely hopeless." Find where you are on the scale first, then decide which way to adjust.
models.example:
You plan to read twenty pages a day. You keep it up for four days, then on day five you're too busy and skip it, and immediately think, "I knew I couldn't stick with it." That verdict wipes out four days of effort and makes starting again on day six even harder.

Try putting it another way: "I read on four days this week. Twenty pages is too much when I'm busy, so next time my minimum is two pages." You're not pretending a missed day doesn't matter, and you're not throwing the whole thing away because of one missed day. That makes the plan easier to keep going.
models.extra: A conflict in a relationship doesn't mean all the past caring was fake, but past caring doesn't mean the current problem can be ignored either. Letting both things be true at once is usually closer to reality.
steps: Notice words like "always," "never," "totally," and "not even once" in what you say.
Find one example, however small, that doesn't fully fit the conclusion.
Swap a label for your whole self with a specific situation and a next step, like "I need to practice my opening."
models.caution: Some things really do need a clear yes or no, like whether you met a deadline. This model isn't about making every rule fuzzy; it's about not inflating one result into a verdict on your whole life.
models.exercise: Write down an absolute judgment that's been hurting you lately. Delete "always," "never," and "completely," add the specific time and event, then read it again.

models.title: Opportunity Cost
models.lead: When you choose something, also look at what you're giving up for it.
models.when: When you think "it's free anyway" or "it's just a bit more time," or you want several things but can't fit them all in, use it to compare.
models.body:
You spend two hours scrolling videos without paying a cent. Does that really cost nothing? Those two hours could have gone to sleep, exercise, or dinner with friends. Opportunity cost reminds us that a choice isn't only about what you pay out; it's also about where else the same time and resources could have gone.

In economics, opportunity cost is the value of the best feasible alternative you give up to get the benefits of a particular choice. It can include money, as well as time, rest, or anything else you value.

The easiest mistake here is to add up the benefits of everything you didn't choose. Skipping a movie, a run, and a book doesn't mean one session of scrolling cost you all three; you could never have fit them all into those two hours anyway. What's worth comparing is the one alternative you'd most likely, and most willingly, have chosen instead.

Imagine the same stretch of time can only take one fork in the road: choose studying and you may give up rest; choose rest and you may give up this round of studying. Opportunity cost looks at the most worthwhile of the options you didn't pick, not the sum of every road not taken.
models.example:
You have three free hours on a weekend afternoon. You could take a side gig that pays $45, or spend time with a friend who's rarely back in town. The gig's payoff is easy to calculate, but it also means that time for seeing your friend is used up. Seeing your friend isn't just a "free chat" either; you're also giving up the money you could have earned.

There's no answer that works for everyone. If you urgently need the income, taking the gig may make more sense; if this meetup will be hard to arrange again, seeing your friend has good reasons too. Laying out the option you're giving up is about choosing with clear eyes, not about converting every relationship and every rest into an hourly wage.
models.extra: A store's sale saves you $3, but the round trip takes an extra hour. If the trip wears you out and makes you miss something you wanted to attend, cheaper isn't necessarily better; if you wanted a walk anyway and can browse along the way, the trip might be worth it. What matters is what else that time would actually do for you.
steps: First identify what's really limited: time, budget, energy, or an opportunity you only get once?
Find the most valuable alternative that's actually feasible if you don't make this choice, without adding up every imagined benefit.
Compare the benefits and costs you care about most on each side, then commit to your choice and don't keep dwelling on every road not taken.
models.caution: Rest and fun have value too; you don't need to spend every minute making money. Options that aren't feasible don't count as real alternatives. Also keep three things separate so you don't count anything twice: the direct cost of spending money, the sunk cost of money already spent, and the opportunity cost of giving up other uses.
models.exercise: Pick something you plan to spend two hours on this week. Write down what you'd most likely do instead if you skipped it, and what each would give you. Don't list ten ideal options; compare just one real, feasible alternative.
models.brief: The same stretch of time splits into two possibilities, studying and resting, with a solid path running beside a dashed path not taken.

models.title: The Socratic Method
models.lead: Asking a few good questions is often more useful than rushing to give answers.
models.when: When you face a sweeping conclusion, a tough choice, or two people talking past each other, it helps you break things down.
models.body:
Socratic questioning means asking, layer by layer, until things are clear. If someone says "This plan is bad," you can ask "What's bad about it?", "What problem are we trying to solve?", or "Has the thing you're worried about ever actually happened?" These questions help everyone move from a vague verdict to specific things they can discuss.

Socratic questioning uses step-by-step, probing questions to clarify concepts, examine reasons and hidden assumptions, and explore the consequences of a view and its alternatives.

It's not the same as aggressive interrogation. Good questioning means looking for answers together, leaving room for "I don't know yet," and being willing to explain your own thinking. If you've already made up your mind and are just asking roundabout questions until the other person gives in, they'll usually just get more defensive.
models.example:
A friend says, "I have to quit. This job has no future at all." Instead of immediately urging him to stay or go, you help him unpack it: "When you say future, do you mean pay, learning, or promotion? What disappoints you most? Would switching companies definitely make it better?"

After talking it through, he realizes what bothers him most is doing the same repetitive work for so long. Now he can consider an internal transfer, building new skills, and outside opportunities all at once. Once the questions get specific, the choices actually multiply, and he doesn't have to pick between quitting on impulse and just gritting his teeth.
models.extra: You can also use it on yourself: why do I feel "it's too late"? Is there a real deadline, or am I anxious because I see others getting ahead? These two answers would lead you to completely different actions.
steps: First check whether the other person wants to be heard or is open to analyzing things together; don't fire off ten questions right away.
Ask slowly around three areas: What does this word mean? What's it based on? What other possibilities are there?
End the conversation on one small, doable action instead of stopping at abstract principles.
models.caution: When someone is very upset, they may first need comfort and rest, not a logic check. Also avoid pressing with "why" again and again; try "What happened?" or "Which part worries you most?" instead.
models.exercise: Pick a conclusion that's been troubling you lately and write three gentle questions in a row. Try to make each question more specific, and don't rush to fill in answers.
models.brief: A layered structure of progressive questioning: a central idea lightbulb is wrapped in several semi-transparent hollow rings; a stick figure with a magnifying glass works through them layer by layer to find an evidence puzzle piece and hidden-assumption pillars at the bottom; wordless speech bubbles lead step by step down to the foundation and then form a revised lightbulb.

models.title: Principle of Falsification
models.lead: If a claim can never be proven wrong, it's hard to know whether it's actually reliable.
models.when: When you notice a method that's "right no matter what happens," or you really don't want to admit your plan isn't working, remember this.
models.body:
Someone says a stone brings good luck: when things go well, the stone is working; when things go badly, the stone shielded you from something worse. Notice that whatever happens, it's never "wrong." The principle of falsification reminds us that to seriously test a claim about reality, you first have to say what outcome would make you reconsider it.

In Karl Popper's philosophy of science, falsifiability means a theory must be incompatible with some possible empirical observations; in other words, there must be possible test results that could refute it.

"Falsification" sounds like looking for trouble, but it's really giving an idea a doorway to be tested. You can love your plan and still be willing to say, "If this doesn't improve things, I'll admit it might not be right for me." That's how you get a chance to actually learn something.
models.example:
You're convinced that "making a plan before bed helps me procrastinate less the next day," so you pick a way to check it in advance: for the next two weeks, record how many of each day's three most important tasks you finish, and also note whether it's making you go to bed later.

If things don't improve, you don't quietly change the standard to "at least I look more disciplined." Instead, you check whether the plan has too much in it, whether the tasks are too big, or whether the method just doesn't help you much. One small trial can't settle everything, but it does leave you fewer excuses.
models.extra: You say "If you work hard, you'll definitely succeed," and whenever someone fails, it's explained away as "they didn't work hard enough." If "hard enough" has no clear standard, the claim is hard to test, and it can easily leave people who've hit setbacks carrying all the blame.
steps: Write your idea as one specific prediction, not just "it'll be better."
Write down in advance which results would lower your confidence or make you willing to try something else.
When the results come in, check them against your original standard first, and don't change what "success" means on the spot.
models.caution: A single failure might mean the method was carried out poorly, or that the original guess was wrong, so check those separately. Questions of feelings, taste, and morality can't all be settled by one experiment either, so don't force it.
models.exercise: Add one sentence to a method you really like: "If ... happens, I'll reconsider." Then see whether you're truly willing to accept that outcome.
models.brief: A testable counterexample: on the left, many white swans support a simple thought bubble saying swans are white; on the right, one clear black swan breaks through the border of that generalization along a bold navy arrow, while an observer checks the black swan with a magnifying glass.

models.title: Burden of Proof
models.lead: Whoever wants others to believe something should be the one to bring the evidence.
models.when: When someone makes you a big promise but expects you to prove them wrong first, this is a good model to reach for.
models.body:
A friend says a new restaurant is amazing, and you can take that as a casual recommendation. Someone else says an app will definitely double your income and wants you to pay a lot for it, and now they owe you much more solid reasons. That's the everyday meaning of the burden of proof: the loudest person doesn't win, and the fact that nobody can rebut you on the spot doesn't mean you're right.

The burden of proof is the responsibility of the party who asserts a fact to provide evidence supporting that claim within the relevant discussion or proceeding; exactly how it is allocated depends on the context and its rules.

Watch out especially for the reversed demand: "Can you prove it doesn't work?" Failing to show something is useless doesn't automatically show that it works. The stronger and more consequential a claim is, the more it usually needs to be backed up with real evidence.
models.example:
Someone in a group chat says, "This course guarantees you'll land a job within a month." You ask what the guarantee is based on, and they reply, "You haven't even taken it, so how do you know it doesn't work?" That doesn't answer your question. You never claimed the course was useless. You only asked what supports a promise you're being asked to pay for.

You can keep going: what kind of job counts as "landing a job"? How many people signed up, and how many succeeded? Are the people who didn't succeed counted too? Where are the conditions of the guarantee written down? Questions like these get you much closer to the information you need for a decision than arguing vaguely about whether to "believe" it.
models.extra: "You say there's an invisible dragon in the room, and I can't prove there isn't" doesn't mean you should start buying dragon food. The person who first asserts the fact needs to explain why everyone should take it seriously.
steps: First figure out whether the other person is sharing a feeling, offering a guess, or asking you to accept something as fact.
Ask them where their evidence comes from and whether there are records or materials you can check.
The more expensive or irreversible the decision, the more carefully you should check the most important evidence.
models.caution: This applies to you too. If you jump from "I haven't seen any evidence" to "it's definitely false," you've made a claim that also needs explaining. And ordinary small talk doesn't need to be treated like a cross-examination in court.
models.exercise: Think of a recent piece of advice that boiled down to "just trust me." Write down the one thing you'd really need to verify, then turn it into a polite, specific question.
models.brief: A claim needs evidence to hold it up: a stick figure holds up a glowing star-shaped claim above a bridge with a missing section, and only three pieces of evidence (a photo, a record icon, and a magnifying glass for observation) placed on the bridge piers can support it. The person making the claim builds the bridge, while the listener stands on the other side checking it, not asked to prove that nothing exists.

models.title: Prototype Theory
models.lead: When we think of a kind of thing, we usually picture a "typical" example first.
models.when: When you're introducing something, teaching a new tool, or sorting things into categories, or when you're tempted to rule someone out because they "don't look the part," this model helps.
models.body:
When someone says "bird," you might picture a sparrow. When someone says "chair," you might picture a wooden one with four legs and a back. Those first images are the typical examples in your head. Prototype theory says we often understand categories through this sense of "how much does it look like one," rather than always starting from a strict definition.

In cognitive science, prototype theory holds that members of a category can differ in how typical they are, and that people often understand a category by organizing it around typical instances and their features.

That's why a penguin might make you hesitate for a second, even though it's just as much a bird. It isn't less qualified; it just doesn't look like the version you know best. Knowing this helps you understand why someone can't make sense of a design, and reminds you not to be boxed in by familiar shapes.

The "center and edges" here are about how typical something is, not a simple test of who's in and who's out. A penguin isn't as typical as the small flying birds we usually picture, but it's still a bird. A bat can fly, but that doesn't make it a bird. Being far from the prototype isn't a reason to exclude something from the category.
models.example:
You set up a new budgeting app for an older relative. The home screen is full of colorful cards and complicated charts. He can't find where to "add an entry" and feels it isn't a budget book at all. You, on the other hand, think every feature is right there, so how could he not know how to use it?

The problem may be that the budget book in his head is a list of rows: date, income, spending, balance. If you first make the entry point look like that familiar layout and introduce the charts gradually, learning gets much easier. You're not cutting features. You're building a bridge between the familiar and the new.
models.extra: The first time someone eats a plant-based burger, they might say, "It tastes good, but it's not like meat." That shows they're using the familiar beef burger as their reference point. Introduced as a dish in its own right, it might be met with different expectations.
steps: Think about what concrete thing the other person will picture first when they hear the name.
Keep a few easy-to-recognize features so people can tell what it's for.
Then explain what's special about it, and check for exceptions that get unfairly hurt by the "typical" image.
models.caution: Typical doesn't mean correct. Someone who doesn't look like your idea of a teacher, programmer, or manager isn't unqualified because of it. Appearance and style aren't the whole evidence of someone's ability or identity.
models.exercise: Pick a profession you know well and write down your first impression of it. Then think of someone who doesn't fit that impression but is great at the job, and notice which features you'd mistaken for requirements.
models.brief: A hub-and-spoke diagram of a prototype and graded members: a typical small bird icon sits in the center, surrounded by a sparrow, a pigeon, a penguin, an ostrich, and a bat. The bird members sit at different distances from the center, while the bat is outside the dashed category boundary. A stick figure compares their features.

bodyDiagram.caption: The center is closer to the typical image, and the edges can be less typical; distance alone doesn't decide what belongs in the category.

models.title: The Reasonable Person
models.lead: Don't use everything you know now to insist someone should have known it back then.
models.when: When something has gone wrong and you need to sort out responsibility, or when you keep blaming yourself with "I should have known," this model offers a different angle.
models.body:
The name can be misleading. It doesn't refer to a perfectly logical, self-interested person. It means a reasonable, careful person, and what such a person would usually notice and do in that particular situation at that time. It doesn't demand that people never make mistakes.

In law, the reasonable person standard is an objective benchmark used to judge what actions or precautions a reasonably prudent person in the same situation would take.

Think of it as a pair of glasses that take you back to the scene: what information was available then? What risks were obvious? Did this person take the care they should have? That way you don't blame someone just because things went wrong, and nobody gets to dodge real responsibility with "well, I didn't know."
models.example:
A friend asks you to look after their pet for a few days and tells you about the food, the water, and the window that must stay closed. You follow the instructions, but a small problem comes up with no warning signs at all. That's a very different situation from knowing the window was open and ignoring it completely.

When you assess what happened, you can't just look at whether something went wrong in the end. You also need to look at what could reasonably have been foreseen and whether the right precautions were taken. This makes looking back fairer: fix the process where the process needs fixing, and own up to carelessness where there was carelessness.
models.extra: Years ago you chose your college major based on a short course description, and only later discovered you didn't actually like it. You can learn from that to ask around more thoroughly next time, but you don't have to expect your 18-year-old self to have had the knowledge you gained over the next ten years.
steps: First reconstruct what was known at the time, leaving out anything that only came to light later.
Ask what a conscientious, responsible person in the same position would usually have checked.
Separate ordinary uncertainty from avoidable carelessness, then talk about how to improve.
models.caution: This isn't "most people cut corners, so I can too," and it doesn't expect everyone to act like an expert. The actual legal rules are their own matter. Here it's just a way to help you look at people's actions fairly.
models.exercise: Think of a decision you still regret. Make two columns: "what I knew then" and "what I only learned later." See whether you've been counting everything in the second column as a mistake you made at the time.
models.brief: A comparison of reasonable care in the same situation: two ordinary stick figures face the same slippery floor and staircase. One sets out a bright warning cone with no text and walks slowly holding the handrail; the other runs and slips.

models.title: Occam’s Razor
models.lead: Check the simple, common explanation first before you spin a big story.
models.when: When you hit a small glitch or a misunderstanding, or something starts to feel more and more like a conspiracy, this model helps you steady yourself first.
models.body:
If your phone suddenly goes silent, you check whether it's on mute before you suspect a broken chip or a hacked system. In everyday terms, Occam's razor means that when several explanations all make sense, you consider first the one that doesn't need a lot of extra assumptions. That's usually less work, and it's easier to check.

Occam's razor is a principle of parsimony: when explanations account for the evidence equally well, prefer the one that introduces fewer additional assumptions.

But "simple" doesn't mean "careless." The rule doesn't guarantee that the simplest explanation is right. If you've checked mute, the volume, and the headphone connection and everything's fine, of course you keep digging. It helps you decide what to check first. It isn't a reason to reject a reality that really is complicated.
models.example:
You sent a friend a message and haven't heard back all day, and a whole plot quickly forms in your head: are they upset with me? Did I say something wrong last time? Did someone stir up trouble? For that explanation to hold, you'd have to be right about a lot of unconfirmed things at once.

Start with a few causes that are easy to check: they're busy, they haven't seen it, or they don't realize it needs a reply. Add a quick note like "I need to confirm by Friday, so just let me know when you get a chance," and you'll often get new information. If there's a clear, ongoing problem, have a real conversation then, rather than letting guesses torment you all day.
models.extra: If a houseplant's leaves are turning yellow, check the watering, the light, the soil, and the change of season before considering rare diseases. It's not that plants never get sick. Checking the most common causes first just makes it easier to find your way.
steps: Write down what you're actually seeing, and hold off on adding motives or a storyline.
Check the common causes first: the ones that need fewer conditions and are easy to verify.
If they don't pan out, keep investigating, and don't ignore new clues just to stick with "simple."
models.caution: "It's too complicated for my taste, so it must be wrong" is not this principle. And don't just pick whichever explanation sounds nicest to you. Evidence matters more than how long the story is.
models.exercise: Pick something you've been thinking about a lot lately but haven't checked. Write down one explanation that doesn't require imagining so many details, then note how you could check it.
models.brief: A parsimony comparison between equally good explanations: the same unlit desk lamp is shown with a short chain of reasoning leading to a loose plug, and a long, winding chain running through many unsupported gears and tangled lines. Both sides point to the same observation.

models.title: Compounding
models.lead: Let what you've already built help you build the next thing.
models.when: When you're committing to long-term learning, building up work materials, or practicing a skill, look at whether each effort leaves behind something you can still use later, not just how much you got done today.
models.body:
Two people each study a little every day. One finds that new knowledge keeps connecting to what they already know; the other always seems to be starting over. The difference may not just be how much time they spend. It's whether what they learned earlier sticks around and keeps getting used in later practice. The compounding effect points us to this kind of process, where what you've accumulated takes part in the next round.

Compound interest originally means adding the interest earned on a principal to the base for future interest calculations, so that the interest itself also grows over time. Borrowed as a thinking model, compounding emphasizes feeding existing results back into the next round, creating a foundation that can accumulate and amplify.

Start with a pure arithmetic example. Suppose $100 grows by a fixed 10% each period and the growth stays in. After the first period you have $110, and the second period is calculated on $110, giving $121 rather than $120. The percentage here is just for illustration, not a promise of returns. When we borrow the idea for learning and work, what we care about is accumulation you can reuse. Human growth can't simply be plugged into a fixed growth formula.

To understand compounding, look not only at whether the total gets bigger but also at whether the arrow carries existing results into the next round. Adding the same amount again and again is just accumulation. Compounding means what you've already built also takes part in the growth that follows. Applied to learning, this picture is an analogy and doesn't guarantee any fixed rate of growth.
models.example:
You start writing articles. With each one, you save a clearly explained example, fix a problem that keeps coming up, and keep a structure that worked as a reference for next time. After a while, new articles no longer start from a blank page: old material is reusable, new structures feel familiar, and it's easier to spot where your writing gets convoluted.

So the value of each piece doesn't stay locked inside that one article. It helps with what you write next. That's the part you can understand through the idea of compounding. If you just copied a paragraph every day that you didn't understand yourself, no amount of saving would give you the same benefit. The key isn't only doing it more often, but the quality of what you accumulate and whether you actually put it to use again.
models.extra: You're learning to cook, and each time you note the heat, timing, and tricky steps that work with your own pots and pans. Later, when you make a similar dish, you can draw on that experience and skip some of the trial and error. That's everyday accumulation and reuse. It doesn't mean your cooking improves by some fixed percentage with every dish. To keep improving, you still need to experiment, correct mistakes, and practice.
steps: Pick something worth building up over the long run, and set a pace you can actually sustain instead of chasing daily doubling.
Each time, leave behind something you'll be able to use later, such as review cards, notes on revisions, a reusable template, or a basic move you've mastered.
Regularly check whether what you've built really helps with new tasks. If it doesn't, adjust your approach, and leave time for rest and review.
models.caution: Sticking with something doesn't guarantee exponential growth. Forgetting, fatigue, the wrong method, and outside changes can all eat away at what you've built, and practice will hit plateaus. When you see problems, you can change methods, scale back, or ask for feedback. Don't use "it'll compound eventually" as an excuse to keep doing something that isn't working.
models.exercise: Pick something you do every week and write down: "When I finish this time, what can I leave behind to make next time easier?" This week, save one small result, then plan a time to actually use it.
models.brief: Existing results are fed into the next stage, with stacks of money gradually building up along a growth curve.

bodyDiagram.caption: What you've already built goes into the next round and becomes part of the growth that follows.

models.title: Entropy
models.lead: Tidying up only lasts a while; to keep things working, someone has to keep looking after them.
models.when: When you're organizing files, maintaining a knowledge base, keeping order at home, or estimating the cost of a long-term project, this model is a good fit.
models.body:
A drawer you just cleaned out looks neat, and a few weeks later it's stuffed with clutter again. A computer folder you just sorted soon fills up with "final," "final 2," and "really final." Borrowing the idea of entropy, the most useful everyday reminder is this: a lot of order needs maintenance. You can't set it up once and walk away.

The second law of thermodynamics states that the total entropy of an isolated system does not spontaneously decrease; entropy is a physical state quantity and can't simply be equated with what we call messiness in everyday life.

To be clear, entropy in physics has a strict meaning, and the second law isn't just a slogan that "everything gets messier." What we're doing here is drawing an analogy: new things keep coming in, old things never get cleared out, the rules for using the system are unclear, and so the system naturally becomes harder to use. Once you know the causes, you can plan for upkeep.
models.example:
You spend a weekend sorting your photos by year and feel you've finally solved the problem. Three months later, new photos are scattered across your phone, your chat history, and your downloads folder, and finding the pictures from one trip takes ages again.

Instead of letting a huge pile build up and reorganizing everything each time, set a few rules: back up once a month on a fixed day, send new photos to a single place first, and delete duplicates as you go. What you're reducing isn't some "destiny of chaos," but the buildup that comes from nobody looking after things or nobody having time to.
models.extra: If a contact list never gets updated, phone numbers go out of date and people's roles change. It may have been complete when it was created, but that doesn't guarantee it'll still be reliable two years later. Part of a resource's value comes from its content, and part comes from someone keeping it up to date.
steps: Pick a place that keeps getting messy again, and look at where new things come in.
Set up a simple way to put things back and throw things out, so tidying takes only a tiny bit of extra effort.
Schedule a small, regular maintenance slot instead of leaving everything for a big cleanup.
models.caution: Don't use "entropy always increases" to scare yourself into thinking everything is bound to collapse beyond repair. Homes, teams, and software can all become more orderly through ongoing effort. You just need to treat maintenance as real work.
models.exercise: Find a place that keeps falling into disorder, design a maintenance action you can finish in five minutes, and give it a specific time.
models.brief: A physics diagram of heat evening out in an isolated system: two large sealed boxes are compared before and after. In the left box, a warm red cup and a cold gray block have a temperature difference, with small dots of heat moving from hot to cold. In the right box, both are close to the same temperature and the heat is evenly spread.

models.title: Survivorship Bias
models.lead: The people who succeeded stand out, while the ones who didn't are usually out of the picture.
models.when: When you see success stories, course results, brands that have lasted for decades, or hear "things used to be built to last," first think about everything that never made it into the picture.
models.body:
You scroll past ten people who succeeded with a certain method, and it's easy to think, "They all did it, so if I copy them, it should work for me too." But what you're seeing may be only the people who are willing to share, still at it, or already made it. People who tried the same method and didn't succeed may have quit long ago and never got the chance to appear in your feed.

Survivorship bias is a form of selection bias: an analysis includes only the cases that passed some filter, kept existing, or were observed, while ignoring those that were eliminated, dropped out, or went missing, which systematically skews conclusions about the whole.

"Surviving" here doesn't have to mean staying alive. It can mean staying in an industry, finishing a training program, or keeping a business running to this day. The problem isn't just that success stories are rare. It's that the process by which they reach you has already filtered out many different outcomes. Looking only at what's left makes success seem too simple and risk seem too small.

It becomes easier to see the problem if you trace the whole path: everyone who started, the filter, and the ones who remain. Success stories usually sit at the far end, after the filtering, while those who quit or failed may have vanished from view. Before judging the whole, you need to bring those missing cases back into consideration.
models.example:
You want to open a coffee shop, so you visit five small shops that are doing well. The owners all say they love coffee, take their product seriously, and put real time into running the business. So you conclude that as long as you're passionate and hardworking enough, a shop should survive.

But the shops you visited are the ones still open and willing to talk to you. The shops nearby that closed last year may have been just as dedicated but ran into problems with rent, foot traffic, or cash flow. A fuller picture means also talking to people who closed, looking up how many shops opened and closed in the same area, and comparing location, costs, experience, and other conditions. Successful people's experience is still worth learning from. It just isn't a guarantee that "doing this will make you succeed."
models.extra: You look at an old piece of furniture your grandparents left behind and think, "Furniture used to be so much better made than it is now." But poorly made old furniture that broke long ago has probably been thrown out, so it never survived for you to see. To compare the overall quality of two eras, you can't pit the few most durable pieces from the last generation against everything from this one, good and bad.
steps: When you see a success story, first ask how many people tried in total, and whether those who quit or fell short are counted too.
Try to find unsuccessful cases from the same period under similar conditions, and learn what they ran into instead of settling for "they just didn't work hard enough."
Treat stories as clues, then check what role method, resources, timing, and luck each played, rather than turning a story straight into a probability of success.
models.caution: Successful people's experience isn't worthless, and failures aren't necessarily more representative. The point is to fill in the information that got filtered out and compare cases with similar conditions. When you don't know the total number of people, admit that you can't estimate the success rate yet, and don't leap from "someone did it" to "anyone can do it."
models.exercise: Find a success story that recently got you excited and ask three more questions: How many people tried in total? Who dropped out along the way? Where are the people who didn't succeed? Write down the information gaps first, without rushing to believe or dismiss the story.
models.brief: A filtering funnel and the invisible failures: many paper airplanes take off at the top, but only a few pass through a filter gate to reach a display stand, while many fall below the gate. A stick figure at first looks only at the display stand; a second, navy observation arrow points down to the overlooked paper airplanes, restoring the full picture.

sources.title: University of Osnabrück MethodsLab · Survivorship Bias

bodyDiagram.caption: What's left is only the part that made it through the filter; the cases that disappeared from view still belong to the original whole.

models.title: Authority Bias
models.lead: A title tells you what someone is good at, but it doesn't make everything they say automatically right.
models.when: When a celebrity endorses something, a speaker has an impressive title, or a team stops discussing because "the boss said so," this model helps.
models.body:
A teacher, a doctor, or a famous entrepreneur has usually built up a lot of experience in their own field and deserves to be taken seriously. But sometimes we stretch that trust to every topic: because someone succeeded in business, we assume they're also reliable on education, history, and nutrition. That's what authority bias commonly looks like.

Authority bias is the tendency to attribute greater accuracy or give more weight to an opinion because it comes from an authority figure, without adequately examining the content itself.

The safer approach isn't to reject experts, but to put your trust in the right place. First see whether the person is talking about their own field. Then look at what evidence they offer, whether they explain where things are uncertain, and what other people who know the subject think.
models.example:
During a livestream, a writer you really admire recommends a paid learning tool. Their books have genuinely helped you, so you want to buy it almost without looking at the features or the price. But being a great writer doesn't mean they know your study habits, or that they've tried every similar product.

You can treat the recommendation as a lead: try the free version first, and check whether you can export your data and whether it actually solves your problem. That way you're not dismissing the writer's experience, but you're also not treating their reputation as reason enough to spend your money.
models.extra: A teacher who's great at teaching math doesn't necessarily know which career suits each student best. A coworker who ran one successful project doesn't prove that the same plan fits every client. Respecting experience while asking about the conditions isn't rude.
steps: First ask: how closely is what they're saying related to their professional experience?
Then look at the specific evidence, the conditions under which it applies, and whether there's anything you should know about, such as a paid partnership.
For important decisions, find at least one independent source instead of just hearing the same celebrity's view repeated.
models.caution: "Experts can be wrong too" doesn't mean any random guess is as credible as professional research. What you should compare is relevant experience and evidence, rather than swinging between blind obedience and opposing every expert on principle.
models.exercise: Take one piece of advice you recently followed and complete two sentences: "What this person is actually good at is..." and "What I still need to check for myself this time is..."
models.brief: Separating the look of authority from the evidence: on the left, a stick figure at a podium wearing a medal uses a big megaphone to present a geometric idea, and the listeners follow automatically. On the right, an ordinary stick figure examines evidence pieces of the same pattern with a magnifying glass. A broken line between the medal and the truth shows that identity alone can't settle the question.

models.title: Inversion
models.lead: When you can't figure out how to do something well, ask instead: how could I be sure to mess it up?
models.when: When you're preparing an event, handing in an assignment, planning a trip, or have a plan that sounds great but you keep worrying you've missed something, try checking it in reverse first.
models.body:
When we're about to do something, we usually ask, "How can I make this succeed?" But that question is so broad that all we come up with is "try harder" or "be more careful." Flip it around and ask, "What would make this hard to pull off?" and the answers tend to be much more concrete: preparing at the last minute, not checking the requirements, putting it off until the end.

Inversion is a way of thinking that analyzes a problem from the direction opposite to the goal: first identify the conditions that would block the goal or cause failure, then look for actions that reduce or eliminate them. It complements forward planning and helps uncover obstacles that are easy to overlook.

Write down those pitfalls, then work out how to avoid each one, and you'll have a preparation checklist you can actually follow. For example, "don't be late" becomes "check the route ahead of time and leave an extra twenty minutes for transfers."

"Inversion" here means checking the same goal from the other direction. It isn't about contradicting everyone, and turning a sentence backwards doesn't make it wise. You still want things to go well. You're just looking for holes by starting from the ways in to failure.

Thinking backwards isn't just reversing the order of the steps. You can start from an outcome you don't want and trace back to its causes, then turn each cause into a preventive action. The causes may sit side by side; they don't have to be forced into one chain where each inevitably leads to the next.
models.example:
You're organizing a get-together with friends this weekend and want everyone to have a good time, but you don't know where to start. First ask, "What would make the trip a waste of everyone's time?" Ideas come easily: sending the wrong address, finding no seats when you arrive, forgetting to ask who can't eat spicy food, and people having no way to get home afterward.

So you send the location in advance, book a table, ask about dietary needs, and check when the last train leaves. These steps may not make the gathering spectacular, but they rule out a few letdowns that could easily have been avoided. With those handled, you can plan games and little surprises with more peace of mind.
models.extra: If you want to use your phone less, first ask, "What would keep me scrolling forever?" All notifications turned on, the phone right by your pillow, and opening short videos every time you're bored. So you might turn off unnecessary notifications, put your phone across the room before bed, and keep a book handy for bored moments. Then keep watching for whether you've just found a new way to procrastinate.
steps: Write down one specific goal, such as "submit a proposal that meets the requirements by Friday."
Flip it and list the three things most likely to make it fail, focusing on ones you can influence.
Turn each one into a preventive action, then check afterward: what else is needed to actually reach the goal?
models.caution: Avoiding the conditions for failure isn't the same as meeting the conditions for success. Showing up on time doesn't mean you'll pass the interview, and complete paperwork doesn't mean the proposal is any good. And don't let this turn into endless worrying: deal with the two or three most realistic risks, then move forward.
models.exercise: Pick a small task you need to finish this week and complete the sentence: "If I wanted this to fail, I would..." Write three answers, then choose one and take a preventive step right away.
models.brief: The reverse structure of inversion planning: on the right, the goal is a reachable flagpole; on the left, a stick figure is setting out. A gray line along the top works backward from the goal through failure points such as a stumbling stone, a broken bridge, and a leaky boat, with the stick figure marking obstacles from back to front and repairing the bridge. Along the bottom, a navy route runs from the start to the goal, avoiding the obstacles that have been identified.

bodyDiagram.caption: Start from the outcome you don't want and look back to find a few possible causes.

models.title: Replication
models.lead: Doing it once might be luck; would it still work with different people, at a different time?
models.when: When you're rolling out a new approach, buying into a so-called secret to success, or about to treat one good result as a lasting ability, this model is especially worth using.
models.body:
The first time you follow a method, the results are fantastic, and it's easy to feel you've found the secret. But that day you may just have been in great form, the task may have been easy, or someone may have helped. Replication reminds us not to look only at one impressive result, but to see whether it shows up again under similar conditions.

In research, replication usually means testing an existing finding with newly collected data, while getting the same result again from the original data and analysis methods mainly tests the reproducibility of the analysis.

In research, having others retest with new data and recalculating from the original data both matter, but they aren't the same thing. For everyday life, it's enough to remember something simpler: keep a record of the process so a second attempt doesn't rely on just "going by feel again." Look at the rounds that failed too, because they may show you where the limits are.
models.example:
You post a short video and it gets ten times your usual views, so you decide, "From now on, I'll always post at 9 p.m." You stick with it, but the results drop back to normal. Looking back, you realize the first video happened to cover a topic everyone was talking about at the time.

If you'd kept notes on the topic, the content, and the posting time, it would be easier to untangle the causes. Posting at 9 p.m. might help, or it might have been an unimportant part of that one success. Only by trying several more rounds will you gradually find an approach that's truly reliable and suits you.
models.extra: You bake a batch of delicious cookies but forget the oven temperature and baking time. Rather than just photographing the result, keeping a record that lets you make them again is what turns a lucky success into a skill you gradually master.
steps: Briefly note what you did when it worked, who it was for, and under what conditions.
Try it again at another time or with a different group if you can, rather than always repeating it with the same small circle.
Look at successes and failures together, and find which conditions, when changed, make a clear difference to the result.
models.caution: One failed repeat doesn't necessarily prove the earlier result was fake; the conditions, sample, or execution may have differed. Many successes don't guarantee it works everywhere either. The goal is to figure out the pattern and its limits, not to get a guarantee that holds forever.
models.exercise: Pick a result you were really happy with and write down five key steps someone else could follow to try it. Where can you still only say "I went by feel"?
models.brief: Side-by-side panels of independent repeat experiments: three different stick figures at three different tables run the same setup of small balls rolling down a ramp, each table with a fresh set of balls. The results at the end are plotted as similar clusters of dots that overlap in a shared area, with a few small differences left visible.

models.title: Third-Variable Problem
models.lead: When two things rise and fall together, look for something behind them that's pushing both.
models.when: When you're reading claims about what a product does, hearing someone share how they succeeded at studying, or trying to pull the reason for success out of a set of numbers, first check whether some common factor could be influencing both sides.
models.body:
In summer, people buy more cold drinks and also run their air conditioners more. You'd never conclude that drinking cold drinks makes people switch on the AC. There's a quieter player that's easy to overlook: hot weather. It drives both things at once, which makes them look closely connected.

The third-variable problem refers to the fact that an observed association between two variables may come partly or entirely from the shared influence of another factor. In causal analysis, such common causes can create confounding, making it hard to judge the effect of one variable on another from the surface association alone.

As a thinking tool, it means pausing every time you hear "I used it, so things got better" and asking: is there something else that affected both whether people used it and whether the result was good? That question helps you avoid giving credit to the wrong thing, and avoid spending money and energy on things that may not actually work.

Spotting a possible common factor only gives you one more explanation. It doesn't mean the case is closed. Next you need to look at the data, ask about the conditions, or set up a better comparison. Several factors may also be at work at once, so there isn't necessarily just one hidden answer.

The clearest picture is a fork: hot weather separately affects cold drink sales and air conditioner use. The two outcomes may move together simply because they share a cause. Drawing a causal arrow between the two outcomes takes additional evidence.
models.example:
Suppose a shop notices that customers carrying umbrellas buy hot drinks more often than customers without them. The owner plans to hand out umbrellas to passersby, hoping to sell more hot drinks. But think first: could it be that rainy days are cooler, which makes people both carry umbrellas and want something hot?

If the weather is what's really at work, handing out umbrellas probably won't repeat the effect. The owner could first split the records by sunny days, rainy days, and temperature, compare under similar conditions, and only then judge whether the umbrella itself makes any difference. The example is a reminder that the most eye-catching thing in front of you isn't necessarily what's driving the result.
models.extra: Say you notice that classmates who often go to the library also tend to get better grades. The library may really help. But it may also be that more motivated students are both more willing to go to the library and more willing to review carefully. To judge the effect of the environment itself, you'd want to compare people with similar motivation and similar starting levels, not just look at who goes to the library and who doesn't.
steps: Write the relationship you've noticed as one sentence: "When there's more A, there tends to be more B."
List conditions that could affect both A and B at the same time, such as weather, experience, timing, or existing habits.
Look for comparisons under similar conditions, or a suitable experiment, to see whether the original relationship still holds.
models.caution: Don't decide that a factor is the cause just because you thought of it. A third variable may also explain only part of the connection. And don't go to the other extreme of calling every correlation fake: some relationships really do include a direct effect, and telling them apart just takes stronger evidence.
models.exercise: Find a line you've heard recently along the lines of "Do A and you'll get B." Write down one condition that could affect both A and B, then write: what would I need to know to judge whether this explanation holds up?
models.brief: An inverted-Y diagram of a common cause: a hot sun at the top sends clear arrows down to a cold-drink sales icon on the lower left and an air conditioner fan icon on the lower right; under each, more stick figures are using the item.
