models.title: Normal Distribution
models.lead: For some things, most cases bunch up in the middle, and very high or very low ones are rare.
models.when: When you're looking at average scores, measurement errors, or how much something varies, it helps you see roughly where a single number falls.
models.body:
If you chart the heights of a large group of adults by how many people have each height, then within a suitable population you'll often see something shaped like a bell: common in the middle, rarer and rarer toward both sides. That's the shape the normal distribution describes. "Normal" doesn't mean anyone is normal or abnormal. It's just a statistical name.

The normal distribution is a continuous, symmetric probability distribution determined by its mean and standard deviation. Its density curve is bell-shaped, with the mean at the center.

To understand it, start with two questions: roughly what number do values hover around, and how widely are they spread out? The first is usually described with the average. The second can be measured with a ruler called the "standard deviation." The more spread out the values, the larger the standard deviation tends to be. Understanding the shape of the chart is more useful than rushing to memorize formulas.

In a bell curve, the high middle means values cluster around that area, and the low ends mean values in those ranges are less common. To compare how often things happen, look at the area under a stretch of the curve. Don't read the height of the curve at one point as the probability of that exact value.
models.example:
Suppose a batch of measurement errors roughly follows a normal distribution centered at 0 with a standard deviation of 1. Then about 68% of the errors will fall between -1 and +1, and about 95% between -2 and +2. These proportions depend on the assumption that the data really is close to normal. You can't apply them to just any set of numbers.

Now switch to household income. A few very high figures can pull the average way up, and the shape is no longer symmetric. If you still read it like a bell curve, you can easily misjudge where an "ordinary" person actually stands.
models.extra: You hear that a class averaged 80 on a test, but you still don't know whether everyone scored close to 80. Most might be between 75 and 85, or half might have scored 60 and half 100. The average alone doesn't show you the distribution.
steps: First draw the numbers as a simple grouped bar chart and see whether it's high in the middle, low on both sides, and roughly symmetric.
If it looks like a fit, use the average to describe the center and the standard deviation to describe the spread.
When the data is heavily skewed, has several peaks, or has a few extremely large values, don't force a bell curve onto it.
models.caution: Not all test scores, incomes, and view counts follow a normal distribution. And people who land in the rare zones aren't a problem. A distribution describes what a group looks like, not how much any individual is worth.
models.exercise: Take a set of numbers you know well, such as your commute time each day for a week. First check for any unusually high values, then ask yourself: if I reported only the average, would I be leaving out something important?
models.brief: A bell-shaped distribution: many small bars of even width line the bottom, tallest in the middle and short at both ends, with a smooth symmetric bell curve over them; many stick figures stand in the middle and fewer at the sides, with a thin vertical line at the center and no labels of better or worse on either side.

bodyDiagram.caption: Values are more concentrated near the middle and less common near the ends. This is one shape a distribution can take.

models.title: Regression to the Mean
models.lead: An unusually good or bad result may simply be followed by a return to your usual level.
models.when: When you're making sense of a sudden high score, a runaway hit, or a slump, or judging a fix you tried right after a low point, it's well worth remembering.
models.body:
When you suddenly ace a test, it may be partly skill and partly the luck of having reviewed exactly the right material. When you suddenly bomb one, you may also have slept badly. Next time your ability hasn't changed much, but luck may not lean the same way again, so the result is likely to be less extreme. This is called regression to the mean.

When two measurements are imperfectly correlated, among other conditions, subjects selected because their first result was extreme tend, on average, to be less extreme on a later measurement. This is called regression to the mean.

It doesn't mean "once your good luck runs out, bad luck is coming," and it isn't some invisible force dragging scores toward the middle. The key is that the performance that caught our attention usually included a dose of chance that isn't easy to repeat. When that chance factor doesn't show up again, the result naturally looks more like usual.

If you connect two results for the same group with lines, you'll often see that those who scored especially high or low the first time are less extreme later. This is an overall tendency. It doesn't mean every single person returns to the average, and it certainly doesn't mean the average is pulling people back from behind the scenes.
models.example:
Your child usually scores around 80 in math, but one time gets only 60. You give them a stern talking-to, they score 78 on the next test, and you conclude, "See, scolding works." But even without the scolding, your child might have bounced back from getting more sleep or being more familiar with the questions.

To know whether the criticism helped, you can't just look at this one jump. You also need to watch how they study, how they feel, and how things change over a longer stretch. Otherwise it's easy to credit a natural rebound to harsh treatment, and then lean on it harder and harder.
models.extra: One day a shop unexpectedly gets a big group order, and its sales multiply several times over. When sales return to normal the next day, it doesn't mean the business has suddenly gotten worse. The day before may just have had one extra factor. Looking at a longer period keeps you from being pushed around by a single day's numbers.
steps: When you see an extremely good or bad result, first check roughly what level the previous few results were at.
Identify chance factors that may have been at play that day, such as your condition, the difficulty, or a one-off event.
When judging whether a method works, don't start at the lowest point and declare success as soon as things bounce back.
models.caution: When ability truly improves or circumstances truly get worse, the usual level changes too. Regression to the mean doesn't guarantee that "bad will automatically get better," and it certainly can't be used to dismiss the value of sustained effort.
models.exercise: Think back to one especially good or especially bad performance. Write down the stable reasons and the chance factors of that day separately. How will you judge yourself more fairly next time?
models.brief: Paired scatter points moving toward the middle after extremes: the left column shows first-round ball-throwing records that are very high or very low, the right column shows later records mostly closer to a gray band in the middle, with thin lines connecting each subject; not everything is pulled to the mean, and a few points remain extreme.

bodyDiagram.caption: Linking two results for the same group shows the second may be less extreme than the first.

models.title: A/B Testing
models.lead: When you can't decide between two options, set up a small comparison that's as fair as you can make it.
models.when: When two headlines, page layouts, or event plans both make sense and you can try them out cheaply, it's a good way to gather evidence.
models.body:
You've made two posters, one with a straightforward headline and one with a teaser. Your friends each have their own favorite, and after a long debate there's still no answer. At this point you can show each version to a different group of people and see which poster does more for your goal, such as getting people to actually sign up.

A/B testing is an experimental method for comparing the effects of two versions: participants are usually randomly assigned to group A or group B, each group is exposed to its version, and the difference is evaluated using a metric decided in advance. As a thinking tool, it emphasizes testing options with comparable observations rather than picking an answer on gut feeling alone.

Its value is in turning "I think this is better" into "under these conditions, here's what we observed." To see the difference clearly, it's best when starting out to change only one key thing. If you're comparing headlines, keep the image, price, and sign-up process the same. Otherwise, even if one version wins, you'll have a hard time knowing which change made the difference.

A formal A/B test usually runs both versions at the same time and randomly decides who sees which, to reduce the effect of the two groups being different to begin with. The results also need to be judged in light of how many people took part, how big the gap is, and how long the test ran. If A gets two more clicks today, you can't immediately conclude it's better forever.

The comparison splits into two paths, but before the split there needs to be an assignment step that's as fair as possible. At the end, both paths are compared on the same metric chosen in advance, and you have to keep track of the denominator: 15 sign-ups only means something alongside the total number of people who saw the poster.
models.example:
Say you're making a sign-up poster for a reading group. Version A's headline is "Let's read together on Saturday" and version B's is "Understand a new idea in two hours." Everything else is the same. You decide ahead of time to use the sign-up completion rate as the main metric, and you have potential participants during the same period randomly see one of the two versions.

When you look at the results, record both how many people signed up and how many saw each poster. If A got 10 sign-ups and B got 15, but B was seen by twice as many people, you can't simply say B worked better. When the numbers are too small or the gap is unclear, you can honestly record it as "can't tell yet" and then decide whether to keep testing.
models.extra: You can also borrow this way of comparing to try memorizing vocabulary in the morning versus in the evening. Give both arrangements similar amounts of time and similarly difficult material, and record how well you remember the words the next day over several rounds. But since this is one person alternating between options, it's affected by fatigue, order, and other factors. It can't count as a strict randomized two-group A/B test, and you certainly can't use it to conclude that everyone should get up early.
steps: First write down the problem you're solving, the difference between the two versions, and which result you'll use to judge which is better.
Assign versions at the same time and at random as far as possible, keep everything else the same, and settle the number of participants or test length in advance.
Compare rates rather than just totals, and check whether the sample is large enough and whether there are extra costs. If the evidence isn't enough, hold off on a conclusion.
models.caution: Don't stop early the moment you see a result you like, and don't keep switching metrics until one version wins. More clicks don't necessarily mean more sign-ups or a better experience. A test only tells you how things went for a particular group under particular conditions. In a different setting, you may need to check again.
models.exercise: Pick an idea you can try on a small scale. Write down version A, version B, the one thing you want to change, and one metric chosen in advance for judging. Then add a sentence: "If this happens, I'll admit I can't see a difference yet."
models.brief: Randomly assigning two versions and comparing rates: on the left, a crowd of identical stick figures is split by a blank lottery box into two paths of similar size; each path sees a different, wordless poster layout, followed by the same number of viewer icons with a few raising hands to show they signed up; at the end, two unscaled bars compare the completion rates by length.

models.title: The Placebo Effect
models.lead: The hope that "this will help me" can sometimes shape how you feel.
models.when: When you're judging a product experience, the comfort of a ritual, or a review that says "it worked the moment I tried it," it helps you think one step further.
models.body:
If you're told beforehand that "lots of people find this really relaxing," you may be quicker to notice feeling relaxed during the same experience. The placebo effect reminds us that experience depends not only on the thing itself but also on expectations, past experience, and how we're treated. The concept comes up mostly in medical research, but here we'll use it to understand where a sense of "feeling better" comes from.

The placebo effect refers to changes in outcomes caused by factors such as expectation, learning, and the treatment context. It is not the same as all of the improvement observed in a placebo group.

It's also important to keep things separate: feeling better after some intervention doesn't mean all of the improvement came from expectation. People often recover simply with time, and a really bad stretch may drift back to normal. To know how much each factor contributed, you need a proper comparison. Don't just attribute any improvement you see to whatever comes to mind.
models.example:
Imagine two groups using software that runs at exactly the same speed. One group sees a message saying "High-speed mode is on" and the other doesn't. If the first group feels it's faster, that may have to do with expectation, but you can't conclude that the actual loading time got shorter. You need to look at the real timings too in order to separate the experience from the speed.

For everyday users, a clear message really can make waiting feel less stressful. But if the product hasn't gotten any faster and a fake message misleads people for a long time, it will damage trust. Understanding psychological effects is about making sense of experience, not about teaching people to use clever wording in place of real improvement.
models.extra: You buy an expensive new pillow and sleep especially soundly the first night. That may be partly the pillow and partly the relief of "finally sorting this out." Watching how you sleep over the next few nights and paying attention to your routine is usually a safer bet than deciding based on the first night alone.
steps: First separate two things: do I just feel better, or has a measurable result changed too?
Think about whether expectation, attention, reassurance, or a sense of ritual was added at the same time.
For effects that matter, look at a proper comparison, and don't treat one experience as the full answer.
models.caution: Expectation can shape part of an experience, but that doesn't mean "believing in it will cure you." Physical health problems should be dealt with in the appropriate way. And don't mock anyone for it being "all in their head": the feeling itself may be real, it's just that the causes need sorting out.
models.exercise: Recall a time something "felt like it worked right away." Apart from the item itself, did your expectations, surroundings, or the extra care you got also change? List them first. There's no need to rush to dismiss the feeling.
models.brief: The path from expectation to subjective experience: two stick figures in similar situations receive identical-looking, wordless neutral objects; on the left, after a wordless speech bubble with a reassuring smile icon, the figure's subjective tension lines decrease, while on the right the changes are mixed.

models.title: Availability Heuristic
models.lead: The easier something is to remember, the more likely you are to think it happens often.
models.when: When the news is flooded with one story, when similar things keep happening around you, or when one especially intense experience is swaying you, it's well worth using.
models.body:
After scrolling past a few reports of plane crashes, you might suddenly feel that flying is dangerous. When two people you know quit their jobs, you might feel that "everyone is switching jobs these days." These impressions don't necessarily come from complete data. They come from the few examples that are easiest to pull out of your memory. This is called the availability heuristic.

The availability heuristic refers to people judging the frequency, likelihood, or importance of events by how easily relevant examples come to mind.

Our memory favors things that are vivid, frightening, or recent, while the plain, abundant stuff of everyday life barely leaves a trace. So "I can easily think of it" and "it's actually common" need to be kept apart. What your mind gives you is a warning light, not necessarily an accurate table of how often things happen.
models.example:
You've recently watched several videos in a row about layoffs, and you start to believe your job could vanish at any moment, so you keep scrolling through similar content late at night. The more you scroll, the more examples pile up in your head and the more anxious you get, yet you haven't learned anything more about the real situation of your own role.

Try gathering information differently: look at how your company's business is actually doing, the work you're responsible for, and any clear recent announcements, then update your resume and make a backup plan. You don't have to pretend the risk doesn't exist, but let your response rest on a fuller set of facts rather than on images repeating in your feed.
models.extra: On a trip to a new city you happen to run into rude service three times, and you decide the whole city is cold and unfriendly. Those three experiences were real, but whether they're enough to represent millions of people deserves a bit of room for doubt.
steps: Ask: do I think it's common because I've seen it a few times, or because I know how many times it happens overall?
Look for the fuller picture, including the ordinary part where nothing went wrong and nothing made the news.
Turn your attention to concrete preparations you can make, and cut back on repeated scrolling that only deepens the impression.
models.caution: A vivid example may genuinely reveal an important problem, and you shouldn't ignore it just because it's only one story. What needs adding is the proportion, background, and scope, not erasing the voices of the people who lived through it.
models.exercise: Write down something that has felt "everywhere" to you lately. How many times have you seen it with your own eyes? How many independent sources is the information from? Have you been seeing the same story over and over?
models.brief: Easy to recall isn't the same as common: inside a stick figure's wordless thought bubble, an exaggerated, vivid plane-incident icon takes up most of the space, while on the ground the actual counts are a large crowd of ordinary everyday vehicles and only a few small plane icons; the arrow from the big memory bubble to a judgment scale is too thick, with a small brick-red warning mark, and a magnifying glass beside it rechecks the full numbers.

models.title: Loss Aversion
models.lead: Losing something you already have often bothers you more than gaining the same amount pleases you.
models.when: When "I can't take a loss" makes it hard for you to switch plans, pass up a deal, or change an existing arrangement, start by looking at your mental starting point.
models.body:
Finding $20 makes you happy, but losing $20 can leave you down for a long time. It's the same $20, yet we often feel losing it more strongly than gaining it. This is loss aversion. There's no fixed ratio that applies to everyone. For now, just notice the imbalance.

In prospect theory, loss aversion refers to the tendency, when people evaluate outcomes relative to a reference point, for losses to carry a stronger psychological impact than gains of the same size.

We also set a mental starting point: what we currently have, the original price, or what we expected to get. Whether a result looks like a gain or a loss depends heavily on that starting point. Sellers, negotiators, and we ourselves can all make the same situation look completely different just by phrasing it another way.

First fix the same starting point in your mind, then compare how "gaining a little" and "losing the same amount" feel. Loss aversion is about reactions possibly being lopsided. It doesn't mean the actual size of a loss is always bigger, or that everyone reacts the same way in every situation.
models.example:
Two jobs both end up paying $5,000 a month. One offers $5,000 from the start. The other first says $5,500, then explains that conditions have changed and lowers it to $5,000. Even if everything else is the same, you may feel more unhappy about the second one, because your mind had already settled on "$5,500 is mine."

That disappointment is understandable, but when you make the decision, come back to the facts: the final pay, the work itself, the stability, and whether the promises are reliable. Feeling that you're "$500 short" and whether this job is ultimately a good fit are related but separate questions.
models.extra: A salesperson says, "If you don't buy today, you'll lose a $30 discount," and you may feel more pressure than if you'd heard, "You can save $30 today." But if you didn't need the item in the first place, not buying may be exactly how you protect your budget.
steps: Find your mental starting point: what am I treating as already mine?
Translate each way of putting it back into actual outcomes, and see what you'd end up getting and giving up in each case.
Give the disappointment a little time, then compare your future options, and don't let "fear of losing" make the call on its own.
models.caution: Loss aversion isn't the same as every reluctance to let go, and it doesn't mean the more you've invested, the more you should keep going. That second idea usually involves sunk costs. Necessary caution can be perfectly reasonable, so don't label it all a mental bias.
models.exercise: Rewrite "if I don't do it now, I'll lose out" as an actual bill: if I do it, how much will I spend; if I don't, what will I really lose? Mark the imagined losses separately.
models.brief: Lopsided feelings about equal gains and losses: the same number of identically sized blank coins on both sides; on the left, coins go into a stick figure's pocket with small lines of joy above the head; on the right, the same number leave, with much larger tangled lines of disappointment above the head.

bodyDiagram.caption: With the same starting point and the same amount, losing and gaining can still feel lopsided.

models.title: Negativity Bias
models.lead: One harsh comment can stick in your head longer than ten kind ones.
models.when: When you can't shake off criticism for a long time, remember only the parts of the day that went wrong, or write off your whole effort because of one bad review, it's a good tool to reach for.
models.body:
You post an article. Ten people say it helped, and one says it's terrible. What you keep replaying before bed is usually that one "terrible." This tendency to be more sensitive to negative information, and to remember it more, is called negativity bias. It helps us notice threats, but it can also push our overall judgment too far.

Negativity bias refers to the tendency of negative events or information to have a greater effect on attention, memory, and evaluation than comparable positive information.

The problem isn't that you're "too sensitive," and the fix isn't forcing yourself to be positive. It's that the way your mind divides its attention may not match the real proportions. Bad news should of course be dealt with, but dealing with one problem and judging the whole thing a failure can be kept separate.
models.example:
In a work presentation, you hit most of your goals and missed only one formatting detail. After your manager points out the mistake, all that's left in your head is "I did a terrible job," and you're still replaying that one minute at home.

You can start by writing down the full facts: what you finished, what you missed, how big the consequences are, and how to avoid it next time. The formatting error needs fixing, but there's no need to erase everything you carefully completed. That makes your review fairer and makes it easier to improve, instead of growing more afraid of handing anything in the more you think about it.
models.extra: After a trip, you might remember only the long wait in line at the very end, which can make you forget that the first two days were a lot of fun. Writing a few lines about the whole trip alongside your photos can sometimes help your memory regain a sense of proportion.
steps: Write down the positive, negative, and ordinary outcomes, and fill in the whole picture first.
Ask how much the problem actually matters, not just how bad it makes you feel.
Give it one concrete action to deal with it, and once that's done, let your attention move on.
models.caution: Not every negative comment should be met with "just let it go." Serious risks, harm, and well-founded complaints need to be taken seriously. What you're adjusting is your overall judgment, not suppressing real problems.
models.exercise: Tonight, write three lines: one thing that went well today, one that didn't, and one adjustment you can make tomorrow. Don't dress it up. Just get the full information down.
models.brief: A few negatives grab attention: a ring of many friendly, wordless thumbs-up cards with one brick-red broken icon; a stick figure's magnifying glass is aimed only at that one negative card, its shadow enlarging it, while all the other positive information remains fully visible.

models.title: The Magic Ratio
models.lead: Good relationships are built from small, everyday responses, not just from making up after a fight.
models.when: When you notice that two people are only handing out tasks and pointing out problems, and rarely express understanding or thanks, treat it as a reminder.
models.body:
The "magic ratio" comes from research on how couples interact and is often summed up as about 5:1 positive to negative interactions during conflict. You don't need to run your relationship with a calculator. The more practical takeaway for everyday life is this: for a relationship to hold up through disagreements, there has to be understanding, care, and repair, both day to day and in the middle of conflict.

Gottman's research on couples linked a ratio of about 5:1 positive to negative interactions during conflict with certain patterns of relationship stability. This ratio is a finding from a specific research context, not a universal law of relationships.

Positive interactions don't have to be compliments, either. Listening all the way through, acknowledging that the other person has a point, saying thank you, and voicing disagreement gently can all help someone feel you're still facing the problem together. What matters is real connection, not reciting lines to hit a quota.
models.example:
Two people are discussing who does the housework. One says, "I'm the one who's been cleaning up lately. You never lift a finger." If the other immediately drags up old grievances, it quickly turns into a fight about who wins. Try a different response: "You really have done more this week. How about we split the two most annoying evening chores?"

This doesn't make the housework problem disappear, but it lets the other person first feel that their effort has been seen. Only then can you talk about who does what. If nothing changes after you've agreed, no amount of nice words will hold things up. Positive responses in a relationship need to be tied to real change.
models.extra: A friend listens carefully to your worries every time you meet, but you never ask how they're doing. The relationship may not run into trouble right away, but if it's one-sided for a long time, the connection will wear thin. One sincere follow-up question may be where responding to them starts again.
steps: Notice specific things people do for you in everyday life, and say thanks when it occurs to you, not only when there's a conflict.
When you disagree, first accurately reflect back part of what the other person means, then explain your own difficulty.
Follow through on the changes you agree to, and repair mistakes early once you notice them, instead of letting them build up into a big blowup.
models.caution: 5:1 isn't a precise rule that applies to every relationship, and it doesn't mean "five compliments earn you one hurtful remark." Insults, control, and repeatedly crossing boundaries can't be traded away with kind words.
models.exercise: Today, pick one person and thank them for one specific small thing they did recently. Don't just say "thanks." Try to explain how it helped you.
models.brief: A sketch of the warmth in a relationship: a small bridge between two stick figures, with several friendly interaction lines above it carrying simple handshake, ear, and heart icons, and one small lightning bolt of friction below; friendly actions help keep the connection during conflict.

sources.title: The Magic Relationship Ratio · The Gottman Institute

models.title: The Curse of Knowledge
models.lead: The better you know something, the easier it is to forget that others don't know the very first step.
models.when: When you're teaching family members to use a device, training a newcomer, writing instructions, or explaining your professional work, you especially need this reminder.
models.body:
Once you can ride a bike, it's hard to imagine why "keeping your balance" is so hard for a beginner. After years of using some software, you may think "just click that button." This difficulty in getting back to the state of not knowing is the curse of knowledge. It often turns a well-meant explanation into a string of shortcuts the other person can't follow.

The curse of knowledge is a cognitive bias in which people who have some piece of knowledge find it hard to fully set aside what they already know, and so struggle to accurately understand the perspective of those who don't.
models.example:
You're teaching your parents to book a doctor's appointment online, and you say, "Just pick the department, enter your details, and pay." But they're stuck on step one: which app, where to get in, why a verification code is needed, and whether they'll have to start over if they close it. To you these are small details, but they're exactly what the other person needs.

Try teaching differently: go through the whole thing with them once, explaining at each step what they'll see and why to tap there, then let them try on their own. When they get stuck, it isn't "how do you still not get it," it's that your explanation needs one more step added. Learning to watch where people get stuck helps more than repeating the same sentence.
models.extra: Someone asks you how to get into running, and you say, "Just control your pace," but they don't even know how to check their pace. Starting with alternating walking and running, picking a suitable route, and how to tell when you're overdoing it is usually far more helpful.
steps: First ask what the other person can already do and what exactly they need to get done this time, rather than starting from the middle of what you know.
Use fewer unexplained abbreviations, and walk through the whole process with one real example.
Have the other person do it once themselves to see which step of your explanation needs more, instead of just asking "Got it?"
models.caution: Keeping things simple isn't looking down on someone. Experienced people may simply be new to this particular field. On the other hand, you don't need to pour every detail on them at once. Cover the task at hand first, then offer more in-depth material.
models.exercise: Pick a line you often say to beginners, like "It's easy, you just..." Circle the words in it that you haven't explained, and try rewriting it as three steps the other person could follow directly.
models.brief: The information gap between expert and beginner: the stick figure on the left has a complete jigsaw puzzle in its head, the one on the right has only one piece; a big arrow trying to leap straight across is blocked by a broken bridge, while below, puzzle pieces placed one by one form a small stepped bridge so the beginner can follow.

models.title: The Minto Pyramid Principle
models.lead: Tell people what you want to say first, then lay out your reasons layer by layer.
models.when: When you're writing an email, making a suggestion, or giving a progress update, or you notice you've said a lot and the other person still can't find the point, use it to reorganize.
models.body:
Ever sat through an update like this? First they tell you who they contacted yesterday, then what came up today, and five minutes later you still don't know what they actually want from you. The Pyramid Principle helps you arrange scattered information into layers, so your listener doesn't have to dig through a pile of details to guess the point.

The Pyramid Principle, developed by Barbara Minto, is a method for organizing thinking and communication: around a single central idea, related points are grouped, summarized, and arranged in levels, so that each higher-level point governs and summarizes the ones beneath it. It emphasizes the supporting relationships between ideas, not just listing information.

At the top goes one central message, such as "I suggest we move the get-together indoors." The next level holds the reasons that support it, like the weather, the venue, and getting there. Only below that come the specific details. However much detail the other person wants, they can follow the relevant reason down and ask.

When you're putting it together, you can work the other way around: lay out your material, group similar pieces, then see what conclusion they actually support. "Lead with the conclusion" is about the order you present things in. It doesn't mean deciding on the answer first and then picking the material that suits you. If the reasons don't hold up, change the conclusion.

You can check the levels from both directions. Looking down: is the central idea backed by reasons and facts? Looking up: can each group of material be summed up as one clear point? Arranging a few points into a triangle isn't enough. The lower levels have to genuinely hold up the ones above.
models.example:
You're planning a weekend picnic with friends. You've checked the weather, asked about the venue, and looked up how to get there. If you replay your whole research process from the start, your friends may finish listening and still ask, "So where are we going?"

Try this instead: "I suggest we switch to eating indoors. First, rain is forecast, so an outdoor plan is shaky. Second, the original spot has no shelter. Third, a restaurant nearby still has tables. If everyone's okay with it, I'll book tonight." Suggestion first, then reasons, then the action needed. Your friends can focus on whether they agree, instead of piecing together what you mean.
models.extra: When you send a coworker a progress update, you might start with "The main work is done, but I need one more day to check the data, so I suggest we submit on Wednesday," then cover what's finished, why it's delayed, and what comes next, each separately. Keeping similar information together makes it easier for them to find what they need to confirm. Not every message has to become a long report.
steps: Ask what the other person needs to know, then write the main thing you want to say as one complete sentence.
Group related material by reason, step, or another clear relationship, and try to have each level answer the same question.
Check that each reason supports the conclusion and is backed by facts. When you speak, start with the central idea and expand as needed.
models.caution: A tidy structure doesn't make the conclusion right, and three reasons isn't a fixed rule. Don't repeat points just to fill the format, and never cut key evidence against you. When you're chatting, comforting someone, or telling a story, it's fine to listen first or set the scene before deciding when to get to the conclusion.
models.exercise: Find a long message you sent recently and write, in one sentence, the thing the reader most needed to know. Then group the rest, delete anything that doesn't explain or support that point, and see if it's easier to follow.
models.brief: Similar pieces of material at the bottom are grouped and summarized, and those summaries support the central idea at the top.

sources.title: Barbara Minto · The Minto Pyramid Principle

bodyDiagram.caption: Facts at the bottom support grouped summaries, and those summaries support the central idea at the top.

models.title: Six Principles of Influence
models.lead: The ways other people sway your decisions often follow a few familiar paths.
models.when: When you're shopping, taking a recommendation, agreeing to a request, or pitching an idea to someone, use it to see where the influence is coming from.
models.body:
Wanting to repay someone who helped you for free is reciprocity. Wanting to stick with something once you've said yes is commitment and consistency. Feeling reassured because everyone else picked it is social proof. Add authority, liking, and scarcity, and you have the six principles of influence used here. They describe what tends to sway people. They aren't six magic phrases that work the moment you say them.

Cialdini's early framework of influence identifies six principles, reciprocity, commitment and consistency, social proof, authority, liking, and scarcity, to explain why people are more likely to accept certain requests or choices.

These influences sometimes help people decide, for example when genuine reviews fill in what you don't know. They can also be exploited, as with fake sales numbers or a countdown timer that keeps resetting. Learning them can make your own communication more sincere and clear, and help you check what's really pulling at you when you feel rushed.

The six are best understood side by side. They're different cues of influence, not a fixed sequence where you do reciprocity first and social proof next. One situation can involve several of them at once, or just one that stands out.
models.example:
You're casually browsing a shopping page. First you see "Everyone's buying this," then a recommendation from an influencer you like, and then a pop-up: "Only 2 left." With several influences stacked together, you suddenly feel that if you don't buy now, you'll miss out.

Try closing the page for a moment and asking, "If nobody had recommended it and there were no countdown, would I still need it?" If the answer is still yes, then check the price, quality, and return policy. You don't have to resist every influence. You're just taking back a bit of control over the decision.
models.extra: A friend once did you a favor for free, and later asks for something clearly beyond what you can manage. You can express your thanks without forcing yourself to say yes because you "owe them." Returning kindness and protecting your boundaries don't conflict.
steps: Identify what's moving you: a favor, a commitment, other people's choices, authority, liking, or scarcity?
Check whether the information is real, for example who wrote the reviews and whether there's an actual reason for the limited spots.
If you're the one influencing others, give genuine reasons and clear terms, and leave them room to say no.
models.caution: Different versions of the framework have added more principles. This one sticks to the original six. And don't assume every ordinary kindness is a sales tactic: what matters is whether it's genuine, transparent, and respects the other person's choice.
models.exercise: Think back to your last impulse purchase and circle the one influence that pushed you most. If you took it away, would you still have bought the same thing?
models.brief: A six-segment wheel of influence factors: a stick figure in the center weighs options, and around it are six separate icons: exchanging gifts, footprints continuing in the same direction, a crowd following along, a medal on a podium, a friendly handshake, and a shelf with just one item left.

sources.title: Robert Cialdini · Influence and the Six Principles

bodyDiagram.caption: Six cues of influence sit side by side, and a real situation may involve several at once.

models.title: Fear of Missing Out / FOMO
models.lead: When everyone else seems to be moving ahead, it's easy to treat even the wrong opportunities as must-haves.
models.when: When scrolling your feed leaves you restless, or you keep saving and signing up for more things than you have time to use, it's a good moment to use it.
models.body:
A friend goes traveling, a coworker picks up a new skill, an influencer says yet another tool changed their life, and suddenly you feel behind. This anxious worry about missing out on good experiences or opportunities is FOMO, the fear of missing out. It keeps you adding new plans, without necessarily bringing you closer to your own goals.

The fear of missing out is an uneasy feeling that others are having rewarding experiences from which you are absent or have missed the chance to take part.

What you see in your feed is usually many different people's best little slice. But you may stitch them together into a life where "everyone else has it all," then expect yourself to keep up on every front. Seeing this helps you tell a real need from the urgency stirred up by comparison.
models.example:
You meant to spend two months working on your spoken English. One week in, you see writing, photography, and AI courses all on sale at once. Each one seems like it could shape your future, so you sign up for all of them. Before long you spend every day just keeping up with course group chats, and your English practice has stopped.

You're not short on opportunities. What's real is that you can only spend your time once. Asking "Which course solves my specific problem for these two months?" and putting the others on a look-later list usually gets you more than forcing yourself to start everything at once.
models.extra: Skipping one get-together doesn't mean losing your friends for good, and not learning a tool yet doesn't mean the world has left you behind. Separating one absence from your long-term relationships and abilities often takes some of the pressure off.
steps: Write down the one thing you most want to move forward right now, and how much time you can realistically give it each week.
When a new opportunity appears, ask what problem it solves and whether you really have to join now.
Sleep on non-urgent choices, and let yourself admire other people's choices without signing up too.
models.caution: Some opportunities really do have deadlines and conditions you can't get elsewhere, and it's worth checking them carefully. Easing FOMO doesn't mean refusing anything new, or calling every urge to try something a lack of self-discipline.
models.exercise: Write down the three new things you most want to join right now. Next to each, add "which part of my current life I'd have to take this time from," then see if you still want it.
models.brief: FOMO's outer ring tugging at attention: a stick figure in the center holds a phone, surrounded by small wordless windows with icons for a party, travel, shopping, and a course. Dashed lines pull at its limbs and gaze, while a plan on its own desk sits forgotten. One converging navy line of sight returns to its own plan.

models.title: Confirmation Bias
models.lead: We easily notice only the information that proves "I was right all along."
models.when: When you've already fallen for a plan, strongly dislike someone, or find your search terms all say "why it's great" or "why it's terrible," it's worth using.
models.body:
You've decided a brand is bad, so a negative review feels like proof, while a positive one must be an ad. You've decided someone is reliable, so even when they stand you up, you find a pile of excuses for them. This is confirmation bias: we don't just pick our information, we also judge the same information by different standards, so our original view can keep standing.

Confirmation bias is the tendency to seek out, interpret, favor, or remember information that supports existing beliefs, while holding inconsistent information to a different standard.

It doesn't mean you're deliberately being unreasonable. The brain likes what's familiar and consistent, and changing your mind can feel embarrassing. So the point of practice isn't to force yourself to argue against yourself. It's to leave room in advance for "I might be wrong," and to take counterexamples a little more seriously.

If you picture the filtering process, you can ask one more question: which information did I keep, and which did I set aside? If supporting material passes easily while contrary material has to meet an unusually high bar, the filter itself needs checking.
models.example:
You want to open a coffee shop and you're already excited about it. When you ask friends, you say, "Doesn't this area really need a cozy little cafe?" They nod politely, and you feel even surer it's a big opportunity. But you never asked where they usually buy coffee, how much they spend, or how often they'd come, and you never looked into why the shops that closed didn't make it.

If you ask about real spending habits and research costs and foot traffic instead, the answers may be less exciting, but they'll protect your investment better. The goal of research isn't to collect agreement. It's to help you avoid pitfalls.
models.extra: You think you're "always unlucky," so you vividly remember the slowest checkout line and the rain when you went out, but rarely note the days you caught your bus just in time. Keeping a steady record might show you a fuller, less one-sided picture of your life.
steps: Before researching, write down your current view and where you're most worried you might be wrong.
Actively look for one serious counterexample, or ask someone who knows the situation to point out the problems honestly.
Hold supporting and opposing evidence to the same standard. Don't swallow one side easily while picking the other apart.
models.caution: Grabbing any random objection doesn't make you objective. Counterexamples need to be relevant and reliable too. In the end, you can still stick with your original choice, as long as you've genuinely checked it.
models.exercise: For a view you're very sure about, finish the sentence: "If I saw ..., I'd be willing to change my mind." If you can't think of anything, ask yourself whether you've already shut the door on new information.
models.brief: A selective filtering funnel: a stick figure holding a circle-shaped opinion icon faces two kinds of evidence, circles and triangles. It puts only the circles in its basket and pushes the triangles aside. A thin arrow and a magnifying glass bring the excluded triangles back for review.

bodyDiagram.caption: Preferred information tends to be kept and inconsistent information tends to slip away, so the filtering itself is worth checking.

models.title: The Golden Mean
models.lead: Doing things well is about the right measure: more isn't always better, and it isn't always splitting the difference.
models.when: When you're showing care, giving feedback, managing your workload, or swinging back and forth between two extremes, it's a good fit.
models.body:
Too little care can feel cold, while too much interference can leave someone gasping for air. Courage helps you act, but ignoring danger completely turns into recklessness. The Golden Mean reminds us that many qualities have to be judged in context: for whom, when, and how much is right.

Aristotle's doctrine of the mean understands certain virtues as a fitting state between excess and deficiency, where what is fitting depends on the particular situation and on rational judgment, not on an arithmetic average.

It isn't a math problem where you find the average. If one person says read one page a day and another says a hundred, fifty isn't automatically the right answer. You need to weigh your goals, time, abilities, and consequences to find a measure you can justify, rather than feeling wiser just because you're standing in the middle.

The mean is more like a fitting spot within a range, and that spot moves with the situation. In a light drizzle, a small umbrella is enough. In a downpour, you might need to change your plans. The sensible choice doesn't have to land exactly halfway between the two extremes.
models.example:
A friend has been feeling down lately. At first you're afraid of bothering them, so you barely get in touch. Then you worry you're not caring enough and start asking every day whether they feel any better, which only adds pressure. You could instead ask what they need first, such as keeping them company when they want to talk, or agreeing to check in every few days.

The right kind of care is neither stepping back completely nor constantly chasing for updates. It comes from understanding what this person needs right now and adjusting what you do. Getting the measure right isn't about nailing it the first time. It's about being willing to watch their reaction, listen to feedback, and adjust a little.
models.extra: When you tidy your room, throwing nothing away can let things pile up, while throwing out every keepsake might leave you with regrets. You could keep the few most meaningful items first, give the rest a set amount of space, and adjust gradually to fit how you actually live.
steps: Think about what problems "too little" and "too much" would each cause here.
Based on the specific person and goal, choose an approach you can explain your reasons for.
Watch the response and adjust if needed. Don't refuse to change just to insist you've got it "just right."
models.caution: Some questions can't be settled by compromise. Mixing truth and lies half and half doesn't make anything more true, and harm doesn't become acceptable because it's "moderate." Bottom lines need to be clear. It's only questions of degree where you discuss how much.
models.exercise: Pick something where you feel you either overdo it or don't do enough. Write one example of each, then plan one small adjustment.
models.brief: The fitting spot moves with the situation: two parallel horizontal lines each run from "too little" to "too much." For a sunny day and a rainstorm, a stick figure slides an umbrella-size slider to a different fitting spot, one leaning left and one leaning right, neither at the mechanical midpoint.

bodyDiagram.caption: The fitting spot moves with the situation and doesn't always land in the exact middle.

models.title: The Golden Rule
models.lead: Before you do something that affects someone else, ask: if it were me, would I be okay with it?
models.when: When you're borrowing something, changing plans, assigning tasks, or giving feedback, a quick role swap can save you from a lot of unintended offense.
models.body:
If you want people to ask before borrowing your things, you should ask before touching theirs. If you want to hear about plan changes in advance, don't wait until the other person has arrived to cancel. The Golden Rule is this simple kind of perspective swap: give others the same respect you'd want for yourself.

The Golden Rule is a reciprocal ethical principle that holds you should treat others the way you would want to be treated.

It's especially good at exposing double standards. When you slip up, "there was a reason"; when someone else does, they're "irresponsible." You want to be understood, but never listen to the other person's explanation. Try swapping places, and a lot of quiet unfairness suddenly becomes obvious.
models.example:
You need to move a meetup with a friend at the last minute and think, "It's only half an hour later." But if you were the one already out the door, standing in the rain waiting, it might not feel like just half an hour. So you explain as early as you can, ask whether the new time works for them, and accept whatever extra hassle it causes you.

Swapping places won't mean you never change plans, but it helps you handle changes more considerately. You're not just counting your own time; you're taking the other person's schedule seriously too. A lot of the trust in a relationship is built slowly through small things like this.
models.extra: You might think "I can message anytime, and they don't have to reply." But if the other person knows you care about quick replies, they may feel pressure. A quick look from their side might lead you to add, "No rush, look at it tomorrow when you're free."
steps: Put yourself on the receiving end and think about what specific inconveniences would come up.
Check whether you're going easy on yourself while expecting others to follow the rules strictly.
At minimum, give advance notice, respect a no, and take responsibility for the effects you cause.
models.caution: Your preferences aren't necessarily someone else's. You might like people to be blunt to your face, while someone else would rather talk in private. The Golden Rule is good for checking basic respect, but for specific preferences you still need to ask.
models.exercise: Think of something today that needed someone else's cooperation. If you two swapped roles, what one small thing would you most want them to do? Go do it now.
models.brief: The symmetrical reciprocity of the Golden Rule: two stick figures hand each other an umbrella across mirror-like symmetrical arrows in the center. A heart bubble on the left, wanting to be cared for, is mirrored on the right as giving the same kindness. Both are equals, and neither controls the other.

models.title: The Platinum Rule
models.lead: For kindness to land, you need to know what the other person needs, not just what you'd like.
models.when: When you're giving a gift, comforting someone, giving feedback, planning a get-together, or keep running into misunderstandings about how to work together, it's especially useful.
models.body:
You love a lively crowd, so you throw your friend a surprise party. But they dread being the center of attention and just wanted a quiet dinner. You put real effort in, yet they don't feel comfortable. The Platinum Rule reminds us: rather than giving based on your own tastes, find out how the other person wants to be treated.

The Platinum Rule is a principle for relating to others that builds on the Golden Rule by emphasizing individual differences, holding that you should, as far as possible, treat others the way they want to be treated.

Finding out doesn't require reading minds. You can just ask. Do you want advice, or do you want to talk it through first? Is now a good time for this feedback, or should we find a quiet moment? Simple questions like these often make people feel more respected than "I'm only doing this for your own good."
models.example:
A coworker has just finished a project, and you want to praise them in the team-wide chat. You also mention the family difficulties they've been going through lately, thinking it shows how hard they worked. But they didn't want their personal situation discussed, and the praise just makes them uncomfortable.

Next time, you could ask first: "You did a great job on this, and I'd like everyone to know what you contributed. Would you rather I say it publicly or tell you privately?" It's the same recognition, but because there's a choice, your intention is more likely to land the way you meant it, and you avoid deciding for someone else what's worth making public.
models.extra: Your friend has just gone through a breakup, so you round up a whole table of people to cheer them up, without asking. But all they want is to sleep. You could ask first: "Do you want company, want to talk, or would you rather be left alone today?" You still care; you've just let them set the pace.
steps: When you're unsure of someone's preference, offer two or three simple options so it's easy to answer.
Trust the needs people state clearly, and don't keep overriding them with "what you really mean is..."
People and circumstances change, so check in again on important arrangements after a while.
models.caution: Respecting preferences doesn't mean agreeing to every request. You can have your own boundaries around time, privacy, and money too. A good relationship is one where both people can express their needs and say no.
models.exercise: Pick someone you spend a lot of time with and ask one question you've always answered by guessing, such as "Do you prefer a spontaneous phone call, or a message first to set a time?" Listen and write down the answer.
models.brief: Helping according to the other person's preference: a stick figure is holding a coffee, first listens to the other person's wordless thought bubble, which contains a teacup, and then hands them a teacup instead.

sources.title: Tony Alessandra · The Platinum Rule Workbook

models.title: Categorical Imperative
models.lead: Don't just ask "Is this good for me?" Also ask "If everyone did this, would I still stand by the rule?"
models.when: When you're about to make an exception for yourself, hide something, or make a promise you don't intend to keep, use it to check yourself.
models.body:
"Categorical imperative" sounds like a stern slogan, but you can start with an everyday question: would you allow other people in similar situations to do what you're allowing yourself? If you keep wanting to be the exception while expecting others to follow the rules, it's worth stopping to think.

One formulation of Kant's categorical imperative is: act only according to a maxim that you could at the same time will to become a universal law, where a maxim is the subjective principle on which a person acts.

The idea comes from Kant's philosophy, and there's a deeper discussion behind it than just "what if everyone did this." As a beginner, hold on to two points: don't tailor rules just for yourself, and remember that other people have their own choices and goals. They aren't tools for you to use.
models.example:
You want a friend to lend you money. You know full well you won't pay it back by the weekend, but you promise "I'll definitely pay you back Saturday" anyway, planning to figure it out later. If this became the rule, "whenever you need help, you can make promises you don't plan to keep," nobody could trust a promise anymore.

Another way is to be upfront: "I'm not sure when I can pay you back. If you need a definite date, it's better not to lend to me this time." You might not get the loan, but you've let them decide based on the real situation, instead of being pushed along by words you never meant to keep.
models.extra: If you don't like people sharing your photos without permission, don't post someone else's just because "I think this one looks nice." They're not your content. They have the right to decide how their own information is used.
steps: Spell out the rule behind your action, not just a nice-sounding reason.
Think about whether the rule still makes sense if everyone in a similar situation followed it.
Check whether the other person can make an informed choice, and whether you're hiding something for your own convenience.
models.caution: This isn't about forcing your lifestyle on everyone. Different needs can be respected. But don't sneak yourself a loophole by inventing a long list of special conditions that only apply to you.
models.exercise: Write down one recent exception where you told yourself "just this once." If someone did the same thing to you for the same reason, would you still find it reasonable?
models.brief: A loop testing whether a rule can be universal: a stick figure tries to cut in front of a waiting line. An arrow from this individual act expands below into everyone cutting in line until the queue knots up, marked with a small brick-red block. Beside it is an orderly line where everyone follows the rule. The focus is whether the principle can apply consistently to everyone, with no legal punishment shown.

models.title: Veil of Ignorance
models.lead: When you set the rules, don't know yet whether you'll end up in the best spot or the worst.
models.when: When you're dividing shifts, chores, or shared resources, or discussing rewards, penalties, and usage rules, it helps to cover up the names and think it through first.
models.body:
Imagine everyone is splitting a cake, but before the cutting is decided, you don't know which piece you'll end up with. You'd probably be more willing to cut the pieces about the same size. The veil of ignorance borrows exactly this imagined state of not knowing where you'll stand, to help people discuss fairer rules.

In Rawls's theory of justice, the veil of ignorance requires those choosing the principles of a society to temporarily not know their social position, background, or certain personal characteristics, in order to reduce the influence of particular interests on their choice.

It doesn't ask you to forget real-world difficulties. It asks you not to plan only around the advantages you have right now. Imagine you could be the newcomer, the person caring for kids, or someone with a disability, and some rules that seemed fine may suddenly need extra safeguards.
models.example:
Several roommates are dividing up rooms, rent, and chores. If you've already picked the biggest room, it's easy to think "splitting everything equally is simplest." Try a different question first: if the rooms were assigned at random, would I still want everyone to pay the same?

That can make it easier to talk about adjusting rent for size, light, and amenities, and to set rules for chores, shared spaces, and unexpected changes. Not everyone has to get an identical arrangement, but you can explain more clearly why the differences are fair.
models.extra: When you're scheduling meetings, if you didn't know which time zone you'd be in or whether you'd need to pick up your kids, you might be more willing to limit evening meetings and offer ways to take part asynchronously. The rules can then fit more people's lives.
steps: List the different positions the rule creates: who might find it convenient, and who might lose out.
Imagine you'll land in any position at random, and look again at whether the basic protections are enough.
Spell out in advance how adjustments, appeals, and special cases will be handled, not just how things work normally.
models.caution: Fairness isn't always everyone getting exactly the same. Accessibility arrangements give extra support to some people, for example, so that they can use things too. A thought experiment offers a way to check, but it won't automatically produce an answer everyone agrees on.
models.exercise: Take a rule you think is perfectly reasonable and stand on the side of the person it's least convenient for. What explanation, protection, or adjustment would you want to add?
models.brief: Fair allocation behind the veil of ignorance: on the left, the identity icons of stick figures of different heights with different bags of resources are separated by a semi-transparent veil. In front of the veil, a group of stick figures with no identity markers decide together on a bridge and ramp everyone can use. The actual identities are assigned behind the veil in a shuffled lottery box.

models.title: Reverse Engineering
models.lead: When you come across great work, don't just say "impressive." Try to see how it was made.
models.when: When you want to learn writing, design, a process, or a product but don't know where to start, this method works well.
models.body:
A clearly written report, a moving video, a small shop that runs smoothly: all of them can be taken apart. Reverse engineering means looking backward from something already finished. What parts is it made of, what order do they go in, and what makes it work?

Reverse engineering is the process of analyzing an existing product or system to identify its components, their relationships, and how it works, in order to gain knowledge of its design or implementation.

The benefit is that vague admiration turns into details you can learn from. You don't have to copy everything someone else did. You can break down the structure first, then try it once with your own material. It's often only when you try to rebuild it that you discover what you really understood and what you guessed wrong.

You can trace reverse engineering back along "finished product, parts, connections, operation." The point isn't just how many parts you can pull out, but also how one part affects the next. Only by knowing these relationships do you gradually understand why it works.
models.example:
You love an article that explains something complex without being dull. Instead of just saving it, you go through it paragraph by paragraph to see how it's written: it opens with an everyday question, breaks the concept into three points in the middle, pairs each point with an example, and ends with an action you can take right away.

Then you pick your own topic and write a section following that structure. When you're done, you ask a friend to read it and see if it's clearer. What you've learned is a way of organizing information, not swapping out a few words and passing off someone else's article as your own.
models.extra: With a delicious dish, you can analyze the texture, aroma, and order of preparation, then try making it at home. It's no loss if the first attempt fails, because by comparing the differences, you start to learn which steps really matter.
steps: Pick a finished piece whose goal is close to yours, rather than starting with something that had far more resources behind it.
Break out the main parts, their order, and the role each part plays.
Rebuild a small section with your own material, and test your guesses against the actual result.
models.caution: A finished product won't tell you how many times it failed or how many resources went into it. Looking simple doesn't mean it was cheap to make. Learning also means respecting the original creator's work and its usage limits. Don't use taking something apart as an excuse to copy it.
models.exercise: Pick something you saved recently but never looked at again. Write down its three parts and what each does, then rebuild the smallest part with your own content.
models.brief: Tracing a finished product back to how it works: on the right, a complete small mechanical alarm clock. To its left, a layer-by-layer exploded view reveals gears, a spring, and arrows showing how motion is passed along. A stick figure uses a magnifying glass to follow how the gears connect, then sketches a simple wordless diagram of the mechanism.

bodyDiagram.caption: Looking back from the finished product to its parts, connections, and how it runs.

models.title: The 4 Cores of Credibility
models.lead: Being trustworthy takes more than being a good person, and more than being good at things.
models.when: When you're choosing someone to work with, handing off a task, or getting along well with someone but still hesitating to trust them with something important, use this to pin down what's bothering you.
models.body:
Who would you hand something important to? Usually you want them to be honest and well-meaning, and also able to do the job and actually deliver. The 4 Cores of Credibility split this into integrity, intent, capabilities, and results. The name sounds like a management course, but the questions are simple: Do they tell the truth? Whose interests do they have in mind? Can they do it? Have they done it before?

Stephen M. R. Covey's credibility framework has four cores: integrity, intent, capabilities, and results. The first two are about character, and the last two are about competence.

Once you separate them, you can see where trust is getting stuck. Someone with a great attitude who keeps misjudging how long things take may need better skills and methods. Someone with strong technical skills who often hides problems may need to work on transparency and how they make commitments. Different problems can't all be solved with "you need to make me feel more confident about this."

The four cores are parallel angles to check, not four levels on a promotion ladder. A person can be very sincere and still lack skill, or be highly capable while their intent leaves you uneasy. When judging credibility, look at what the task at hand needs most, and whether each area is backed by real evidence.
models.example:
You ask a friend to take photos at an event. He's enthusiastic and genuinely wants to help, but he's never shot fast-moving scenes indoors. If you hand him the whole job and the photos come out blurry, your friendship could take a hit too.

A better plan is to look at his work beforehand, explain the key needs, let him do a test shoot, and if needed, ask someone experienced to cover the crucial moments. You're not rejecting his goodwill. You're matching the responsibility to his skills. Being honest about limits builds trust on its own.
models.extra: You promise your family you'll sort the bills once a week, and you do it for several weeks in a row. That reassures them more than a single promise like "leave all the finances to me from now on." Trust often comes from small, visible track records, not one big declaration.
steps: Get specific about why you're uneasy: is it fear of something being hidden, doubt about motives, or uncertainty about skill and delivery?
Make commitments smaller and their boundaries clearer, and build confidence with one delivery that can be checked.
Share progress and risks early, instead of explaining why it couldn't be done only after it fails.
models.caution: This isn't a formula for giving someone's character an overall score. Being inexperienced at one thing doesn't make a whole person untrustworthy, and systems, resources, and cooperation also affect results.
models.exercise: Pick one area where you'd like others to trust you more. Write down one small promise you can keep this week in a way the other person can see, then deliver it on time.
models.brief: Four pillars holding up a bridge of trust: a shield with a check mark, a heart facing outward toward others, well-used tools, and a finished puzzle stand for integrity, intent, capabilities, and results. Two stick figures walk toward each other from either end of the bridge; each pillar stands separately, with no text.

bodyDiagram.caption: Integrity, intent, capabilities, and results all shape credibility, and each needs real evidence.

models.title: Minimum Viable Product / MVP
models.lead: Start with a version small enough to try that can still answer a real question.
models.when: When you have an idea for a business, course, community, or tool but don't yet know whether people really need it, this is the best way to start testing it.
models.body:
When you want to do something big, the easiest place to get stuck is "once I'm fully ready." A minimum viable product, usually shortened to MVP, encourages you to put in a small amount first and see whether the people who'd actually need it are willing to use it. The point isn't to make something shoddy. It's to check, as early as possible, the part you're most likely to have guessed wrong.

In the Lean Startup method, a minimum viable product is used to start a process of real feedback and learning with relatively little investment, testing key assumptions, rather than simply delivering a product with fewer features.

Say you want to open a shop: sell a small batch first. Want to build a tool? Start by helping a few people do the same task by hand. What you're testing is the need, how people use it, or whether they'll pay, not showing others that "I've already built lots of features." Decide what you want to learn first, then decide how much to build.

An MVP isn't a straight line that ends once it's built. It's a learning loop: make a version that can test the key idea, let real use bring feedback, then adjust based on it. The most valuable thing the loop teaches you might be that your original idea doesn't hold up.
models.example:
You want to build an app for organizing travel plans, and you're already picturing maps, budgets, carpooling, and sharing. Instead of jumping into months of development, find a few people who are about to travel and help them plan their routes using a spreadsheet and chat. Watch which information they keep asking for and which nobody ever looks at.

If all they need is a shared schedule they can edit together, you've skipped building a pile of features no one would use. If nobody even wants to try the hands-on service, you find out sooner whether you picked the wrong audience, the wrong need, or the wrong pitch. A small version makes mistakes cheap. It doesn't guarantee the idea will succeed.
models.extra: If you want to start a book club, first get four people to read the same short piece and see whether the discussion flows and whether they want to come back. That tells you more than designing a full year of sessions and a fee structure up front.
steps: Write down the one thing you're most worried you've guessed wrong, such as "does anyone really need this every week?"
Design a small version that reaches real users, even if you start with off-the-shelf tools and do the work by hand.
Agree in advance on what you need to see to keep going and what would mean changing course, so you don't push on just because you can't bear to waste what you've put in.
models.caution: A small version still has to keep its basic promise. Don't trade safety, privacy, or honesty with users for speed. A half-finished thing that nobody tries and that can't answer any question doesn't become valuable just because you call it an MVP.
models.exercise: Shrink a big plan you've been putting off into "a version one real person could try this week." Write down what you want to learn from that trial.
models.brief: A short testing loop: a stick figure builds a simple cart from a few wooden pieces that can carry weight. A real user pulls the cart to move a small box, and feedback, shown as an eye icon, flows back to the repair tools. Beside it, the outline of a large, complicated, unfinished cart is shown in pale gray for contrast.

bodyDiagram.caption: Test results may support the next step, or they may point to changing your assumptions. Feedback doesn't only mean success.

models.title: Minimum Effective Dose
models.lead: Find out how much is already enough before you automatically keep adding more.
models.when: When your plans are always too heavy, when you won't start because you can't do the full version, or when you suspect you're putting in more than you need to, this is well worth using.
models.body:
With practice, meetings, or organizing files, adding a little sometimes makes things noticeably better, but adding more after that barely helps. The minimum effective dose asks: for the goal in front of me, what's the least I can do that will still work? This is about effort in work and daily life, not about adjusting medication doses on your own.

In the context of everyday productivity, the minimum effective dose is the smallest amount of input needed to produce the intended effect. It depends on a goal, subject, and measure that are clearly defined in advance.

It's good for lightening a starting plan that's too heavy. Maybe you meant to read for an hour a day and gave up completely once things got busy. Switch to a sustainable ten minutes, and you actually get started. Still, be clear about the goal first: ten minutes may be enough to build a habit, but not enough to prepare for an exam a month away.

When you look at effort and effect together, you'll see that "the point where you just reach the goal" deserves more attention than "the more effort, the better." First decide what result counts as enough, then find the range of effort that reliably gets you there. If the goal or conditions change, look at that range again.
models.example:
Your team holds a half-hour sync meeting every day, but most of it is people taking turns reading out their progress. First make the goal clear, "make blockers visible," then try having people write updates before the meeting and only discussing things that need someone else's help. The meeting shrinks to ten minutes.

After two weeks, check: did any problems slip through? Did collaboration slow down? If nothing important was lost, there's no need to add back twenty minutes just to seem thorough. If something important really was missed, add back what's needed. Cutting back is something you test, not something you slash by gut feeling.
models.extra: A note to a friend doesn't have to be long. One line that shows you remember what they're going through and says something specific and heartfelt can mean more than a page of clichés. The goal is for them to feel remembered, not to hit a word count.
steps: Write the goal as a result you can check, not just "do better."
Start with a small input that's easy to keep up, and give it some time to observe.
If it's not enough, fill the specific gap. If it is enough, stop there for now, and don't treat doing more as automatically being responsible.
models.caution: "The least" isn't the only goal. Long-term training, reliability, and handling surprises may all need some margin, and not every task can be squeezed down endlessly. The right amount matters more than chasing the minimum.
models.exercise: Pick a habit you always feel you "don't have time for" and design a five-to-ten-minute starter version. Write down what it can achieve and what it can't yet.
models.brief: An effect threshold and minimal input: a stick figure gradually adds batteries to a flashlight. A small but sufficient beam just lights the page that needs reading, with a clear line marking the target level of light. Piling on many more batteries only adds to the load without changing the goal of reading that page clearly.

sources.title: Tim Ferriss · Excerpt on the Minimum Effective Dose from The 4-Hour Body

bodyDiagram.caption: First decide what goal counts as enough, then look for the range of effort that reaches it.

models.title: The 5 Ws and 1 H
models.lead: To make something clear, start by answering six basic questions.
models.when: When you're assigning a task, planning a get-together, reviewing what went wrong, or asking someone for help, this comes in especially handy.
models.body:
"Sort out that event this weekend." Would you know what to do after hearing that? Who's in charge, which part to do, when it's due, where it happens, why it's being done, and how: none of it is clear. The 5 Ws and 1 H are these six questions: who, what, when, where, why, and how.

The 5 Ws and 1 H is a framework for organizing information and analyzing problems that fills in the basic elements of a situation through six types of questions: Who, What, When, Where, Why, and How.

There's nothing mysterious about it. Like checking for your keys and phone before you leave the house, it helps you avoid leaving things out. Other people don't have all the background that's in your head, and you yourself may only "feel like" you've thought it through.
