Running through the six questions often shows that what's really missing isn't effort, but one clear sentence of explanation.

The six questions work best as parallel checks on the same situation, with no fixed starting point. Think of them as six windows: if one is empty, it reminds you that you may not have made clear the people, the time, the place, the purpose, or the method.
models.example:
You ask a friend to "help book somewhere for dinner." He picks a reasonably priced restaurant, and then it turns out someone is vegetarian, someone can't arrive until after seven, and the place has no private room. Everyone tried hard. The requirements just weren't clear at the start.

Next time you could say: "Saturday at seven, six people, near the subway station. We want to celebrate Sam's birthday, the budget is about $15 a person, and one of us is vegetarian. Could you find two places with quiet seating so we can decide together by Thursday?" A little more detail saves a whole string of back-and-forth later.
models.extra: "My computer's broken" is hard to help with. Make it "After today's update, my laptop at home turns on but won't connect to Wi-Fi. My phone works fine on the same network, and I've restarted once," and it's much easier for someone to know what to ask next.
steps: Write down the six questions, and fill in the information that actually affects getting the task done first.
Spell out who's responsible, the deadline, and what counts as done, instead of saying "ASAP" or "roughly."
Flag anything you don't know and confirm it first, rather than pretending it's already arranged.
models.caution: It's a checklist, not a rule that every message needs six paragraphs. Sometimes two sentences cover everything. Complex projects also need budget, dependencies, and risks, so the six questions aren't a one-size-fits-all template.
models.exercise: Rewrite a vague request you sent recently. Don't make it longer yet. Just add the two pieces of information the other person was most likely to guess wrong.
models.brief: A six-spoke analysis diagram: in the center, a house-and-box icon for a moving task, with six branches reaching out to a person, boxed items, a clock without numbers, a map location pin, a target for the purpose, and tools with steps.

bodyDiagram.caption: The same situation can be checked from six angles: people, object, time, place, purpose, and method.

models.title: 2×2 Matrix Diagram
models.lead: When things pile up, use two key questions to sort them into four boxes.
models.when: When you're organizing tasks, comparing needs, planning a budget, or a group can't agree on priorities, this is a great fit.
models.body:
When you're facing a dozen to-dos and your head is a mess, pick two important dimensions first, like "how big is the impact?" and "how much effort does it take?" Draw one line across and one line down, and you get four boxes: high impact and low cost, high impact and high cost, low impact and low cost, low impact and high cost. That's a 2x2 matrix.

A 2x2 matrix is an analytical tool that uses two dimensions, each split into two levels, to form four quadrants, so options can be sorted by their characteristics and compared more easily.

Its value is turning "everything's important" into differences you can actually discuss. You don't have to calculate everything to the decimal point. You just need to let yourself and others see why some things go first and others wait. But the two questions have to be the right ones. Otherwise, however neat the drawing, you've only packed the mess into four boxes.

What makes the four quadrants useful is laying out both dimensions at once. First be clear about what the horizontal and vertical axes each compare, then decide where high and low split. If the dimensions are vague, no matter how neatly you draw the boxes, they won't help you judge.
models.example:
You want to make your home more comfortable, and your list includes changing light bulbs, fixing a leak, repainting the walls, buying decorations, and replacing a big cabinet. Sort them by "impact" and "cost," and fixing the leak and replacing the dead bulbs probably come first, while the decorations can wait.

Repainting and replacing the cabinet may have a big impact, but they take money and time, so plan them separately. Once things are sorted, you won't give up just because you can't do every upgrade at once, and the small decorations that are easiest to buy won't soak up all your energy.
models.extra: You can look at a study plan the same way: do the exercises that help your goal a lot and are easy to start first, and set aside materials that take ages but don't help much. Not everything that looks like studying deserves the same effort.
steps: First get clear on what you most want to solve right now, then pick two comparison dimensions that really matter for it.
Set a rough standard for "high" and "low," place each item, and mark the ones you're unsure about.
Handle the few items most worth doing first, then look into any information that could change how things are sorted.
models.caution: You're the one who drew the box edges. If two tasks differ only slightly, don't treat them as worlds apart just because they landed in different boxes. Important conditions like safety and deadlines may also need a separate check.
models.exercise: Draw four boxes on paper and place five of this week's to-dos using "how much does it help?" and "how much time does it take?" Then pick the one most worth finishing first.
models.brief: A clear four-quadrant grid: two perpendicular axes split the picture into four areas. The ends of the axes show icons for a short clock and a long clock, and for a small target and a large target. In each area, task icons of different sizes and positions are being sorted by stick figures, emphasizing that two dimensions are compared at once.

bodyDiagram.caption: Crossing two dimensions gives each type of option its own place.

models.title: Decision Matrix
models.lead: Putting your options in one table is clearer than flip-flopping between them in your head.
models.when: When you're choosing a rental, a device, a course, or a collaboration tool, or whenever each option has its own pros and cons, this works well.
models.body:
When buying a computer, you might be drawn to the price one moment and decide looks matter the next, until the more you look, the more confused you get. A decision matrix means first listing the criteria you care about, then running every option through the same criteria. Some criteria matter more, so you can give them more weight.

A decision matrix compares candidate options against a shared set of criteria, combining the ratings with criterion weights where needed, to make each option's relative strengths and weaknesses clear.

The table doesn't decide for you. It shows you what you're trading off. One especially important point: filter out anything that fails your bottom line first. If a computer can't even run the software you need, a nice color or lots of freebies can't make up for it.

In the matrix, each column should measure every option with the same ruler. Criteria may also differ in importance: when renting, safety and commute might not be outweighed by a heap of small perks. Scoring organizes your judgment. It doesn't turn a subjective choice into an absolutely objective answer.
models.example:
You're torn between three rentals. First write down your hard requirements: a maximum budget, an acceptable commute, and basic natural light. Rule out the ones that clearly don't fit, then compare how quiet they are, storage, everyday convenience, and how easy the landlord is to deal with.

You really loved the decor in one of them, but after filling in the table you realize the extra commute every day would eat up a lot of your rest time. You might still choose it because you love it. You just know now exactly what that love costs. Choosing with clear eyes feels better than discovering the price afterward.
models.extra: One job may pay more while the other offers more growth. List the commute, the work itself, stability, and how each fits your life side by side, and you'll know better why you're choosing, instead of being swayed by whichever perk you heard about most recently.
steps: List your non-negotiable requirements first. If an option doesn't meet them, don't let its other strengths earn it points.
Pick three to five main criteria and note which one matters most to you. Don't list too many.
Score the options or write their pros and cons, then shift the weights around to see whether the result flips easily.
models.caution: The numbers come from your own judgment. Multiplying them by weights doesn't make them objective truth. If two options are close, don't put blind faith in the total. Go back to the most important differences, then look for more information or try them out.
models.exercise: Draw a small three-column table for a real choice: criteria, option A, option B. Write the one thing you're least willing to compromise on first, then fill in the rest.
models.brief: A matrix comparing options on shared criteria: three differently shaped candidate objects on the left, and three columns of icon-only criteria across the top: a clock, a coin, and a shield. The nine cells use a few solid dots to show how each option performs, and a stick figure points to the one that best fits the goal according to the criteria.

bodyDiagram.caption: Every candidate option is compared against the same set of criteria.

models.title: Venn Diagram
models.lead: Some people or things belong to two groups at once, and the overlap deserves its own look.
models.when: When you're sorting groups of people, explaining rules, looking for shared needs, or discussing "who meets all the conditions," this is very handy.
models.body:
You have friends who can cook and friends who are free on weekends, and the two groups aren't exactly the same. Draw each group as a circle, and the overlap is "people who can cook and are also free on weekends." A diagram that uses circles to show what things share and how they differ is called a Venn diagram.

A Venn diagram is a way of picturing relationships between sets. It uses regions and their overlaps to show relationships such as intersection, union, and complement, helping you see which conditions members satisfy at the same time.

It's especially good for making clear the difference between "meets both" and "meets either one." It sounds like just a few words, but in practice the plans that result can be very different. Draw the combination you're really looking for first. It's less error-prone than everyone forming their own idea of "either is fine" or "both are needed."

The overlap means "meets both at once." It isn't simply the two sides' numbers added together. If the two circles are people who like reading and people who like podcasts, the middle is the people who like both, and the rest of each circle holds what's unique to that group.
models.example:
You want to host a board game night. Some friends love board games, some are free on Saturday, and some live fairly close. Looking at the three conditions separately, you can see that not everyone who loves playing can come this time, and living nearby isn't the only thing that qualifies someone to join.

First be clear about the truly necessary conditions, like "wants to come and is free that day," then treat distance as something to consider when sorting out transportation. The diagram helps you check whether conditions are getting mixed up, and keeps you from leaving out the right people because of an irrelevant criterion.
models.extra: The things you love, the things you're good at, and the things people need might overlap somewhere. This diagram can help you ask the question, but whether that overlap really exists, and whether it can support a living over the long run, still takes trying things and finding out.
steps: Write down clearly what each circle stands for, so people can tell whether something fits.
Mark whether you're looking for the intersection ("and") or the union ("or").
Try a few real or made-up examples to see if anything has been left out or put in the wrong place.
models.caution: When you sketch circles freehand, their sizes don't mean anything about how many people are in them. When the overlaps between several groups get too complicated, a table may be clearer. There's no need to make things hard to read just to draw a diagram.
models.exercise: Draw two circles: "things I want to do" and "things I have time to do this week." In the overlap, put one action you're going to actually start.
models.brief: Three semi-transparent, hollow, overlapping circles: each holds a small icon of a book, headphones, or a person, and the overlapping areas hold combined icons for meeting two or all three conditions. A stick figure uses a pointer to examine the shared central area.

bodyDiagram.caption: The three positions show, in order: meeting only the first condition, meeting both, and meeting only the second condition.

models.title: Decision Tree
models.lead: Spell out "if I do this, what happens next?" and your choice gets a lot less tangled.
models.when: When you're deciding whether to try something out first, how to set up a backup plan, or when one choice could lead to several different outcomes, this is a great fit.
models.body:
Some decisions aren't just about the next step. They lead to more forks down the road. A decision tree draws those forks as branches: what can I choose, what might happen after I choose, and what do I do next in each case? It makes the costs easier to see, and shows you which information is worth looking into first.

A decision tree uses branches to represent available actions, possible events, and their outcomes, adding probability and value estimates where needed, to help analyze the paths a decision can take.

It's important to tell apart two kinds of branches. Some are yours to choose, like whether to buy a ticket. Others are out of your control, like whether it rains on the day of the event. Separating what you can decide from what you can't helps you plan far more than asking yourself "but what if it rains?" over and over.

The forks in the tree mean two different things. One is an action you can choose. The other is something you still can't decide after you've chosen, like the weather. Only by keeping them apart can you see which step you control and what uncertainty each path still faces.
models.example:
You're planning an outdoor get-together this weekend. You could book a lawn right away, or choose a venue that can move indoors. Follow each path further: what happens if it's sunny, what if it rains, how much does canceling cost, and is there enough time to switch locations at the last minute?

If people are traveling a long way and canceling last minute would be costly, paying a bit more for a place with backup space may be worth it. If it's just a few people nearby meeting on short notice, keeping a cancelable booking may be enough. The same "weather risk" leads to different choices because what follows costs different amounts.
models.extra: If you want a pet, don't just draw the branch "happy after adopting." Also draw what you'll do when you travel for work, when the pet gets sick, or when you move. The point isn't to scare yourself off, but to let both your affection and the long-term responsibility into the decision.
steps: Start by drawing the two or three actions you can actually choose right now. You don't need to add every possibility you can imagine.
For each action, add the most important things that could follow, and write down the costs and any ways to recover.
Find the unknown that's most likely to change your choice, and put your effort into finding it out first.
models.caution: Drawing branches doesn't mean you know the probabilities. Be honest about uncertain numbers: compare a few scenarios, and don't make up precise figures that fool you into thinking you've worked it all out.
models.exercise: Pick a choice you're facing soon. Draw two main branches and write two possible outcomes for each. Which one needs a way out planned in advance?
models.brief: A decision tree spreading left to right: on the left, a stick figure faces a square choice node that splits into icons for an outdoor activity and an indoor activity. The outdoor branch then hits a round weather-event node that splits into sun and rain, leading to outcomes under an umbrella and in the sunshine. The indoor branch leads to board games.

bodyDiagram.caption: A choice splits into different paths, and along those paths you may meet events you can't decide.

models.title: Pros and Cons List
models.lead: Write down the pros and cons so the loudest thought doesn't take over your head.
models.when: When you keep going back and forth on a choice like moving, changing jobs, or signing up for a course, writing it down usually helps more than thinking in circles.
models.body:
Sometimes it's not that you haven't thought about a choice, it's that your thoughts keep spinning: today you only see the upsides, tomorrow it's all worries. A pros and cons list puts both sides on paper so they're present at the same time. That way you can see more clearly what you're actually hoping for and what you're afraid of.

A pros and cons list is a decision-making method that records the factors for and against a choice side by side, making the relevant benefits, costs, and concerns easier to compare.

But it's not about counting ten items on the left and eight on the right and letting the left win. One serious cost can matter more than ten small conveniences. Look at how much each item weighs, whether it's real, and whether there's some other way to reduce its impact.
models.example:
You're thinking of moving closer to work. The pros: less commuting, more sleep, and enough energy left to cook after work. The cons: higher rent, being farther from friends, and having to move. Once it's written out, you realize the key question is really just "how much more do I pay each month, and how much usable time does it buy me?"

So you actually travel the route once, check the rent and moving costs, and consider whether working from home a few days a week could improve things instead. The list helps you step out of your emotions and find the numbers you need to check and the terms you might negotiate.
models.extra: "I'll have fun at the party" and "I'll get to see my friends" may be the same kind of benefit, so there's no need to split them into two votes. On the other hand, "it'll affect my important exam tomorrow morning" may be just one line, but it deserves serious attention.
steps: Write the benefits, the costs, and what you don't know yet separately, so guesses don't blend in with facts.
Circle the two or three items that really affect your life. You don't need to treat every small point as equally important.
Check these key items first, then see whether you can make adjustments that shrink the costs.
models.caution: Don't count the same benefit three times by phrasing it three ways. Safety, health, or bottom lines you can't accept shouldn't be brushed aside just because there are lots of upsides.
models.exercise: Spend five minutes writing a pros and cons list, with no more than five items on each side. Then circle the most important one on each side and see whether those two are the real choice you're facing.
models.brief: An icon version of a side-by-side pros and cons list: in the center, a suitcase for the choice at hand, with two parallel wordless lists on either side. The left shows icons for scenery, companions, and rest; the right shows a coin, time, and fatigue. Each item is a different size to suggest different importance, and a stick figure compares them one by one.

models.title: Cost–Benefit Analysis
models.lead: Don't just look at what it costs to buy. Look at what you'll pay later and what you'll get back.
models.when: When you're buying equipment, subscribing to a service, choosing how to get around, or deciding whether an upgrade is worth it, this comes up easily.
models.body:
A cheap printer may come with expensive ink cartridges, and an automation tool still takes time to set up after you buy it. Cost-benefit analysis means laying out and comparing the main things you give and get over a period of time. Costs aren't just money. They include learning, upkeep, the space something takes up, and the other things you can't do because of it.

Cost-benefit analysis systematically compares the relevant costs and expected benefits of an action against a clear baseline for comparison and within a defined time frame. When outcomes can be measured in money and spread over time, the time value of money usually needs to be considered too.

"Benefits" can't always be turned into money either. Ease, convenience, and time with family are worth considering too. Work out the parts you can calculate, and list the hard-to-price parts separately. There's no need to slap a dollar amount on every kind of happiness just to look scientific.
models.example:
You want to buy a dishwasher, and the price makes you think it's too expensive. But if you only compare the purchase price, you miss installation, supplies, and space, and you also miss the washing-up time you'd save every day. First estimate how often your household cooks, whether your dishes are a good fit, and who'll load and maintain it, then compare that with keeping on washing by hand.

In the end it might be worth buying, or it might not pay off because you rarely cook. The key is to calculate based on how you'll actually use it, and not to take the ad's "saves you an hour a day" as a benefit you're guaranteed to get.
models.extra: A supermarket farther away saves you $2 each trip, but the round trip takes an extra forty minutes. Whether it's worth going can vary from person to person. But once you factor in travel costs, time, and energy, you'll know better what you're choosing.
steps: Be clear about what you're comparing and over what time frame, such as how buying versus not buying would play out over the next year.
List the main costs of buying, learning, using, and maintaining, and also list the benefits you'd really get.
Run the key numbers once with optimistic estimates and once with conservative ones, and see whether your conclusion still holds.
models.caution: Money that's already spent and can't be changed shouldn't decide on its own whether you spend more later. And the time you save won't automatically turn into income, so don't count every imagined benefit as money in the bank.
models.exercise: Pick a tool you're thinking of buying. Besides the price, list three more costs, then write down how many times a week you'd really use it. See whether your original "great deal" needs rethinking.
models.brief: A cost-benefit scale over the same time frame: one side holds the coins, clock, and tools you'll need to put in later, and the other holds a basket of results and a small growing tree for the expected gains. Along a limited timeline below, two thin paths compare continuing with keeping things as they are, while a stick figure checks the baseline conditions.

models.title: Supply and Demand
models.lead: When more people want something and less of it is available, the price usually starts to move.
models.when: When you're looking at changes in rent, ticket prices, holiday goods, or lines for a service, use this to pull the causes apart.
models.body:
Supply is how much sellers are willing to offer. Demand is how much buyers are willing and able to buy. Both depend on price, and both are shaped by other factors too. If everyone loves something but nobody will actually pay that price for it, that isn't the same as strong real demand.

In economics, demand and supply describe the quantities that buyers and sellers, respectively, are willing and able to buy or offer at different prices over a given period, with other conditions held constant.

Two things are easy to mix up. In one, you buy less because the price went up. In the other, something in your life changed, so you want more even at the same price. The first is the price itself shaping your choice; the second is your need to buy changing. Telling them apart makes it much easier to understand why something suddenly becomes hard to find or more expensive.

When you read a supply-and-demand chart, separate moving along the same curve from the whole curve shifting. A change in price corresponds to a different point on the curve. A change in conditions like costs or preferences may mean you have to redraw the curve. Not every change can be explained as the same kind of thing.
models.example:
When it starts raining, suddenly lots of people outside the subway station want an umbrella, but the little shop nearby only has so many in stock. They may sell out fast, or the price may go up. Once the sun comes out, that last-minute demand fades, and the same umbrella may not have many eager buyers.

This doesn't mean any price hike by a seller is fair. Real transactions also involve rules, promises, and questions of fairness. The supply-and-demand lens just helps you see who might be changing their behavior behind a price change, and how quickly stock can catch up.
models.extra: If new office buildings go up near your neighborhood, demand for lunch might rise. But if ten new restaurants open at the same time, competition changes too. Noticing "more people" is where the analysis starts, not a guarantee that opening a shop will make money.
steps: Ask separately: what has changed for the buyers, and what has changed for the sellers?
Think about whether there are substitutes, and how long it takes to restock or expand production.
Don't read every cause off a single price; keep an eye on costs, seasons, rules, and competition.
models.caution: Supply and demand is very useful, but it can't explain every price. Market power, information gaps, and institutions all shape transactions. And high demand doesn't automatically mean something is worth starting a business in or investing in.
models.exercise: Pick something that got more expensive recently. Write down two possible changes in demand and two possible changes in supply. Which ones do you have facts for, and which are just guesses?
models.brief: Crossing supply and demand curves with both sides of the market: on unlabeled axes in the center, a navy downward curve crosses a brick-red upward curve; on the left, a vendor with boxes of goods; on the right, a customer with coins; dots and a price tag are linked by plain lines.

bodyDiagram.caption: The solid and dashed lines show supply before and after conditions change. A shift of the whole curve is different from moving to a new point along the same curve.

models.title: Critical Mass / Tipping Point
models.lead: Some things barely respond as you add a little, then suddenly change once they reach a certain point.
models.when: When you're running a community, organizing events, trying to understand how a platform grows, or noticing that plenty of people have joined but things still won't get going, this is worth using.
models.body:
Say you start a mutual-help group chat. With only a few members, questions often go unanswered. As more people join and they bring a wider range of skills, replies come faster and more people want to come back. Critical mass and tipping points both remind us that some changes don't happen at a steady pace. Once certain conditions are met, a process may start to sustain itself or speed up noticeably.

Critical mass is the key quantity or density needed for a process to continue or sustain itself; a tipping point usually emphasizes the marked change or acceleration that happens once a system crosses a threshold.

But don't rush to translate this into "we're just one hundredth person away." What actually matters may be the number of active people, how connected they are, how often they use something, or how reliable it is, not some magic total. You need to see which kind of interaction is actually holding the system up.

The key isn't just "more," but whether the system has crossed the conditions it needs to keep running. Widely spaced dominoes may not keep falling; they only pass the push along when they're close enough together. In real situations, the threshold also depends on connections, quality, and context. It's not a headcount that works everywhere.
models.example:
You want to set up a regular weekend badminton game, but with twenty people in the group chat it still rarely happens, because everyone is free at different times. What finally makes it stick isn't packing the group to fifty. It's finding eight people who are often free at the same time, and fixing a court and sign-up rules.

What got filled in was steady enough participation and organization. When each game goes smoothly, people are more willing to sign up early, and organizing gets easier. Scale and feedback changed together, which is what gave the game a chance to last, not an impressive member count.
models.extra: If a neighborhood swap board is always full of outdated posts, more people won't necessarily make it useful. Only when it's updated promptly, covers enough categories, and gets quick replies will people check it often. How densely it's actually used matters more than the sign-up numbers.
steps: Identify the key interaction that keeps things running, such as replies, matches, or participation.
Look at what's missing: numbers, density, overlapping schedules, or one important role.
Track things on a small scale to find where the change happens, rather than treating a round number as a guaranteed threshold.
models.caution: Not every project has a clear tipping point, and piling on numbers doesn't guarantee a breakthrough. Without real value, more people can simply make the problems bigger.
models.exercise: Think of something you feel would "work if only a few more people joined." Write down exactly what those extra people would need to do for it to actually get better.
models.brief: Self-sustaining only past a threshold: on the left, a few scattered dominoes are spaced too far apart to pass on the push; on the right, a dense row of dominoes keeps falling after the first nudge, with the key gap circled in navy.

models.title: The Paradox of Choice
models.lead: When there are too many options to compare, freedom of choice can turn into a burden.
models.when: When the more you shop the more confused you get, when you keep putting off starting a course, or when you keep comparing options after you've already decided, this is a good one to use.
models.body:
You open a food delivery app and half an hour later you still haven't picked anything. You go to buy toothpaste, and the more specs you read, the more you worry about missing a better one. The paradox of choice says that in some situations, more options make it harder to get started and more likely you'll regret your pick afterward. That's because you're not only judging each option; you also keep imagining the ones you gave up.

The paradox of choice holds that under certain conditions, adding options can increase the burden of comparison, delay decisions, and lower satisfaction, though this kind of choice overload doesn't show up in every situation.

Not everyone dislikes lots of options, though. Someone who knows cameras well may enjoy a wide range, while a beginner just wants to know which few suit them. What matters is whether you have a goal, criteria for comparing, and a point where you can stop searching, not just the total number of options.

Think of choosing as a funnel that opens up and then narrows: first accept that there are many possibilities, then use clear criteria to rule out the ones that don't fit, and finally compare a small number of candidates. Narrowing down is about easing the work of comparing, not cutting things at random until only one is left.
models.example:
You want an ordinary office chair. At first you only care that it's comfortable and reasonably priced. After a week of reading reviews, you start worrying about every detail: armrests, materials, mesh, the base. The more you research, the less you dare to order.

Go back to how you'll actually use it: how many hours a day you sit, where you feel uncomfortable, what your budget is, and whether you can try it or return it. Narrow it down to three chairs that meet your basic needs, actually try them, then decide by a set time. The goal is to get a chair that works for you, not to prove there's no better one anywhere on the market.
models.extra: When you're meeting friends for dinner, asking "what do you want to eat?" can drag on forever. Asking "noodles, hot pot, or something light?" first, and then picking a specific place based on what people can't eat, often makes it much easier. Cutting down how many comparisons people face at once works better than deciding for everyone.
steps: Decide on your two or three most important needs, plus the budget or time you won't go beyond.
Use those criteria to narrow things down to a few comparable options, and stop adding new candidates.
Set a "this is good enough" standard, and let yourself stop searching once something meets it.
models.caution: Fewer options aren't always better. When the differences are real and the information is clear, a wide choice can be very valuable. And don't hide alternatives that matter to other people just to make things simpler.
models.exercise: For one decision you're stuck on, set three requirements, at most three candidates, and a deadline. When time's up, choose based on your requirements, and don't keep postponing because "maybe there's something better."
models.brief: From an explosion of branches to a focused decision: on the left, a stick figure faces branches fanning out into many nearly identical cups, with tangled lines above its head; on the right, the options are filtered first so only a few distinguishable cups remain, and the stick figure can compare them more easily.

bodyDiagram.caption: First open up the possibilities, then use clear criteria to narrow them down to a few candidates.

models.title: Trade-Offs
models.lead: Choosing more of one thing often means getting less of another; spelling out the cost actually makes choosing easier.
models.when: When you're trying to satisfy too many goals at once, your commitments keep piling up, or every option leaves you a little dissatisfied, this is the one you need.
models.body:
When you travel, you'd like it to be cheap, close, comfortable, and flexible, but you usually can't get the best of all of them. At work, you'd like things done fast, broad in scope, and high in quality, and that takes resources too. Making trade-offs means admitting your conditions are limited and deciding what to protect this time and where you're willing to accept a little less.

A trade-off is accepting a sacrifice or cost in one respect in order to gain an improvement in another, under constraints; it's a common decision situation when several goals can't all be fully met at once.

It sounds like "compromise," but it can actually help you take charge. You're not being forced to give things up without understanding why; you're choosing with the cost in view. At the same time, don't give in too early. Some goals that seem to conflict can both improve with a different arrangement, so it isn't always either-or.

If two goals draw on the same pool of time or money, the possible options often form a boundary: move a bit further toward one, and you may have to give up some of the other. First check whether the constraint is real, then decide what you're willing to trade. Don't assume by default that all your goals conflict.
models.example:
You're about to move, and you want a place close to work, with a big room, and low rent. Three apartments each have one of those strengths, and you keep waiting for the perfect one to show up. Start by ranking what you really need. If what you need most right now is sleep and rest, the commute might come first. If you'll mostly work from home for a long time, space might matter more.

You can also look for new combinations: a neighborhood with easier transit connections, sharing with a friend, or changing your move-in date. Exploring which conditions you can change first, and then being clear about which cost you'll accept, is more useful than constantly blaming yourself for "never being satisfied with anything."
models.extra: If you want to spend time with family but also go to a friend's party, you might stop by briefly, meet your friend another day, or let them know ahead of time that you'll miss this one. A trade-off doesn't always mean dropping one side completely. Sometimes it means rearranging time and scope.
steps: List the things you want most, then mark the one you're least willing to give up this time.
For each one, ask: if I protect this, what extra cost comes with it, and what do I have to give up?
First look for ways to change the conditions; if you still can't have both, make a clear trade-off.
models.caution: Don't let an unreasonable arrangement hide behind "life is all about trade-offs." Some conflicts come from processes or how resources are divided, and you can push for improvements. And don't treat a real bottom line as a minor item you can give up any time.
models.exercise: For a choice you're about to make, finish this sentence: "This time my priority is ..., I'm willing to accept ..., but I won't accept ...." See whether you can make it specific.
models.brief: Trade-offs with limited resources: a stick figure holds a rope of fixed length linking two sliders; pulling one up raises a speed and wind icon while the other, a magnifying glass for careful checking, drops; below, several possible balance points are shown instead of a single best one.

bodyDiagram.caption: Under the same constraint, improving one goal may mean giving up part of another.

models.title: The 80/20 Rule / Pareto Principle
models.en: 二八法则与帕累托原则
models.lead: Don't spread your effort evenly; first find the few things that change the outcome most.
models.when: When you have a lot going on but little visible progress, or you don't know which problems to fix first, this is worth using.
models.body:
Sometimes only two or three out of ten tasks really move things forward, and a pile of recurring small glitches may come mostly from a few causes. The 80/20 rule is a reminder that contributions are often uneven, so it's worth finding the part that carries the most weight first. "80" and "20" are a common shorthand, not an exact ratio every situation has to fit.

The Pareto principle summarizes the uneven distribution of inputs and outcomes: a small share of causes or activities may contribute a large share of results, with 80:20 being a common approximation rather than a fixed law.

It's not about teaching you to slack off, either. It helps you put limited energy where it's most useful. If you spend every day polishing a document's formatting but never get around to understanding your readers' questions, you may be very diligent and still miss the thing that would improve the content most.

If you line up each item's contribution from largest to smallest and add them up as you go, it becomes easier to see whether results are concentrated in a few factors. What you're looking for is real evidence of an uneven distribution, not an assumption that the top two items must account for 80 percent.
models.example:
You want to improve your spoken English. Every day you save ten articles about learning methods and try out different apps, but you rarely actually speak. Looking back after two weeks, you notice that the most helpful moments were a ten-minute chat with a friend in English and carefully fixing two expressions you kept getting wrong.

So you set aside most of your time for speaking practice and reviewing mistakes, and leave only a small window for saving resources. It's not that everything else was useless. You just make sure the high-impact part actually happens first, then put any leftover energy into the secondary things.
models.extra: If your household spends a lot of time cleaning every week, most of it might come from a few spots where dust and clutter build up. Changing how you use the entryway storage, the shoe cabinet, and the countertops is more likely to cut down repeated work than wiping every corner a little more.
steps: Look back at recent effort and results, and find which things clearly moved you forward once they were done.
Put the two or three most important ones that you can actually influence into fixed time slots.
Check again after a while, so last month's priorities don't stay your priorities forever.
models.caution: Rare but costly things, like backups and safety checks, shouldn't be ignored just because they make up a small share. And don't turn "the vital few" into an excuse to only do the tasks you like and leave all the responsibility to others.
models.exercise: Circle three items on this week's to-do list. If you could only finish those three, would you still make real progress this week? If not, think again about what really matters.
models.brief: A few key tasks contribute most of the results through wide flowing bands, while the remaining tasks contribute less.

bodyDiagram.caption: A few factors may contribute most of the results; adding them up makes it easier to see whether the contribution is concentrated.

models.title: Win–Win
models.lead: Figure out what each side really wants, and sometimes nobody has to lose.
models.when: When you're negotiating a collaboration, splitting chores, arranging schedules, or noticing that two sides keep fighting over the same resource, this is a good one to use.
models.body:
You say, "I have to deliver early." I say, "I need time to do it properly." It sounds like someone has to back down. Win-win thinking starts by unpacking the surface demands: why are you in a hurry? Which part am I worried about? Could we change the scope, the timing, or the approach so both sides' core needs are taken care of?

Win-win is an approach to negotiation aimed at mutual gain; it emphasizes identifying each party's interests and exploring arrangements that are worth more to everyone than their respective alternatives.

Win-win doesn't mean everyone gets exactly the same thing, and it doesn't promise that every conflict has a happy solution. It's more about the order you go in: first try to create a better arrangement, then decide how to divide things up, instead of treating the other person as someone you have to beat from the start.

You can picture the two people's interests as two circles and look for goals that overlap. But mutual gain doesn't only come from the overlap; it can also come from differences that complement each other. If one person wants the orange peel and the other wants the fruit, the point is to rearrange the exchange, not just split the overlapping part.
models.example:
Two roommates: one wants to open the window for fresh air, the other gets cold at night. As long as the argument is only about "open or closed," it's hard to settle. Talking it through, it turns out the first one mainly minds the cooking smells, and the second mainly worries about a draft while sleeping.

So they agree to air out the place for a set time after cooking, close the window before bed, and then deal with the kitchen ventilation. Once the needs were pulled apart, a better solution appeared than "each putting up with half." It's not that the better talker won. Both of them got closer to living comfortably.
models.extra: A client wants to see results tomorrow, and the team needs a week. If the client really only needs something for an internal demo tomorrow, the team can deliver a small presentable piece first and finish the rest as planned. The key was asking, "What do you need it for tomorrow?"
steps: Have each side say what outcome they care about most, instead of repeating their original demands.
Look for things that can be adjusted, such as timing, scope, order, resources, or how risk is shared.
Compare the new plan with what each side would do without a deal, and make sure both really are willing to accept it.
models.caution: If one side is forced to accept and the other says "it's good for you too," that isn't win-win. When someone keeps crossing lines or things are clearly unfair, you can say no. You don't have to agree just to keep the relationship looking good.
models.exercise: Think of a current disagreement. Write down "what I'm asking for" and "the result I actually want." Then try writing the same for the other person, and find a chance to check whether you guessed right.
models.brief: Expanding the shared gain: two stick figures want the orange peel and the orange flesh respectively, shown in wordless thought bubbles; in the center, a single orange is split into peel and flesh, each going to the person who values it, so both get the part they care about more.

bodyDiagram.caption: The overlap is shared interest; differences outside the overlap can also lead to complementary exchanges.

models.title: Second-Order Thinking
models.lead: Don't just look at what happens right away; ask one more question: and then what?
models.when: When a decision looks like a great deal right now but might affect long-term habits, how work is shared on a team, or how other people behave, it's worth asking one more step.
models.body:
When you first come up with a fix, you often see only the most direct benefit: skip one check and you deliver faster today; handle all the hard problems for your coworkers and the trouble disappears right away. Second-order thinking asks us to look one step further. Once the check is skipped, will mistakes flow into the next stage? If you always finish things for others, will the same problems just come back next time?

Second-order thinking is a decision-analysis approach: beyond the direct results of an action, it traces the indirect effects those results cause, how other people respond, and the follow-on changes that unfold over time.

"Second-order" doesn't mean you may only think two steps ahead, and it isn't about who's smarter. It reminds us to connect the action, the direct result, and what follows, especially how others will respond and whether existing rules will change because of it. The same decision can also have different effects in the short term and the long term.

Take learning a new skill: at first you're slower and it's more tiring, but later you may be more independent and save time. Second-order thinking can show you the cost hidden behind an immediate benefit, and also the value that comes after an immediate struggle. It helps widen what you're comparing, rather than automatically rejecting fixes that work quickly.

When drawing it, put "what action you take" on the left, then connect "direct results" and "later effects." Where there are different possibilities, branch out; use dashed lines for links without enough evidence. The point isn't to draw long chains of arrows, but to spell out why each step might lead to the next.
models.example:
You lead a small team, and whenever someone hits a hard problem, you take it over and do it yourself. The first-order result is obvious: the task gets done quickly and the schedule stays on track. Keep asking "and then what?" and another possible path appears: your coworkers don't get a chance to practice and come back to you next time; you get busier and busier, and your own important work keeps getting pushed back.

That doesn't mean you should never help again. First judge whether it's urgent. If it has to be handled right away, finish it together. When there's time, have your coworker propose a plan first, then give hints, check the key steps, and ask them to finish it themselves. It may take a bit more time now, but it can cut the cost of taking things over again and again later.

This chain of changes is just a guess to be tested, not proof that helping once will make someone dependent. Try it on one common type of problem for two weeks, see whether your coworkers finish more on their own and whether you spend less time on that kind of problem, then adjust.
models.extra:
To sleep ten more minutes each day, you always leave packing tomorrow's things until right before you head out. You get a bit more sleep now, but what may follow is rushing to find things, forgetting documents, and having to go back for them. What you really need to compare is the time and energy of the whole morning, not just the moment you get up.

Try spending five minutes the night before getting things ready, and see after a week whether your mornings are less frantic. If packing ahead doesn't help, look for other causes. Factoring in later effects also means letting the facts correct what you first imagined.
steps: First write down the most direct benefits and costs of the decision, without skipping the immediate issues.
Then ask "and then what?" two more times: how will others respond, what new tasks or opportunities will come up, and which parts are uncertain?
Compare the short-term and later effects, pick a small approach you can adjust, and check your predictions against real feedback.
models.caution: Thinking far ahead doesn't make your predictions accurate. Each extra link can bring in new assumptions, so don't turn a chain of "maybes" into "definitely," and don't only imagine the worst case. Ordinary small things don't need endless analysis, and in an emergency, deal with the immediate risk first. Second-order thinking focuses on later effects, opportunity cost focuses on the alternatives you give up, and a feedback loop requires results to come back and affect the starting point. You can use all three together, but they aren't quite the same.
models.exercise: Pick a decision you're about to make and write three columns: "direct results," "what might happen next," and "who will change what they do because of it." Choose the item that affects the decision most and is least certain, and think about how you could check it first.
models.brief: Looking far down a chain reaction: a stick figure gets ready to gently push the first domino with one hand while watching what follows through a telescope; the first chain splits into two more distant possible paths, one driving gears and a seedling, the other affecting a block on a support. Off-white background, dark gray line art, navy arrows, small touches of brick red, no text.

bodyDiagram.caption: From left to right: taking over the task, finishing it now, and being asked for help again next time. The branches on the right show the possible added time pressure and fewer chances to practice. The dashed lines indicate these later effects still need to be checked.

models.title: Murphy’s Law
models.lead: Don't count on everything going smoothly every time; leave a backup route for the parts that matter.
models.when: When you're rushing to an important trip, giving a presentation, saving important files, or organizing an event, running through this once is usually well worth it.
models.body:
The more pressed for time you are, the more you dread hitting traffic; right before you present, the laptop refuses to connect to the projector. Murphy's Law uses exaggeration to remind us that the steps that could go wrong are worth thinking about in advance. It's not saying bad luck is guaranteed. It's saying don't let a whole plan depend on perfect conditions to succeed.

Murphy's Law is an adage drawn from experience about errors and accidents; it reminds people to take the steps that could fail seriously, rather than being a scientific law claiming every mistake will inevitably happen.

Useful preparation doesn't have to be complicated. Backing up important files, leaving a little extra time when you head out, and explaining to someone else how to take over can all greatly reduce the panic when something goes wrong. Rather than imagining every possible disaster, the more useful thing to practice is asking: if something really does go wrong, how can I keep going?
models.example:
You're presenting slides online, and since the file is saved in the cloud, you feel safe. Before the event, ask one more question: if the internet goes down, you can't log in, or you get disconnected, can the host carry on?

So you download a local copy, send the host a PDF ahead of time, and briefly explain where it would be fine to pause. The prep may take ten extra minutes, but it turns "one small glitch and everyone sits waiting" into "someone knows what to do next." The value of a backup plan is that it actually works when you need it.
models.extra: When you travel, securely backing up your ID details and noting down key ways to get in touch doesn't mean you expect to lose things. It means that if it does happen, you won't be completely stuck.
steps: Find the few steps that would bring everything to a halt if they failed; you don't need to treat every small thing as a disaster.
Set up a simple, independent backup or alternative for each of them.
Actually try the recovery process once, so you're not relying on a backup file you've never opened.
models.caution: Adding endless safeguards also costs money and adds complexity. Plan your preparation according to how big the impact is and how hard recovery would be, and don't let guarding against accidents swallow your whole life.
models.exercise: For an important plan coming up, write three lines: which step you're most worried about going wrong, how you'd spot it early, and who does what if it does go wrong.
models.brief: A backup route for when things fail: the main power cord has a possible break point; a stick figure checks the weak connector first and prepares a backup battery, and both the normal path and the backup path can light the bulb.

models.title: Positive and Negative Reinforcement
models.lead: A reward can make a behavior happen more, and so can taking away something unpleasant.
models.when: When you're building a habit, trying to understand product notifications, designing feedback for learning, or finding that "I gave a reward and it didn't work," use this to break it down.
models.body:
"Positive reinforcement" and "negative reinforcement" are easily misheard as reward and punishment. Start with this: both increase a behavior. Positive means adding something; negative means taking something away. Whether reinforcement happened depends on whether the behavior actually shows up more often afterward, not just on your good intentions.

In operant conditioning, positive reinforcement increases the likelihood that a behavior will occur again by adding a stimulus, and negative reinforcement does so by removing a stimulus; punishment, by contrast, aims to reduce a behavior.

For example, if you get feedback you like after tidying up and then become more willing to tidy, that may be positive reinforcement. If an annoying chime stops once you buckle your seatbelt, and so you buckle up more promptly in the future, that may be negative reinforcement. Punishment works in the other direction, making a behavior less frequent, and it isn't the same thing as negative reinforcement.

For both kinds of reinforcement, follow the loop forward: after a behavior, was something you like added, or something unpleasant reduced, and is the behavior more likely next time? The difference lies in how the consequence changes the environment, not in which one sounds harsher.
models.example:
You want to build a habit of practicing piano every day, so after each practice you let yourself listen to a performance you love. If that consequence makes you more willing to start, it may be working as positive reinforcement. Just "setting up a reward" isn't enough, though; you have to see whether the habit actually increases.

Another example: a device keeps beeping until you shut the door properly. If the beeping stopping makes you more likely to close the door next time, that's negative reinforcement. The "negative" here doesn't mean the behavior is bad. It just describes something being taken away.
models.extra: Every time a pop-up nags you to upgrade, you click "Remind me later," and it disappears right away. If that relief makes clicking it more of a habit, your behavior is being steered by the consequence, even though the designers originally wanted you to upgrade.
steps: Write down clearly the behavior you want more of, such as "practice for ten minutes," not just "be more disciplined."
Check what gets added or taken away after the behavior, and whether that consequence really matters to the person.
Watch how the behavior changes over a while, and keep an eye out for going through the motions, cheating, or added stress.
models.caution: Not all praise works for everyone, and rewards can make people focus only on the prize. And never deliberately create discomfort to control someone, so they can only get relief by complying. Understanding the mechanism also means respecting boundaries.
models.exercise: Pick a habit that keeps happening and write down "what comes before, what the behavior is, and what you get or escape afterward." Don't rush to judge it as good or bad; just see the chain clearly first.
models.brief: Two parallel reinforcement loops, both increasing a behavior: on top, a stick figure finishes tidying a desk, gets a small star, and is more willing to tidy next time; below, a stick figure buckles a seatbelt in a car, the harsh reminder sound waves disappear, and they are more willing to buckle up next time.

bodyDiagram.caption: On top, a pleasant consequence is added; below, an annoyance is removed. Both can make a behavior more likely to happen again.

models.title: Intrinsic Motivation
models.lead: Some things you're happy to do simply because doing them feels good.
models.when: When studying is hard to stick with, a hobby has turned into a chore, or you want to help someone else get more actively involved, this is a good place to look.
models.body:
You lose track of time while drawing, feel satisfied when you crack a tough problem, or grow flowers just because you love watching them slowly come up. These may all involve intrinsic motivation: not doing it for grades, bonuses, or other people's likes, but because the activity itself is worth your time. It explains why you want to keep going with some things even when nobody is pushing you.

In self-determination theory, intrinsic motivation means engaging in an activity for the interest and satisfaction inherent in the activity itself, as distinct from acting for a separable external outcome.

To support this kind of drive, give yourself some choice, make your progress visible, and stay connected with people who support you. The theory sees autonomy, competence, and relatedness as important needs. In plain words: "I get some say," "I can do this, and I'm getting better," and "there are people here who understand me."
models.example:
You used to love taking photos, then you started running an account, and every time you went out you only thought about which shots would get more likes. Gradually, picking up the camera made you think of numbers and comparisons, and the joy of watching the light faded.

You could set aside some time to shoot only what you want, with no need to post it, and aim your practice at improving a particular skill rather than needing every photo to win. You don't have to dislike outside recognition. Just leave the activity itself some room to breathe, so results don't take over all the fun.
models.extra: If a child loves drawing and you always ask how they placed in the competition, drawing may slowly become nothing more than "turning in results." Try asking what they drew and which part they like best, paying attention to the exploring, not just the outcome.
steps: Ask yourself whether there's some small part of this that you'd happily do even if nobody knew.
Give it a reasonable amount of choice and small challenges you can complete, and add a bit more difficulty once you see progress.
Look for support and shared interests, and cut down on unnecessary rankings, nagging, and the feeling of being watched.
models.caution: Having intrinsic interest doesn't mean you don't need rest, and it doesn't mean others can skip paying you fairly. Dull but necessary tasks still need to be divided fairly; they can't be solved just by saying "you should love it."
models.exercise: For an activity you used to enjoy that now feels stressful, set aside twenty minutes of "no grading" time. Do only the small part that interests you, and notice how it feels different.
models.brief: The interest loop of the activity itself: a stick figure is absorbed in a geometric puzzle, feels happy after finishing it, and then eagerly tries a new puzzle; a short loop links interest, engagement, and satisfaction.

models.title: Hawthorne Effect
models.lead: When we know someone's watching, we may act differently, and that isn't necessarily thanks to the new method.
models.when: When you're judging a check-in routine, a short pilot, public accountability, or a new policy, it's well worth asking this one extra question.
models.body:
With a teacher standing beside you, you might sit up a little straighter. When a team is piloting a new system, everyone may be extra conscientious. The Hawthorne effect is often used as a reminder that being observed, studied, or given extra attention can itself change behavior, so how people perform during a trial isn't necessarily how they'll perform normally.

The Hawthorne effect usually refers to individuals changing their behavior because they are aware of being observed or studied; the direction and size of the effect need to be tested case by case.

The name comes from early workplace studies, but how to interpret those studies has been debated for a long time. You don't need to memorize the story. Just remember one checking question: if results look better, is it because the new setup really is better, or because people know for now that "someone is watching"? It could also be both.
models.example:
You try posting a daily study check-in to a group chat, and in the first week you're especially motivated and read noticeably more. You decide you've found a method that will work forever. A few weeks later, the group goes quiet and your own check-ins start slipping.

That first week's progress wasn't necessarily fake. It may genuinely have been boosted by attention and novelty. The next step is to find a setup you can stick with even when fewer people are watching, such as a fixed place, a manageable amount of work, and self-testing for feedback. Turning a short-term push into a long-term habit takes other ingredients too.
models.extra: You buy a new budgeting notebook and record everything carefully for the first few days, then gradually forget about it. Maybe the notebook really is good, or maybe novelty was doing the work. Keeping it up for a few more weeks is a safer test than deciding after three days to buy one for the whole family.
steps: Note whether, besides the new plan itself, there's also added supervision, reminders, praise, or novelty.
Don't judge by the first week alone; keep watching for a while after the buzz has died down.
If it only works with attention, count that attention as a cost instead of pretending it will last on its own.
models.caution: "Working harder when watched" doesn't happen to everyone, and it can also turn into nervousness, people-pleasing, or avoidance. The Hawthorne effect can't explain every improvement. It's just one possibility worth ruling in or out.
models.exercise: Think back to a new routine that worked especially well at first and then slackened. Apart from the tools and methods, what extra attention or expectations were there in that first week?
models.brief: Two scenes of behavior changing under observation: the same stick figure does the same block-building task. On the left, in a natural state, the posture is relaxed; on the right, after noticing a researcher's eye and clipboard, the posture is more deliberate and careful. The result dots are spread differently on each side, with neither marked as better.

sources.title: Levitt & List · A Reanalysis of the Original Illumination Experiments

models.title: The Forgetting Curve
models.lead: Feeling like you know it right after reading doesn't mean you can recall it on your own a few days later.
models.when: When you're memorizing vocabulary, preparing for an exam, reading a technical book, or saving lots of material you never seem to remember, this is very useful.
models.body:
You look over a page of notes and everything seems familiar, but when you close the book you can barely recall a couple of key points. That's not strange: feeling familiar with something and being able to pull it out of memory yourself are not the same thing. The forgetting curve reminds us that memories fade over time, and if you want to use something in the long run, you need to retrieve it again later.

The forgetting curve describes how memory retention changes over time. It often shows a fairly quick drop after learning followed by a leveling off, but its exact shape depends on factors such as the material, how it was learned, and retrieval practice.

The most practical approach isn't just rereading, but actively recalling after some time has passed: explain it without looking at the material, work a problem, or apply it to a new example. Making a bit of effort to remember often tells you more about what you truly know and what's still shaky than gliding through the page again.

When reading a forgetting curve, first check what kind of material it describes, how it was learned, and how it was tested. The boost after review doesn't mean it will never drop again. The trend on the chart is there to help you schedule recall practice, not to predict exactly how much each person will forget on which day.
models.example:
You read your lecture notes three times for an exam and feel like you know nearly all of it, yet you keep getting stuck on practice questions. Try a different routine: after each short section, close the material and write down the core points. The next day, try answering questions first and only look back at what you missed. A few days later, check again.

At first this may make you think, "How did I forget so much?" But really it's exposing the gaps earlier. You no longer wait until the exam to discover that you can only recognize sentences and can't answer on your own. You can also adjust your review based on what you actually forget, instead of rereading everything equally.
models.extra: When you've just learned a new dish, cooking it a few days later without watching the video, then filling in whichever step you forgot, usually turns it into your own skill better than rewatching the same video every day.
steps: After studying, close the material and explain or write out the main points in your own words.
Try again after a gap; review more of what you can't recall, and space out what you've already mastered.
Find your own example for each concept so the memory connects to real use.
models.caution: Don't treat some fixed online schedule of days and forgetting percentages as a universal manual for humans. Difficulty of the material, your background, and practice all affect memory, and the right rhythm for you has to come from actually checking.
models.exercise: Close this page now and try to say the one question the forgetting curve most reminds you to ask, plus how you'll review something you're currently learning tomorrow.
models.brief: Memory fading over time and review: a navy curve drops quickly and then levels off; beside it, another curve rises and falls again at a few unnumbered time points where a small stick figure doing recall practice pulls out puzzle pieces.

bodyDiagram.caption: The top row shows a memory gradually fading; the bottom row adds recall practice partway through, after which retention may turn out differently.

models.title: Prisoner’s Dilemma
models.lead: Both people are afraid of getting the short end, and both may end up with it.
models.when: When two people or two teams could cooperate but keep guarding against each other out of fear of free riders or of losing out by going first, use it to examine the rules underneath.
models.body:
Two people are working on something together. Clearly, cooperating would be better for both, yet each can't help thinking: "If they do their part, I can slack a bit and come out ahead. If they don't, I'm certainly not going to work for nothing." So both choose not to cooperate, and the work turns out worse. That's the tension the prisoner's dilemma is meant to show us.

The prisoner's dilemma is a classic model in game theory: in the standard one-shot, two-player game, not cooperating is each player's dominant strategy, yet the payoff to each when both don't cooperate is lower than when both cooperate.

In the classic story, two suspects are questioned separately. As the puzzle is set up, no matter what the other person chooses, confessing gets you a somewhat lighter punishment. But if both confess, both are punished more heavily than if both had stayed silent. This is a hypothetical structure of choices, not a description of how real criminal cases work.

Its most useful reminder is that when cooperation fails, it isn't always because someone has "bad character." It may be that the rules make not cooperating look like the better deal. To improve the outcome, besides showing good faith, look for ways to make contributions visible and commitments enforceable, so neither side has to protect itself by guessing.

To read the four-box grid, let the rows be your choices and the columns the other person's, each ordered "cooperate, don't cooperate." Look at both people's payoffs in each box. Then compare your two options down the same column, and the other person's two options along the same row. That's how you see why individual choices can lead both sides to a worse result.
models.example:
Suppose you and a classmate agree to each organize half of the review notes and then share them. To make the relationships clear, we'll use hypothetical "net payoff scores": the help the notes give you minus the effort of organizing them. Higher is better, and these aren't real measurements. If both of you do your part, you each get 3. If you don't and your classmate does, you get 5 and they get 0. The reverse gives you 0 and them 5. If neither of you does it, you each get 1.

From your side: if your classmate does their part, skipping yours moves you from 3 to 5. If they don't, skipping yours moves you from 0 to 1. Your classmate makes the same comparison, so neither of you does it and you each get 1, worse than the 3 each you'd get by cooperating. That's the dilemma: the choice that looks better to each person on their own doesn't leave the two of you better off together.

In real life, you can change how you cooperate: each hand in a small portion first and continue once the quality checks out, and spell out each person's tasks and deadlines so contributions can be verified. That changes the conditions for cooperation, rather than just asking the other person to "trust me."
models.extra:
Two neighboring teams both need to maintain a shared document. Maintaining it takes time, while just reading the other team's updates is easy. If both try to free-ride, the document gets more and more outdated until it's useless to everyone. Whether this is a strict prisoner's dilemma depends on how each side really weighs the time against the value of the information, but it's a reminder to ask "who bears the cost, and who gets the benefit?"

You could try rotating updates, defining what each team maintains, recording contributions, and having both sides flag gaps promptly. The key is to make the effort and the payoff of cooperating line up more easily, rather than repeatedly blaming the other side for not taking the initiative.
steps: Write down each side's two choices, list the four combinations, and see who each outcome favors.
Check why not cooperating is tempting: is it easy to free-ride, are commitments impossible to verify, or is there a fear of not being paid back?
Start with one small, verifiable round of cooperation with clear deliverables, feedback, and a way out, then decide whether to continue.
models.caution: Not every bumpy collaboration is a prisoner's dilemma. The classic one-shot model requires that not cooperating is better for you no matter what the other side does, yet both not cooperating is worse for both than both cooperating. Real-life payoffs, relationships, and motives may not fit that setup. Repeated cooperation, public information, or rule changes may change the outcome, but success isn't guaranteed. Understanding the dilemma doesn't mean always giving in; protecting your boundaries and knowing when to walk away matter just as much.
models.exercise: Find something where you and someone else are both waiting for the other to go first. Draw four boxes and fill in the outcomes for "we both do it," "only I do it," "only they do it," and "neither of us does it." Then write down one small arrangement that would lower the risk of going first.
models.brief: Two-sided choices and a shared loss: two stick figures on separate sides each decide whether to put a gear into a shared machine or keep it on their own side. A faint small scene above shows a bridge connected after cooperation; the main scene below shows both taking their gears back, the bridge broken, and both stuck. No text; a narrative scene rather than a matrix.
