models.title: False Dichotomy
models.lead: When you hear "it's either this or that," look for a hidden third path first.
models.when: When you're facing high-pressure persuasion, a big decision, or a choice between two options you don't want, it's especially worth using.
models.body:
"Either quit right now or put up with it forever." "If you don't buy it now, you'll never get one." "If you don't agree with me, you're on their side." Statements like these squeeze a choice down to two extremes, possibly leaving out waiting, adjusting, doing it in stages, or combining options. That's a false dichotomy.

A false dichotomy is a logical fallacy that presents options that don't exhaust the possibilities as if they were the only two choices, thereby hiding other workable paths.

It's different from a genuine either-or. Some deadlines really do mean you either apply or you don't, but before deciding you can often still check the conditions, look for alternatives, or negotiate the timing. Finding one more path isn't about never deciding. It's about not being forced to choose between two extremes someone else has drawn for you.
models.example:
You want to learn to draw, but you feel it's "either quit my job and go to art school, or never get to study it seriously." In fact, you could start with a short course, practice at a set time every week, ask a teacher to look at your work, or spend six months figuring out which direction you like and what's realistic.

These options may not replace all professional training, but they let you learn more about yourself before taking on a major cost. You might become surer that you want to switch careers, or find it suits you better as a long-term hobby. The point of a third path is to give your decision more information, not to guarantee you'll get both.
models.extra: If you want to go to a party but worry it'll run late, you can go for just the first half. If you can't afford new equipment, you can rent or borrow first. If you can't take on a whole task, you can say which part you can handle. Adjusting the scope often opens up new choices.
steps: Write down the two options you've been handed and check whether they really cover every possibility.
Try to think of one variation each in timing, scope, order, and how you take part.
Return to your real constraints, rule out what isn't workable, and then decide in earnest.
models.caution: Not every conflict has a third path. Some rules and bottom lines really are clear-cut. And once you've come up with new options, check their costs too, rather than stalling indefinitely on "there must be another way."
models.exercise: Pick a difficulty you've been describing as "either... or..." and write at least one step-by-step plan, then see whether it's actually workable.
models.brief: From a false dichotomy to finding a third path: above, a confused stick figure stands squeezed between two large doors, seemingly with only two choices; below, an observer pulls back a side curtain to reveal a workable third bridge, and the original two-way frame is opened up.

models.title: Feedback Loop
models.lead: Some results loop back and drive their own causes, so things snowball or gradually settle down.
models.when: When habits keep relapsing, work keeps piling up, a relationship gets tenser with every argument, or some progress starts building on itself, it's a great fit.
models.body:
The later you go to bed, the sleepier you are during the day. You procrastinate your way to evening, tasks pile up, and at night you're even more reluctant to sleep. It isn't a straight line; it has looped into a circle. A feedback loop is this kind of process where "the result comes back and affects the next round." Seeing the whole loop makes it easier to find a way in than just blaming one link.

A feedback loop is a process in which a system's output returns through a chain of cause and effect to influence its input; reinforcing loops amplify change, while balancing loops tend to counteract deviation.

Some loops amplify change, like getting better at practice and so wanting to practice more. Others pull deviations back, like an air conditioner easing off once it reaches the set temperature. When people say positive feedback and negative feedback, they mean amplifying versus counteracting change, not simply good versus bad. A loop that makes a problem snowball is also amplifying change.

An ordinary process only shows what happens in what order. A feedback loop adds a line that comes back: how does this result change the next action? Coming back around, it might push the change further and further, or correct the deviation. A loop doesn't automatically mean progress.
models.example:
You don't understand part of your job, so you're afraid to ask. The less you ask, the slower you are; the slower you are, the more you worry people will notice, and so you're even less willing to ask. Just telling yourself "don't be anxious" may not break the chain.

Instead, change one small link first: set aside a time each day to ask two specific questions, or ask someone to do the first pass with you. Understand a bit more and you finish a bit faster; once your progress improves, asking questions isn't so scary. You don't have to wait for every problem to disappear. Just find an entry point that can start a positive change.
models.extra: Customer support replies slowly, so users keep sending follow-ups, which creates more tickets and even slower replies. Showing clear progress updates and cutting down duplicate submissions may break the cycle better than simply pushing the support team to hurry.
steps: Draw the problem as three or four connected arrows and see whether it loops back to the start.
Find a link you can control with a small change, not necessarily the most visible consequence.
Give the change some time, then watch whether the whole loop starts to weaken or change direction.
models.caution: The arrows you draw are only your understanding and still need to be checked against the facts. Changes may be delayed, and ramping up your intervention too soon can leave you lurching back and forth. Also, don't overlook new influences from outside the system.
models.exercise: Draw a recurring frustration as a loop, and next to each arrow write "how does this affect the next step?" Circle one spot where you could make a small change this week.
models.brief: A closed loop of drawing, observing the deviation, adjusting, and coming back to the next round of drawing.

bodyDiagram.caption: On the left, two links reinforce each other's change; on the right, the returning effect counteracts deviation. Positive and negative feedback don't mean good and bad.

models.title: Law of Diminishing Returns
models.lead: Keep pushing on the same thing, and each extra bit of effort may bring back less and less.
models.when: When you keep revising, studying leaves you more and more drained, adding people isn't speeding things up, or you're unsure whether to keep investing, it's well worth using.
models.body:
When you tidy a room, the first twenty minutes of putting things away make an obvious difference. The next hour spent rearranging a few knickknacks doesn't improve much. Diminishing returns reminds us to look at the value of "doing a bit more," not just "how much I've already done." Things aren't necessarily getting worse; each additional unit of effort just brings less extra benefit.

The law of diminishing marginal returns states that, with technology and some inputs held fixed, continuing to add more of one input will eventually yield smaller and smaller increases in output.

In economics this idea comes with specific conditions, such as other resources staying the same for now. Brought into daily life, one question is already very useful: is what's really holding back the result still a lack of effort, or have time, space, method, or feedback become the limit? Pick the wrong limit and you'll just wear yourself out adding more.

It helps to separate "how much you get in total" from "how much this extra unit of input adds." The total harvest may still grow, but the extra harvest from each additional bucket of water is getting smaller. Diminishing refers to the added part, not to the total necessarily starting to fall.
models.example:
You're preparing a ten-minute talk. The first two hours, spent making the structure and examples clear, improve it enormously. The next three hours go to swapping fonts and tweaking single sentences, and then when you present, you discover the audience didn't understand a concept in the middle at all.

By now, polishing the look adds very little. Spending ten minutes having a newcomer listen to a run-through might help more. It's not that details never matter; it's that the most valuable place to invest has shifted, and you need to shift with it instead of piling more effort into the same spot just because you've already spent so long on it.
models.extra: With only one pot in the kitchen, two people cooking may be faster, but five people crowded around the stove at once tend to get in each other's way. The problem isn't necessarily that anyone isn't trying hard; the fixed space has limited what extra hands can do.
steps: After each stretch of work, ask what specifically just improved.
Find the part that's most limiting the result right now, and see whether you need a different method or more resources.
Compare continuing with this small step against resting, asking for feedback, or starting something else, and see which is more worthwhile.
models.caution: Smaller gains don't mean the total gain is negative, and they don't mean "effort is pointless." Some long-term skills need steady accumulation and don't show much in the short term. Judge with your goal and time frame in mind.
models.exercise: Pick a task you've been working on for a long time and write down the most likely improvement the next half hour would bring. If you can't say, should you invest differently?
models.brief: Added output shrinking under fixed conditions: a fixed-size vegetable plot under the same unchanging sun; a stick figure keeps adding same-sized buckets of water, each new harvest basket is smaller than the last, but the total harvest still grows.

bodyDiagram.caption: Above, each added unit of input is the same; below, the matching added harvest gets smaller each time. That doesn't mean the total harvest is falling.

models.title: Cashflow Quadrant
models.lead: Looking at where money comes from and what it requires of you tells you more than a job title does.
models.when: When you're considering a side gig, freelance work, starting a business, or changing how you work, use it to sort things out instead of rushing to change your identity.
models.body:
The Cashflow Quadrant roughly divides income roles into four: employees who draw a salary, the self-employed who mainly take on work themselves, business owners who organize a business to run, and investors who put assets to work. You can treat it as a few different lenses for looking at income, not a staircase you must climb step by step.

Robert Kiyosaki's Cashflow Quadrant distinguishes employees, the self-employed, business owners, and investors by income role. It is a framework for observing personal finances, not a complete classification of careers or wealth.

One person can be in several positions at once. What matters is how much time each income stream takes, what risks it carries, how stable it is, and what happens if you step away for a few days. The framework can raise questions, but it doesn't guarantee that any quadrant is freer or more profitable.

The four quadrants are for looking at income sources and roles side by side, not four levels you must climb in order. The same person may have both salary income and investment income, and spanning boxes doesn't automatically mean lower risk or a better life.
models.example:
You work as a designer at a company and take on personal projects on weekends. Your salary is an employee role, while the side projects have a self-employed flavor. Later you team up with partners and divide the work, so it starts to rely on a team and processes, but you also take on more responsibility for finding clients, managing, and delivering.

If you also hold investment assets, that adds another source of income and of risk. A new label doesn't automatically make life easier. Rather than envying a quadrant that looks more impressive, write down the real effort and pressure involved, and see which arrangement fits your abilities, your family, and your stage of life.
models.extra: Someone who runs a small shop is the boss in name, yet still has to open and close the doors personally every day. Whether there's a team, processes, and backup arrangements often says more about whether they have time freedom than the title does.
steps: List your income by source, not just a single job title.
For each one, add how much time it takes, what skills it needs, what you could lose, and whether it can last steadily.
When considering a change, first try to learn about the day-to-day work and responsibilities, not just the success stories.
models.caution: "Passive income" can also require a lot of upfront work, ongoing maintenance, or the risk of losses. Don't call employees inferior, and don't treat starting a business or investing as a guaranteed path that suits everyone.
models.exercise: Pick a way of earning money you envy. Besides "how much can it make," write down three questions you'd ask someone who does it: what do they do each day, what's hardest, and how do they cope when income is bad?
models.brief: Four quadrants of income roles: the four boxes show a stick figure receiving a share of coins in a company job, providing a service alone with tools to earn income, a collaborating team and process machine running continuously, and putting resources into different assets that flow back as returns.

sources.title: Rich Dad · The Cashflow Quadrant and the Four Ways to Earn Income

bodyDiagram.caption: The four boxes are different income roles, and the same person can be in more than one at a time.

models.title: Parkinson’s Law
models.lead: Give a task loose time, and sometimes it puts on weight to match.
models.when: When tasks always drag to the last minute, you keep grinding on small details, or all you have is "do it today" with no clear boundaries, it's a great fit.
models.body:
An ordinary email could be written in ten minutes, but because you've given yourself the whole afternoon, you keep reworking the opening, checking your wording, and waiting to be in a better frame of mind. Parkinson's Law sums this up as: work expands to fill the time available for it. It's an observational reminder, not a natural law that can calculate every work schedule.

Parkinson's Law is an organizational observation made by Cyril Northcote Parkinson; its core idea is that work can expand to fill the time scheduled for it.

The useful move is to give a task a reasonable timebox and first spell out what counts as done. You're not using an alarm to force yourself to work at top speed; you're cutting unnecessary expansion. When time's up, you can decide whether to extend based on quality and remaining risk, rather than using "it could still be improved" as a reason never to deliver.

Putting the same task into time containers of different lengths makes it easy to see which work is necessary and which is just detail that swelled with the deadline. But the container can't be so small that the necessary work doesn't fit; a reasonable deadline still has to respect the task itself.
models.example:
You need to write an internal note for colleagues, and the only goal is to let everyone know the problem, the proposed solution, and what needs deciding. You planned to "get it done today," but the morning goes to picking a template and the afternoon to adjusting the layout, and the core message still isn't clear.

Instead, give yourself forty minutes to write a one-page draft people can discuss, flag anything you're unsure about, and then spend ten minutes checking it. You'll likely get feedback sooner and learn what actually needs filling in, rather than polishing the unimportant parts alone all day.
models.extra: Spending a whole day sorting your inbox may never feel finished. Setting twenty minutes to handle the emails that need replies, and leaving filing for another time slot, actually lets the truly important actions happen.
steps: Before starting, spell out what done looks like, for example "one page covering three questions, ready for tomorrow's discussion."
Set a realistic timebox for the first version, and break complex tasks into several chunks.
When time's up, check what's still missing and add time only for the necessary parts, instead of tweaking endlessly.
models.caution: Shorter deadlines aren't always better. Creative work, research, and tasks that depend on others genuinely need time and a buffer, and this idea shouldn't be used to push people into unrealistic schedules.
models.exercise: For one small task, set "how finished it needs to be" and a twenty-five-minute timebox. When time's up, note what's actually missing, then decide whether to continue, rather than assuming an open-ended extension.
models.brief: A task swelling to fill its time container: two transparent horizontal time frames, one long and one short; the same rubbery task outline expands to fill each frame. In the long frame the stick figure procrastinates and fiddles with details; in the reasonably short frame it focuses and finishes.

bodyDiagram.caption: The solid part is the necessary work; the dashed part shows details that expand as the time allowed grows.

models.title: Maslow’s Hierarchy of Needs
models.lead: People need more than money and good grades: they also need security, connection, respect, and growth.
models.when: When team morale is low, you can't get yourself motivated, or you've offered plenty of rewards and still can't help someone, use it to look a little wider.
models.body:
Maslow's hierarchy of needs is often drawn as a pyramid, starting with basics like food and sleep, moving up through safety, belonging, and esteem, and ending with reaching your potential. Set the name aside, and its most useful reminder is this: to understand why someone has no energy or why they care about something, you can't focus on just one goal.

Maslow's hierarchy of needs explains human motivation through physiological, safety, love and belonging, esteem, and self-actualization needs, though these needs don't always appear in a strict, non-overlapping order.

When someone isn't getting steady rest, just urging them to grow may not be enough. When someone doesn't feel accepted, handing out a few more prizes may not fix their loneliness. At the same time, real life doesn't require "clearing" one level before you can think about the next. People whose circumstances aren't perfect can still pursue love, creativity, and meaning, and many needs often exist together.

The layered diagram helps you remember the categories of needs, but it's easy to misread as a strict level-by-level game: if a lower need isn't fully met, higher needs can't appear. It helps to keep the overlaps and cross-level links in mind; people may care about safety, relationships, and creativity all at once.
models.example:
You try to lift your spirits by setting bigger goals, but the more you write, the more frustrated you feel. Looking back at your recent life: you're often short on sleep, your work schedule changes at any moment, and it's been ages since you had a real conversation with a friend. What you're missing may not be a grand ambition, but a basic daily life and sense of connection that have both been squeezed.

First steady your sleep a bit, drop one unnecessary task, and set up a relaxing chat with someone, then look at your study and work plans again. You're not losing your drive by doing this; you're giving your drive solid ground to stand on.
models.extra: A new colleague who doesn't speak up in meetings may not lack ideas. They may simply not know yet whether they'll be laughed at for saying something wrong. A safe atmosphere for discussion and being taken seriously can sometimes help more than another round of "everyone, please be more proactive."
steps: Check several areas: whether the body is cared for, whether life is stable, whether there's support, whether there's respect, and whether there's room to grow.
Identify the most obvious gap right now, and don't just fill it with the method you know best.
Make one concrete adjustment first, then listen to your own or the other person's feedback to see whether you guessed the need right.
models.caution: This framework works best as a checklist of questions, not a fixed order that applies to everyone. Don't assume that someone with a low income has no need for beauty, ideals, or respect.
models.exercise: Next to rest, sense of security, relationships, respect, and growth, write one sentence each about how things really are lately. Pick the area that's lacking most and plan one small improvement.
models.brief: Five levels of needs that can overlap: five semi-transparent tiers or mountain layers, marked in turn with food and water, a house and shield, friends holding hands, a recognition medal, and creative stars. A stick figure can move between levels via several flexible side paths, and the dashed boundaries are not absolute gates.

bodyDiagram.caption: Several kinds of needs can connect at the same time; one level doesn't have to be fully met before another appears.

models.title: Diffusion of Innovations Curve
models.lead: Early adopters showing up first doesn't mean everyone else will follow for the same reasons.
models.when: When you're promoting a tool, organizing a new activity, introducing a workflow, or something gets good early reviews but never catches on, it's well worth using.
models.body:
When something new comes out, some people want to try it right away, some wait until friends have used it, and some won't switch until the old one breaks. The diffusion of innovations curve groups people by when they adopt, helping us see that people at different stages often have different worries and expectations.

Rogers's diffusion of innovations theory groups adopters by relative time of adoption into innovators, early adopters, early majority, late majority, and laggards, as a way to understand how innovations spread through a social system.

The percentages often shown on the chart, like 2.5% and 13.5%, are best treated as segments in a model, not numbers every industry must match. What matters more in daily life is that early users willing to put up with hassle and later users who need something stable and easy can't be approached with the same pitch.

Charts like this often show two curves. One shows how many new people join at each stage, which may start low, rise, and then fall. The other shows how many have adopted in total so far, which usually only keeps adding up. The two curves answer different questions, so don't read a falling number of new adopters as all the existing users leaving.
models.example:
You recommend a new budgeting app to your family. You love that it categorizes spending automatically and makes charts. But your parents are worried about losing their account, who to contact if something goes wrong, and how to keep their old records. You keep showing off the new features, and they still don't want to switch.

Helping them with moving their data, account recovery, and the basic steps may work better than showing off more advanced charts. Adopting later doesn't mean being stubborn; their costs, the information they need, and their situation differ from yours. The job of spreading something is to lower real obstacles, not to blame others for not being forward-thinking enough.
models.extra: A neighborhood starts taking online bookings for its facilities. People comfortable with smartphones adapt quickly, but others may need in-person help and a simple way in. Offering a transition option does more to expand real use than writing the problem off as "they don't want to learn."
steps: First learn why the people who are willing to try it now actually came, and what they're willing to put up with.
Then ask what the next group worries about most, instead of only talking to people who already like it.
Add stability, examples, migration help, and support so adopting makes sense, rather than just turning up the promotion.
models.caution: The same person may jump on new phones but be very cautious about financial tools. These categories aren't permanent personality types, and adopting late can be a good decision that fits someone's needs.
models.exercise: Pick a tool you'd love to recommend and write down three things, besides "it has great features," that others might worry about. Which of them do you already have a way to help with?
models.brief: The timing structure of innovation adoption: a smooth bell-shaped band runs left to right. At the front, a few stick figures try a new tool; in the middle, the majority follow; at the back, a few join later, with communication lines spreading through the group.

bodyDiagram.caption: The top chart shows how many new people join at each stage; the bottom chart shows how many have joined in total up to that point.

models.title: Gallup Q12
models.lead: If you want to know why a team has lost its spark, don't just ask whether everyone is "satisfied."
models.when: When team morale is low, people keep leaving, or you want to know whether the way things are managed actually helps the people doing the work, start with these questions.
models.body:
Gallup's Q12 is a tool for measuring employee engagement. As a beginner, it's enough to understand what it pays attention to: Do people know what's expected of them? Do they have the right resources? Is their contribution noticed? Do they have support, connection, and room to grow? These questions get much closer to what work actually feels like than "Why aren't you more motivated?"

According to Gallup's description of Q12, it is an employee engagement measurement tool made up of twelve items that focus on workplace conditions linked to job performance.

This page introduces that way of looking at things. It doesn't reproduce the full proprietary survey or offer an official score. For most readers, the most useful part is breaking a vague morale problem into small things you can talk about and change, rather than measuring a number and calling it done.
models.example:
A small team has been delivering more slowly lately, and the manager is planning a team outing so everyone can "get their enthusiasm back." But after a few conversations, it turns out people get different priorities every day, finish a task only to hear it wasn't the important one, and raise problems without ever getting a clear answer.

A more effective fix might be to set the week's priorities, make clear who makes the final call, and follow up on feedback. An outing can help people relax, but on its own it can't fix confused goals. What really brings people back is often everyday work that finally makes sense and can actually move forward.
models.extra: You can also use these questions to look at your own job. Instead of asking "Am I working hard enough?", ask "Do I know what matters most? Do I have the tools? Does anyone give me feedback?" Some difficulties call for asking for support, not just carrying them alone with self-blame.
steps: Ask about specific things that happened recently around goals, tools, recognition, support, and growth.
Let people know how their feedback will be used, so they worry less that honesty will cost them.
Pick one or two things you can change and act on them, then tell everyone what changed and what's still unresolved.
models.caution: Don't pressure people into giving high scores so the results look good, and don't use scores to label individuals as "disengaged." Formal use of Q12 requires following Gallup's licensing and methods.
models.exercise: Pick the point at work where you get stuck most often. Write down one concrete example and the kind of support you'd like. Turn "the environment is bad" into a request people can discuss.
models.brief: A ring of twelve nodes for conditions of engagement: around a stick figure working in a team, twelve separate small icons stand for clear direction, tools and resources, using one's abilities, recognition, care, growth, being heard, purpose, quality of coworkers, a close colleague, feedback, and learning. Only generic icons are drawn, with no original Gallup survey items and no numbers.

models.title: Flow
models.lead: You get absorbed most easily when the task is just within reach and you know what to do next.
models.when: When you're studying, practicing a skill, writing, or doing work that needs long stretches of focus, use this to set up your tasks better.
models.body:
Maybe you've had an afternoon like this: you were so focused on writing, making something, or playing a game that when you looked up, the time had flown by. Flow is that state of deep absorption. It's often linked to clear goals, quick feedback, and a good match between the challenge and your skills.

The concept of flow, introduced by Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi, describes a mental state in which a person is highly focused, fully absorbed, and experiences their actions as smooth and effortless. It is often associated with clear goals, immediate feedback, and a match between challenge and skill.

Tasks that are too easy get boring, and tasks that are too hard get frustrating. But a good match doesn't mean no effort. It means you can still see progress after the effort. You don't need to chase flow in everything. Start by adjusting your surroundings and your tasks so focus comes more easily and absorption has a better chance to happen.

Challenge and skill have to be looked at together. As your skills grow, a task that used to be engaging can become boring; push the challenge too high, and you may get anxious. Flow is more like a matching zone that shifts with conditions than a precise line that always applies.
models.example:
You've just started learning guitar and try to play a whole complicated song along with an expert's video. Half an hour later, all you feel is discouraged. Switch to one slightly challenging bar, slow it down, listen clearly for which beat is off, then join the pieces bit by bit, and it can feel completely different.

The goal gets smaller, the feedback gets faster, and the difficulty becomes reachable. You may start wanting to play a few more rounds instead of being crushed every time by how far you are from the whole song. You can't summon flow at the push of a button, but well-designed practice can cut down on unnecessary stalls.
models.extra: When you do a jigsaw puzzle, you can spot small differences in color and shape at a glance and see right away whether a piece fits, which makes it easy to stay absorbed. Vague tasks with no feedback often need you to add similar small goals yourself.
steps: Set one clear, small goal for this block of time instead of just saying "I'm going to study hard."
Adjust the difficulty: break it down if it's too hard, and add a specific challenge if it's too easy.
Cut down on notifications and switching back and forth, set up feedback that shows your progress, and leave room for breaks.
models.caution: Losing track of time isn't always valuable flow. Scrolling through videos can also make it hard to stop. Still check whether it fits your goals and whether your body needs rest, rather than just chasing the feeling of absorption.
models.exercise: Choose a specific goal for the next thirty minutes, write down how you'll know you're making progress, and then shut off the one thing most likely to interrupt you.
models.brief: A diagonal channel where skill matches challenge: on a two-axis plane with no text, a wide navy channel runs from bottom left to top right, with a stick figure inside it focused on a jigsaw puzzle. Above the channel, a person facing too much challenge looks tense; below it, a person facing too little looks bored. The channel extends upward as skill and challenge rise together.

bodyDiagram.caption: When challenge and skill match, it's easier to become absorbed, and the matching zone shifts as you grow.

models.title: Strengths-Based Thinking
models.lead: Don't spend all your energy on "what I'm bad at"; also look at how you contribute most easily.
models.when: When you're choosing what to study, assigning roles, or have long seen only the ways you fall short of others, this is well worth using.
models.body:
Strengths-based thinking encourages you to notice the abilities you use well again and again, the ones other people genuinely benefit from. Some people are good at explaining complicated things, some are good at catching what's been missed, and some can bring strangers together. Putting those abilities into the right tasks and continuing to practice them often builds confidence and results more easily than staring at your weak spots forever.

A strengths-based approach emphasizes identifying, developing, and using the abilities and resources a person or system already has in order to improve performance and growth, while managing the weaknesses that must be addressed to reach a goal.

But a strength isn't a label like "that's just how I'm made." It depends on real performance, the conditions where it works, and feedback, and it still needs basic skills underneath it. If you're good at coming up with ideas, you still need to explain and follow through. If you're good with details, you also need to keep small issues from holding up all your progress.
models.example:
On your team, you always feel behind the others because you're slow at writing long reports. But whenever a discussion gets messy, people come to you to lay out the problem clearly and sketch how things connect. Looking back at those moments, you may realize that what you're good at is sorting things out and explaining them on the spot.

You could talk it through first, record it, and then turn it into a report. You could also team up with someone who's good at writing things up, while still practicing basic writing. It's not that you never write again. You've found an entry point that suits you better, and you're using the abilities you already have to help cover what you lack.
models.extra: You're not good at speaking off the cuff in a big group, but you can write very clear questions ahead of time. You could send a discussion outline first and then gradually practice speaking up. Finding a way that works is an easier place to start than forcing yourself to become someone else first.
steps: Look back at three tasks you did well and got specific feedback on, and find what they have in common.
Ask under what conditions this ability works best, instead of just giving yourself a name for a strength.
Actively seek out suitable tasks, use tools and teamwork to support your weak spots, and build up the basics you need.
models.caution: "I'm not good at it" can't be an excuse to never learn or to hand every hassle to someone else. Strengths can also be overused; for example, being thorough can turn into endless nitpicking, so adjust to the situation.
models.exercise: Ask a friend who knows you well: "What's something you'd especially want to come to me for help with? Can you give a specific example?" Then compare the answer with your own experience.
models.brief: Using strengths while managing necessary weaknesses: one stick figure uses a long pole they're skilled with to cross a gap in a task, while a teammate fills in a small step for a weakness that must be covered. On the left, five ability bars of different lengths, with the tall bar standing out as support for the goal and the lowest, riskiest bar reinforced.

sources.title: Gallup · How to Develop and Use Your Strengths

models.title: Cognitive Dissonance
models.lead: When what we do doesn't match how we see ourselves, we often rush to explain it away.
models.when: When you regret a purchase, find yourself defending a bad decision, or notice that the more you explain the less sure you feel, this is well worth using.
models.body:
You think of yourself as frugal, but you impulsively buy something you don't need, so you say, "I'll definitely use this someday." You see yourself as reasonable, but after an argument you keep pointing only at the other person's faults. When your beliefs, actions, and self-image clash, it feels uncomfortable. That state is called cognitive dissonance.

Leon Festinger's theory of cognitive dissonance holds that when related beliefs or behaviors are inconsistent with each other, people feel discomfort and are motivated to reduce the inconsistency or change how they interpret it.

To feel better, we might change what we do, adjust what we think, or find excuses to cover up the conflict. Knowing how this works lets you pause when you're rushing to defend yourself: Am I really explaining, or am I mainly trying to prove "I couldn't have been wrong"?
models.example:
You spent quite a bit of money signing up for a course. After a few sessions, you realize the content isn't right for you, but because you're afraid to admit you misjudged it, you keep telling friends, "The more I listen, the deeper it gets." Every time it feels painful, you put in more time anyway, trying to prove the original decision was worth it.

You can separate two questions. Signing up based on the information you had then is understandable. Now that you know it doesn't fit, you can adjust. Admitting a choice didn't suit you doesn't mean you're a foolish person. Going a bit easier on your self-image makes it easier to spend your time from here on in a better place.
models.extra: You value being on time, yet you've been late several times in a row. Instead of insisting "I'm actually a punctual person," look at where your routine for getting out the door needs to change. Gradually bringing your actions closer to what you value takes less effort than guarding a perfect label.
steps: Notice the moments when you suddenly really want to prove "I'm not wrong," and slow down first.
Write down where the conflict is: between your actions and your values, or between new evidence and an old judgment.
Choose one action that actually improves things, such as stopping further investment, admitting the mistake, or revising your plan.
models.caution: When someone changes their mind, they're not necessarily making excuses; they may have new information. This concept is best for checking yourself first, not for diagnosing every disagreement from a distance.
models.exercise: For a recent choice you're not happy with, write two sentences: "At the time, I was going on..." and "What I know now that I didn't then is..." What small next step could change based on the new information?
models.brief: The tension between belief and action: a stick figure has a small tree icon in its head for protecting trees, but its hand drops paper on the ground, and two mismatched lines between them create a tangle. Below, two responses split off: one changes the behavior by putting the paper in a recycling bin, while the other just throws a thin cover over the original behavior to stand for excuse-making, marked with a small brick-red warning.

models.title: IQ vs. EQ
models.lead: Thinking clearly and handling emotions well are different abilities, and both can be practiced in concrete ways.
models.when: When you're judging yourself or others, trying to communicate better, or looking for the cause of a learning difficulty, it helps to first describe the ability in concrete terms.
models.body:
People often say someone has "a high IQ but low EQ," but that easily becomes a vague label. IQ is usually tied to standardized tests of cognitive ability, while EQ has several different theories and ways of measuring it, often involving recognizing, understanding, and managing emotions. They aren't two bars that cancel each other out, and neither can account for everything about how a person performs.

IQ usually refers to an intelligence score from standardized tests of cognitive ability, while emotional intelligence involves abilities such as recognizing, understanding, and regulating emotions; its exact definition and measurement vary by theoretical model.

In everyday life, a more helpful question is: what specific ability is actually missing here? Is the information not sorted out, or do you interrupt people as soon as you get nervous? Can you not solve the problem, or can you not say that you need help? The more specific the problem, the clearer the direction for practice.
models.example:
A coworker is quick at analysis, but whenever someone disagrees, he immediately raises his voice. People say he has "low EQ," and he feels others only want to hear nice things. The more each side thinks about it, the further apart they get.

If the conversation shifts to specific behaviors, there's a way forward: let the other person finish, restate the point of disagreement, pause when he notices himself speeding up, and then respond to the evidence. He doesn't need to start going along with everyone or give up his professional judgment. He just needs to get better at "noticing emotions and choosing how to respond."
models.extra: You're very good at understanding a friend's sadness but don't know how to manage your own anxiety. That's not a contradiction. Recognizing, expressing, and regulating emotions are different sides of the picture, and a phrase like "having EQ" can't sum them all up.
steps: Replace labels like "smart," "immature," or "low EQ" with the behaviors you actually saw.
Tell apart a lack of knowledge, a lack of practice, and too much pressure, instead of putting it all down to personality.
Pick one action you can practice, try it in a real situation, and ask someone for specific feedback.
models.caution: There's no single EQ number that can precisely determine how successful someone will be in life. Being good at pleasing people doesn't mean strong emotional skills, and being good at analysis doesn't mean someone can't care about others.
models.exercise: Turn one ability label you often use into a concrete action. For example, change "I need to improve my EQ" to "Next time I disagree, I'll restate what the other person said before responding."
models.brief: Cognitive and emotional abilities complementing each other: two areas side by side. In one, a stick figure solves a geometric puzzle to show cognitive reasoning; in the other, a person recognizes a teammate's expression and helps them calm down to show emotional skill. The two areas converge on a shared team goal.

models.title: Big Five Personality Traits
models.lead: People aren't five fixed models; each of us sits somewhere along several personality scales.
models.when: When you're trying to understand differences in how people get along, figure out working styles, or feel trapped by a personality label, use it to see people in more detail.
models.body:
The Big Five describes differences along five directions: how open you are to new things, how conscientious you are in getting things done, how outgoing you are, how agreeable you are, and how easily your emotions swing. It sounds a bit academic, but you can think of it as five separate scales, not five boxes where you have to pick one.

The Big Five is a framework that describes differences in personality using five continuous dimensions, openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, and neuroticism, each of which also includes more specific facets.

Everyone has a position on each scale, along with more detailed patterns. Being introverted doesn't mean you can't communicate, being agreeable doesn't mean having no principles, and being highly conscientious doesn't mean you'll never procrastinate. Personality describes fairly stable tendencies; it can't replace actually watching how someone behaves in a specific situation.

The five dimensions are like five independent scales, not five boxes where you can only pick one. A person can be fairly outgoing, fairly conscientious, and very open to new things all at once; one trait standing out doesn't let you guess everything else.
models.example:
You notice that big parties wear you out, so you decide you're "not suited to any job that involves communication." But looking back, you're very good at understanding people's needs one-on-one, and you can give a clear presentation when you've prepared ahead.

That difference suggests you may not enjoy sustained, intense social stimulation, but you're not lacking in communication skills altogether. Knowing your tendencies can help you plan rest, choose how you communicate, and practice the skills you need, instead of shutting doors early because of a label.
models.extra: A very detail-oriented person can be quite laid-back on vacation, and someone who loves a crowd still needs time alone. People have tendencies, but they're also shaped by their goals, relationships, and how they feel that day. Don't expect every behavior to match the label.
steps: Change "I'm that kind of person" to "In certain situations, I tend to..."
Look at behavior across many situations and over a longer time, not just one test or one mood.
Use what you learn about your tendencies to improve your surroundings and teamwork, while leaving room for practice, change, and exceptions.
models.caution: Tests have error, and self-ratings can be swayed by how you feel at the moment. "Neuroticism" is the standard term for one dimension, not an insult or a diagnosis. Personality results shouldn't be used to judge someone's worth or limit their opportunities.
models.exercise: Rewrite one label you use for yourself as a sentence with context: "When..., I usually..., but when..., it can be different." See whether it's closer to the real you.
models.brief: Sliders for five continuous personality dimensions: five horizontal sliders side by side, each with its knob at a different position, forming a unique profile next to a single stick figure. The ends of each slider use simple icons for exploring vs. familiar, planned vs. spontaneous, social vs. solitary, cooperative vs. competitive, and calm vs. sensitive.

bodyDiagram.caption: Each of the five dimensions has its own position, and only together do they show how a person differs.

models.title: DISC
models.lead: Four styles can help you talk about communication, but don't use four letters to box a person in.
models.when: When a team wants to talk about differences in communication but can't say exactly where things clash, use it as a starting point, then come back to specific behaviors.
models.body:
DISC is common in workplace training. It usually sums up behavioral preferences in directions like Dominance, Influence, Steadiness, and Conscientiousness, though the names differ between versions. You can think of it like this: some people want the conclusion first, some need interaction, some value stability, and some care more about evidence and details.

DISC is a set of tools and frameworks that describe behavioral style using dimensions such as Dominance, Influence, Steadiness, and Conscientiousness or Compliance; the scales, naming, and interpretation may differ between providers.

Its practical value is mainly in opening a conversation: "How would you like me to hand this over to you?" It isn't for taking a test and then declaring who's fit to lead or who's naturally bad at teamwork. The quality and purpose of different assessments need to be judged separately, and it shouldn't be treated as the same body of evidence as all personality research.

The four boxes can help you remember behavioral tendencies side by side, but don't take that to mean everyone fits neatly into one fixed box. Different tools may define and score things differently, and the same person can act differently in different tasks or relationships.
models.example:
You're giving a coworker an update and start with twenty minutes of background, while they keep asking, "So what do you need me to decide?" You think they're impatient; they think you're not getting to the point. If you open with the conclusion and the decision you need, then add background and data afterward, it's much easier to connect.

This kind of adjustment doesn't even require knowing which letter either of you is. Simply asking "Do you prefer to see the summary first or the process first?" is often more accurate. The model offers a set of possible preferences; only a real conversation can confirm what this person needs this time.
models.extra: The same person may want to decide quickly on a familiar task but want to read more before tackling something new. Preferences shift with the situation, so don't refuse to hear what someone needs right now just because "that's not what the test said."
steps: Treat style words as guesses, and check them with the other person through real questions.
When communicating, try adjusting the order, level of detail, and pace, and see whether it makes working together easier.
Turn the preferences that work into small agreements you both can follow, rather than just remembering a color or a letter.
models.caution: Don't assume someone is timid because they were labeled the "Conscientious type," and don't let a "Dominant type" overstep boundaries because of their label. Labels can't replace standards of behavior and mutual respect.
models.exercise: Ask someone you often work with: "When I give you information, what part is the hardest for you?" Turn their answer into one specific adjustment and try it next time.
models.brief: Four behavioral tendencies that shift across situations: four quadrants show small stick-figure scenes of pushing ahead directly, interacting and expressing, providing steady support, and checking carefully. An ordinary person in the center connects to the different scenes with dotted lines, showing that behavior changes with the situation.

bodyDiagram.caption: The four behavioral tendencies can be used side by side as a reference, and the same person acts differently in different situations.

models.title: Six Thinking Hats
models.lead: In a discussion, agree first on which angle you're using right now, so one person's idea isn't instantly shot down by another.
models.when: When brainstorming keeps getting interrupted, meetings have everyone talking past each other, or you keep flipping between excitement and worry on your own, this works well.
models.body:
Six Thinking Hats uses six colors for different focuses: the white hat looks at facts, the red hat shares feelings, the black hat looks for risks, the yellow hat looks at value, the green hat thinks up new ideas, and the blue hat organizes the discussion. You don't need to wear actual hats. Everyone just needs to know what this round is mainly about.

Edward de Bono's Six Thinking Hats is a parallel thinking method that uses six hats, white, red, black, yellow, green, and blue, to organize information, feelings, risks, value, creativity, and process management respectively.

What makes it useful is that the team no longer splits permanently into "optimists" and "fault-finders." Everyone thinks up ideas together, then checks them together, giving creativity some room to grow and giving risks an official time to be raised. Every angle has its place, so no one has to talk over others to be heard.

The six hats work best laid out side by side, so the same group can take turns switching viewpoints. They aren't six fixed personality types, and they don't have to be used in the same order every time; the order should serve what the current discussion needs.
models.example:
A few friends are planning a trip. As soon as someone suggests camping, another asks what happens if it rains, a third starts adding up costs, and someone else just thinks it sounds exhausting. Everyone is raising something important, but because the angles are all mixed together, the conversation starts to feel like everyone is against each other.

You could start with the white hat to confirm the dates, number of people, and budget, then use the red hat for everyone to say what they really want the trip to feel like. Next, come up with a few options and compare their benefits and risks, and finally decide who will look into what. The order can change. The point is to separate tasks that were tangled together, without rushing to label each person's position.
models.extra: It works for decisions you make alone too: first write what you know, then your feelings, then the benefits and risks, and finally some alternatives. Splitting them into columns is often much clearer than having them all argue in your head at once.
steps: Start by stating what this round is meant to solve, and use the blue hat to handle timing and next steps.
Focus on one angle at a time; when it's time for ideas, write them down first and save risks for their agreed slot.
Before wrapping up, sum up the facts, disagreements, unknowns, and who's responsible, rather than leaving just a pile of interesting ideas.
models.caution: You don't have to go through all six hats in a fixed order every time. An urgent problem might call for looking at risks first, and if the facts are unclear, gather information first. This framework helps you organize a discussion; it won't prove that a plan is right.
models.exercise: For one small decision, write six lines: facts, feelings, risks, benefits, new ideas, next step. Write just one sentence per line and see which angle you'd been missing.
models.brief: Six viewpoints on the same problem: in the center is a small bridge that needs repair, and around it the same group of stick figures takes turns trying on six hats of different colors. Next to the white hat is an icon for observing data, the red hat a heart, the black hat a crack for risk, the yellow hat a sun for benefits, the green hat a sprout for creativity, and the blue hat a loop for organizing the process.

models.title: Hanlon’s Razor
models.lead: Before deciding someone is out to get you, remember they may simply not have noticed, not have understood, or not have done it well.
models.when: When a vague action irritates you, you want to confront someone right away, or you keep feeling there's a hidden meaning in what people say, use this to leave a little room for checking.
models.body:
A friend doesn't reply to your message, and you feel ignored. A coworker leaves you off an email, and you feel deliberately shut out. Hanlon's Razor reminds us that, without clear evidence, we should first consider carelessness, gaps in information, ability, and circumstances, instead of jumping to the most hurtful explanation of someone's motives.

Hanlon's Razor is a rule of thumb about attribution: when carelessness, misunderstanding, or limited ability can fully explain a behavior, you shouldn't assume malice first without evidence.

This isn't about always making excuses for other people. It's about separating "what happened" from "why they did it." The first can usually be checked; the second is often just a guess. Checking first often spares you some of the torment of imagining the worst, and makes it easier to find what really needs to change.
models.example:
You send a coworker a long message asking them to confirm something, and they don't reply for a whole day. The more you think about it, the angrier you get, convinced they don't take you seriously. Later you find out the message got buried among hundreds of group chat messages, and they thought you were just sharing materials, so they never noticed the question at the end.

You could send the thing that needs confirming as a separate message, give a deadline, and agree that important tasks need a reply. If it keeps happening even after a clear agreement, then note the impact and talk about responsibility. Not assuming malice the first time is not the same as never setting boundaries.
models.extra: A noisy neighbor might not know the walls are thin, or might have been told already and not care. Explaining the specific impact and making a request first, then seeing how they respond, usually tells you more than starting off by yelling through the wall.
steps: Write down the observable facts, such as "The confirmation message I sent yesterday hasn't been answered," and strip out guesses about motives.
Check whether the other person saw it, understood it, knew the deadline, and was able to do it.
Adjust your judgment based on how they respond and whether it keeps happening, and act when it's time to change the process, discuss responsibility, or protect yourself.
models.caution: When there's clear deception, threats, or ongoing harm, you don't need to keep covering the evidence with a charitable assumption. Even without malice, there can still be consequences; responsibility and boundaries don't disappear just because "it wasn't on purpose."
models.exercise: Take a recent moment when you thought "they did it on purpose" and rewrite it as one sentence of fact with no motive. Then list two possible reasons and one question you could gently ask to check.
models.brief: Shifting from a single guess of malice to checking the evidence: an unanswered envelope with no text sits in the middle. On the left, a stick figure's head holds a pale gray, spiky shadow of malice as an assumption; on the right are icons for ordinary explanations: a missed inbox, a busy clock, and a disconnected network cable. A magnifying glass leads to a checking conversation, and a shield at the edge shows that ongoing harm still calls for boundaries.

models.title: Anchoring Effect
models.lead: The first number you see can quietly pull on every judgment that follows.
models.when: When you're looking at discounts, discussing a quote, estimating how long something will take, or notice yourself adding and subtracting around a number that came up first.
models.body:
You only meant to buy an ordinary backpack. First you see one priced at $300, then one at $120, and suddenly the second one feels "pretty cheap." But if the first one you'd seen cost $30, $120 might have seemed expensive. The backpack didn't change; the reference point that got into your head first did.

The anchoring effect is the tendency, when estimating or judging, to rely too heavily on the first number or reference point encountered, and to adjust insufficiently after receiving further information.

That first reference point works like a ship's anchor, pulling later estimates in its direction. It might come from an original price, a number someone else names first, or even an answer you guessed offhand. It's not that we ignore new information completely; sometimes we just don't adjust enough.

Once you understand anchoring, you can first find yourself an independent basis: what do similar things usually cost, what do I actually need, and what's the most I'm willing to pay? Then, when you see the number the other side offers, it's easier to tell whether you're comparing value or just comparing how far you've moved from the first number.

When comparing, you can keep the item and conditions fixed and change only the reference point that appears first. The item is the same on both sides, yet how expensive or cheap it feels can differ; that difference tells us to check the starting point, not that the item itself has changed.
models.example:
You want to buy a desk, and the page says "Was $299, now $119." You feel like you're saving a lot and even start worrying about missing out. But you haven't checked whether anyone ever actually paid the original price, what similar desks usually sell for, or whether the size fits your room.

Cover up the "$299" for now, list what you need in terms of size, material, and sturdiness, and then compare three products with similar features. Finally, ask: if the page just said $119, with no crossed-out original price, would I still want to buy it? You can still buy it; the reason just comes from your real needs and comparison, not from being pushed along by an original price.
models.extra:
When a team discusses how long a task will take and the first person says "about two days," everyone after tends to add or subtract around two days. But if the task has unfamiliar parts, that starting point may have no basis at all.

You can have everyone write down their own estimate and reasoning independently first, then break the task down together and check how long similar past work took. Judging independently first doesn't guarantee the influence disappears completely, but it cuts down on everyone just circling the same number.
steps: Write down your own needs, the basis for your estimate, or your acceptable range before you look at the number the other side gives you.
Find a few pieces of truly comparable outside information and check the conditions, rather than just comparing price tags.
Set the first number aside for now and ask again: looking only at the facts, how would I judge this?
models.caution: A number that shows up first isn't necessarily worthless. Well-founded past prices, real time records, and a clear budget can all be reasonable reference points. The anchoring effect reminds us to check whether a reference point is reliable, not to deliberately choose the opposite. A judgment is shaped by many factors, so you can't conclude someone was anchored just from the final price.
models.exercise: Find something that strikes you as "a great deal" or "too expensive," and write down which number you're comparing it with. Cover that number up, then estimate again using three real conditions.
models.brief: A stick figure tries to make an independent estimate on a measuring scale, but its wrist is held back by a heavy anchor attached next to the initial price tag; in the distance, a magnifying glass points to comparable items.

bodyDiagram.caption: Both rows show the same item on the same scale. Light dots mark different starting reference points, and dark dots mark the estimates pulled by them; the positions only illustrate the direction of the influence and are not experimental data.

models.title: Framing Effect
models.lead: Say the same thing a different way, and how we feel and choose can shift with it.
models.when: When you're reading promotional material, comparing options, or talking about risk, or when you notice that a different wording clearly changes how you feel.
models.body:
"Nine out of ten people finished" and "one out of ten people didn't finish" describe exactly the same result. But the first makes you notice success, and the second makes you focus on failure. The framing effect is about how the way something is presented shapes how we understand it.

The framing effect is the phenomenon in which the same problem, or equivalent options, lead to different judgments and choices depending on how they are presented, which aspect is emphasized, or how they are described.

We can never see information completely apart from how it's expressed. What goes in the headline, whether benefits or costs come first, whether you use head counts or percentages: each can pull attention to a different place. The problem is that we may believe we're choosing based on the full facts when we've actually seen only the side that was emphasized.

One practical habit is to restate the same information from the opposite direction: how many finished, and also how many didn't; what you'll gain, and also what you'll pay. Putting both versions side by side usually helps more than just swapping in a nicer-sounding word.

A side-by-side comparison should use the same group, the same denominator, and the same standard, changing only where the emphasis falls. That way you can see it's the angle of description that changes, not the data or conditions being quietly swapped out.
models.example:
One course description says: "Of last term's 100 students, 90 completed every exercise." You feel the course would be easy to stick with. Another page says: "Of last term's 100 students, 10 didn't complete every exercise." Now you start worrying you won't keep up.

If both are about the same group of people and the same definition of "completed," the two sentences don't contradict each other. First write them together as "90 completed, 10 didn't," then ask how much time the exercises take, what counts as completing them, and whether those students were in a situation like yours. It's fine to notice how the wording makes you feel, but the decision needs these concrete details.
models.extra:
You're planning a weekend activity and say it "takes up two hours." Your friend feels their downtime is being squeezed. Say instead that "the rest of the time is still free," and it sounds more relaxed. If the activity takes the same time either way, you've only moved the spotlight.

When you talk it over, lay out the whole plan: two hours for the activity, travel time on top, and which hours are free. The point isn't to pick the wording that wins the other person over, but to let both of you decide while looking at the same schedule.
steps: Translate the description back into concrete people, numbers, time frames, and conditions, and check first whether the two versions really are equivalent.
Restate it from the complementary angle: write down both who finished and who didn't, both the gains and the costs.
Decide based on your own goals and the full set of conditions, not just the first feeling one sentence gives you.
models.caution: Two statements that sound alike don't necessarily say the same thing. With "$15 a month" versus "$180 a year," you still need to check whether you must pay annually and whether you can cancel; if the conditions differ, it's more than a framing difference. The framing effect also doesn't mean every way of putting things is manipulation. Clear, complete presentation genuinely helps people understand.
models.exercise: Pick one description that excited or worried you. Write down the side it emphasizes and the side it leaves out. After rewording it, did the facts change? How much did your feeling change?
models.brief: The same plate of ten dots is highlighted through two different viewing frames: the left frame focuses on nine plain dots, the right on one brick-red dot. Two stick figures react differently, while the underlying facts stay the same.

bodyDiagram.caption: Two bars with the same total and the same split. The top one emphasizes the finished part, the bottom one the unfinished part. What stands out changes, but the underlying numbers don't.

models.title: Outcome Bias
models.lead: A good result doesn't prove the decision behind it was a good one.
models.when: When you're reviewing a project, judging someone else's decision, or tempted to copy everything after one success or scrap the whole process after one failure.
models.body:
One person checks the weather and leaves extra time, yet still arrives late because of a sudden traffic shutdown. Another person doesn't prepare at all but gets there on time because the roads happen to be clear. If we only look at who made it, we may call careful preparation useless and mistake a lucky break for a good method.

Outcome bias is the tendency, once a result is known, to let how good or bad it was shape our judgment of the decision's quality, without properly separating the information available at the time of the decision from chance factors that came up afterward.

To judge a decision, start by going back to that moment: What information could you have known? Which risks were foreseeable? Did you reasonably compare alternatives? Then look separately at why the outcome happened. That way you can tell whether the method needs improving, or whether you prepared sensibly and still ran into something unexpected.

Results obviously matter. It's just that a single success or failure can rarely explain the whole process on its own. Looking at process and outcome together keeps you from blaming everyone for bad luck, and from rewarding a risky approach just because it happened to work.

A four-square grid can split "Was the process sound?" and "Was the outcome good?" into two separate axes. A sound process can still meet a bad outcome, and a poor process can get lucky for a while. When you evaluate, check both axes rather than collapsing them into one.
models.example:
You and a coworker each prepare an online presentation. You test your equipment ahead of time and have backup files ready, but the internet cuts out during your session. Your coworker doesn't test anything, and their setup happens to run smoothly. In the review, someone says, "See? All that preparation was pointless."

A more useful review checks things separately: Did your testing cover the problems you could foresee? Did your backup plan help once the connection dropped? What sensible improvements could you make next time? Your coworker's smooth run doesn't mean it's fine to skip the checks from now on. The outcome of one event can offer clues, but it can't turn all your preparation into a waste.
models.extra:
A team uses the same sensible hiring process to pick two new people. Later, one does well and the other doesn't. Looking only at results, it's easy to think one decision was brilliant and the other a complete mistake.

Start by comparing what was known at the time, the criteria used, and whether any checkable issue was missed, then use their later performance to improve the process. If the same kind of mistake keeps showing up, change the criteria; don't wave away a recurring signal by calling it "just luck."
steps: Before you look at the final result, write down the goal, evidence, alternatives, and known risks at the time of the decision.
Separate the controllable factors in the outcome from the accidental ones, and check whether anything was missed that could have been spotted at the time.
Keep the parts of the process that worked, fix the parts that can be improved, and keep watching whether results over many rounds support your original judgment.
models.caution: Telling luck apart from skill is hard, and "the result doesn't reflect the process" can't be used to dodge responsibility. Knowingly ignoring a major risk is different from preparing as well as you could and then hitting an unforeseeable change. Problems that keep recurring are evidence too. Use them to update your process instead of brushing them off as chance.
models.exercise: Think of something that recently went well or badly. Cover up the ending, list three reasons behind the decision at the time, and ask: if the ending had been the opposite, would I suddenly judge those same reasons differently?
models.brief: A carefully checked plan and a plan that skipped its checks each pass through a wheel of uncertainty; the first lands on a disappointing result while the second happens to get a star. A stick figure uses a magnifying glass to look back at the original decision process.

sources.title: Baron and Hershey · Outcome Bias in Decision Evaluation

models.title: Theory of Constraints
models.lead: How fast the whole line moves often depends on its tightest spot.
models.when: When work is piling up, upstream and downstream steps keep waiting on each other, or everyone is busy but the total amount finished still won't go up.
models.body:
In any workflow, everyone being busy doesn't mean more gets finished in the end. The front end keeps taking on tasks, only one person in the middle can review them, and the people downstream are left waiting. Pushing the front end to go faster may just make the pile waiting for review even taller.

The bottleneck idea usually refers to the Theory of Constraints: with the system's goal in mind, identify the key constraint limiting overall output, coordinate the other parts around it and improve it, then keep checking where the next constraint appears.

It reminds us to ask first where the whole thing is stuck. Not which person looks slowest, but which limit is actually blocking final delivery. The limit might be a machine, staffing, scheduling, approval rules, or even the team's agreement about priorities.

Once you find the constraint, first cut down the time it loses to interruptions and wasted work, and only then think about adding capacity. Other steps need to cooperate too, rather than creating more backlog just to look efficient themselves. After one bottleneck improves, a new limit may show up somewhere else, so this is a process of adjusting round after round.

A flow diagram lets you see incoming volume, processing capacity, and where things wait, all in one place. The real bottleneck caps overall throughput. Speeding up the steps before or after it on their own won't necessarily increase final delivery, and may only add to the waiting.
models.example:
A small coffee shop can take 40 orders an hour and pack 40 drinks an hour, but its espresso machine can make at most 20 cups an hour. Speeding up the register alone won't let the shop hand out 40 coffees an hour; it'll just leave more customers standing in line.

Start by making sure the machine never runs out of supplies, that cleaning and shift changes are well planned, and that remakes are kept to a minimum. When taking orders, tell people the wait time, and consider pre-orders or capping orders in a given time slot. If the demand persists, then weigh whether another machine is worth it. Keep watching after the changes, too: if packing starts to back up, the bottleneck may have moved.
models.extra:
You're publishing articles. Writing can produce three a day and layout can handle four, but review can only get through one a day. If the team tells everyone to "go a bit faster," you may just end up with more half-finished pieces.

First make sure everything sent for review is complete, handle similar issues in batches, and set clear review hours so the reviewer doesn't have to keep chasing people with questions. Judge the improvement by how many articles actually get published and how long things wait, not by counting how much each person has on their plate.
steps: Map the process from start to final delivery, noting each step's capacity, waiting time, and backlog.
Find the step that truly limits the overall goal, first cut its idle time, rework, and unrelated interruptions, and have the other steps work around it.
After improving it, check whether overall delivery went up, then look for the constraint again instead of treating the old bottleneck as the permanent answer.
models.caution: The step that takes the longest isn't necessarily the bottleneck; judge it alongside demand, how much can run in parallel, and where things actually pile up. Some processes have several constraints, along with fluctuations and quality requirements, so don't chase speed at the expense of safety and quality. The Theory of Constraints is much broader than "find the slowest person and hurry them up." What matters is the goal of the whole system.
models.exercise: Sketch four to six steps of something you do often. Mark where things most often queue up, then write down one small change that could reduce the waiting or rework at that point.
models.brief: Process channels of different widths, with task blocks piled up only in front of the narrow central section. A stick figure adjusts the central gate while the other sections arrange themselves around it, emphasizing overall flow.

models.title: Goodhart’s Law
models.lead: Fixating on making the number look good can pull you away from what you actually wanted.
models.when: When the numbers you're measured on keep improving but user experience, quality, or real ability isn't keeping pace, or when people start working out how to "hit the target."
models.body:
You want to build a reading habit, so you make a rule: fifty pages a day. At first, the number reminds you to open the book. Later, to meet the quota, you start picking pages with less text and flipping past anything hard to understand. The page count looks great, but your understanding hasn't grown with it.

Goodhart's Law warns that when a measure originally used to track a goal is heavily relied on as a target for evaluation or control, the ways people adapt and optimize for it can weaken its ability to represent the real goal.

Page count was only ever one clue about how your reading was going. Once rewards, evaluation, or your own sense of satisfaction are all tied to it, behavior can start to revolve around the number. Goodhart's Law prompts you to check: when this number improves, is the thing I actually care about improving too?

The problem isn't that every metric is useless; it's treating a stand-in signal as the end goal. Use numbers to spot changes, then judge them together with quality, real feedback, and any side effects, so the metric helps you observe instead of defining everything that matters.

A side-by-side comparison should give "how the number looks" and "the real effect" a place of their own. The two may improve together or drift apart. The point is to check how they're connected, not to assume every number is lying.
models.example:
A customer support team wants to help users more promptly, so it measures "tickets closed per person per day." Before long, some people close complicated issues too early or ask users to submit them again. The number of closed tickets goes up, yet users' problems may still be unsolved.

Start by spelling out the real goal: users' problems get properly resolved without overly long waits. Then look at whether issues were resolved, whether people had to ask for help again, user feedback, and handling time, and spot-check specific cases. Adding a few more numbers isn't a cure-all either; keep watching how people adapt to the new rules.
models.extra:
If you treat "how many thinking models I've read" as your learning score, you might quickly mark all 87 entries as read but be unable to say how even one of them applies to real life. The read count records what you've browsed; on its own, it can't prove how much you understand.

Keep the progress bar, but add a small action that's closer to the real goal: pick a model and write an example from your own life, explain it again a few days later with the page closed, or note how you adjusted after actually using it once. What really helps is the change in how you think.
steps: Write the real goal in one sentence, then explain why your current metric represents it and what it might miss.
Think about how someone could improve the number without improving the goal, and actively look for loopholes or likely side effects.
Check the metric against quality feedback and specific cases, allow the rules to be revised, and keep watching whether behavior is being pulled off course.
models.caution: It isn't a law of physics saying every metric must fail, and it isn't an argument against recording data. Whether a metric is useful depends on the goal, the incentives, the setting, and how it's checked. The popular line "when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure" is a later, widely circulated paraphrase; it works best as a reminder to check for risks.
models.exercise: Pick a number you often chase, such as pages read, streak days, or tasks completed. Write down the real goal, describe one situation where the number improves but the goal doesn't, and think of one way to check for it.
models.brief: A stick figure chases an ever-rising gauge bar while a curved arrow veers away from the real bullseye beside it; another stick figure uses a magnifying glass to check the distance between the metric and the goal.
