models.title: Implementation Intentions
models.lead: Decide in advance: when this happens, I'll do that.
models.when: When your goal is clear but you keep forgetting to start, hesitate in the moment, or keep reacting in a way you don't want in the same situations.
models.body:
"I'll exercise more from now on." "I'll read when I have time." They sound sincere, but when evening comes, you often don't know at what moment to begin. Implementation intentions take a wish one step further: instead of only saying what you want to achieve, you agree ahead of time on exactly what you'll do in a specific situation.

An implementation intention is a way of planning that turns a goal into action by linking a specific situational cue to a corresponding behavior in advance, forming an "if this situation comes up, then I'll do this action" plan.

For example: "After dinner, once I put my dishes in the sink, I'll change my shoes and go out for a ten-minute walk." There's a cue you can recognize and an action that's clear enough. When the moment comes, you don't have to decide on the spot whether to do it today or what to do first. Getting started has a clearer way in.

The same approach can handle obstacles: "If it's still raining when it's time to go out, I'll do a suitable activity at home instead." The plan isn't meant to control every change, just to arrange ahead of time the step where you're most likely to get stuck.

The flow diagram starts from a recognizable cue and connects it to one concrete action. If there's a common obstacle, a simple backup path can branch off. What matters in the diagram is "when to start and what to start with," not turning your whole life into a complicated flowchart.
models.example:
You want to read every night, but you always forget about it while scrolling your phone. You could write the plan as: "At night, after I brush my teeth and put my phone on the charger in the living room, I'll read two pages by my bed." Leave the book somewhere within reach, and two pages makes it easy to know when you're done.

After a few days, you notice you often brush your teeth too late, so you change the cue to right after you've cleaned up from dinner. The plan has to fit your actual life. If you keep failing at the same point every day, check whether the conditions and the action suit you before blaming yourself for lacking willpower.
models.extra:
In meetings, when someone suddenly objects, you tend to jump in right away with explanations. You could decide in advance: "If I hear an objection, I'll first note down one specific concern the other person has, then check my understanding in one sentence."

This doesn't guarantee the conversation will go smoothly, and it won't make your emotions vanish instantly, but it gives you an alternative action you can practice. After the meeting, see whether you did it, then decide whether the action needs to be made simpler.
steps: Pick a small goal you genuinely want to pursue, and pinpoint the specific moment where you most often get stuck.
Write it as "If this cue happens, I'll do this action," making sure the cue is recognizable and the action doable.
Get the things you need ready and try it for a while, adjusting the cue or action based on what you record, and set up a simple backup plan if needed.
models.caution: It can't replace actually wanting the goal, or having the ability, time, and resources. A cue that's too vague, an action that's too big, or a goal that simply doesn't suit you can all make the plan fall through. Don't write dozens of rules at once, and don't decide it doesn't work because you missed it once; look at whether the setup is reasonable and what the real obstacles are.
models.exercise: Finish this sentence: "If ________, I'll ________." Shrink the second half down to a small action you can do today, and check that what you'll need when the cue hits is already prepared.
models.brief: A stick figure stands beside a clear doorway-threshold cue and naturally follows a navy arrow toward an open book and a desk lamp; where an obstacle appears, a simple backup path leads to a small doable step.

bodyDiagram.caption: First spot the cue, then do one concrete action and check it's done. The dashed line below shows a backup action you can plan ahead for when a common obstacle comes up.

models.title: Retrieval Practice
models.lead: Close the book, try to say it yourself, then see what you missed.
models.when: When you've finished a book or course and want to check whether you really understand it, when you're getting ready to review, or when you notice you "get it" while looking but lose it once the material is gone.
models.body:
When you read a passage, you may feel you understand every sentence. Then you close the page, try to explain it, and suddenly can't put it clearly. That doesn't necessarily mean you're bad at learning. "It looks familiar" and "I can pull it out of memory" were never the same thing.

Retrieval practice, also called active recall, is a way of studying in which you pull previously learned information out of memory without looking at the material for the moment, then strengthen your learning by checking it and getting feedback.

Retrieval practice adds a step of pulling things out: before looking at the answer, try to explain, jot down the key points, or solve a problem, then go back to the material to check. It helps you find where something only looks familiar, and it turns the act of retrieving into part of the practice.

It doesn't have to feel like a stressful exam. Start by recalling one small section, allow yourself to leave things out, then fill in whatever you forgot or got wrong. What matters is genuinely trying to retrieve and using feedback to correct yourself, not reciting the original word for word on the first try.

A cycle diagram can separate two steps: first trying to recall without the material, then opening it to check. Use what you find to correct the next round. It's not about reading the answer while telling yourself you've already memorized it.
models.example:
You've just read the entry on sunk cost and think "money already spent shouldn't decide your next step" is easy. Close the page and try to answer: What counts as an investment you can't get back? Should refundable fees be taken into account? When is it still reasonable to keep going?

Write down your answers, then open the entry to check. If all you remembered was "don't stick with it," fill in what you missed: what you should compare are the benefits and costs from now on, and if something still has future value, it can make sense to continue. A few days later, explain it again using a different everyday example. That tests your understanding far better than staring at one familiar sentence.
models.extra:
You're learning a work procedure, and rereading the instructions makes it feel very familiar. In a safe practice setting, close the instructions, write out the key steps first, then try to run through it once, and finally check for gaps and mistakes.

If the task involves danger or something important, don't skip the official checklist just to do it "from memory." Practicing to learn and doing the real thing have different requirements, and a checklist is still a tool for reducing mistakes.
steps: After finishing a small chunk, close the material for now and bring the content back to mind using questions, a blank page, or your own words.
Open the material again to check, pinpoint what you left out, misunderstood, or couldn't support, and correct it right away.
After some time, retrieve it again with different questions or situations, combining spaced review with application so you don't just memorize fixed answers.
models.caution: Retrieval practice isn't rote memorization, and it can't replace first understanding the material, getting needed explanations, and hands-on practice. If you haven't understood the content at all, go back and build the basics, then narrow the scope of your practice. Don't keep repeating mistakes you haven't checked. It's fine for practice to be a little hard, but you don't need to treat suffering as proof that learning is working.
models.exercise: Close this page and write, in your own words, the difference between retrieval practice and rereading, plus one thing you could practice today. Then come back, check, and fill in one thing you missed.

models.title: Nonviolent Communication
models.lead: Stating facts, feelings, needs, and a request clearly gets heard more easily than an accusation.
models.when: When you want to voice frustration, ask for what you need, or sort out who does what, or when you notice conversations turn into mutual blame the moment they start.
models.body:
"You're always so irresponsible." Once that's said, the other person may start explaining or hitting back before they've even figured out what happened. Nonviolent Communication tries to help us break that sentence apart: what specifically happened, how I feel, what I care about, and what one thing I'd like the other person to do next.

Nonviolent Communication is a communication framework developed by Marshall Rosenberg. It emphasizes separating observation from evaluation, identifying feelings and needs, and making specific requests the other person can respond to, while also understanding the other person's feelings and needs.

For example: "Both of the last two times, the materials came in later than we agreed. I'm feeling a bit anxious, because I need time to check them. Next time, if you can't make it, could you let me know in advance roughly when you'll send them?" This doesn't guarantee the other person will agree, but it gives both of you a starting point for discussing the facts and the arrangements.

The four common parts are observations, feelings, needs, and requests. Keep observations as specific as possible, describe your own emotions as feelings, explain what you value as needs, and make the request a doable action. These are clues to help you sort out what you mean, not a fixed formula to recite every time you speak.

When you're listening, you can also try checking: "Are you worried there isn't enough time, and want to confirm what matters most first?" This is a question, not a claim about what the other person really thinks. Expressing yourself and understanding the other person take back-and-forth checking.

A four-step diagram can separate facts, emotions, needs, and actions. Follow it to check whether blame has slipped into what you're saying, and leave a path back for the other person to respond. The diagram isn't meant to turn a request into an order the other person must carry out.
models.example:
You and a coworker agreed the materials would be sent by 3 p.m., but both of the last two times they arrived after 4. You were about to say "You always hold everyone back," but instead you say: "The last two times we agreed on 3, and I got the materials after 4 both times. I have to finish a summary by 5, so I'm feeling a bit stressed right now. I need at least half an hour to check things. Could you tell me today which parts are already done?"

Your coworker might say they've been handed a more urgent task at the same time. From there, you could talk about sending the key parts first, splitting the work differently, or setting a new time. If they can't manage it for now, you can still explain your time constraints and bring the coordination issue to whoever is responsible. Swapping blame for a request doesn't mean giving up on responsibility or boundaries.
models.extra:
A family member has the TV on loud at night, and you're tempted to say, "You never think about me at all." Instead, start with the specific situation: "The sound is coming into the bedroom right now. I haven't fallen asleep yet and I'm getting a bit irritated. I'd like some quiet to rest. Would you be willing to turn it down or use headphones?"

They may just want to relax and might not realize the sound carries. The two of you can find something that works together. If you say "I feel like you're selfish," adding "I feel" doesn't change that what follows is still a judgment about the person. Keeping judgments separate from your own emotions makes it easier for the conversation to continue.
steps: Start with specific things that can be checked, and drop words like "always" and "never" as well as judgments about character.
Identify your own feelings and needs, then make one specific, doable request in a single sentence.
Listen to the response and check your understanding, then discuss what's workable; if it can't be done, state your boundaries clearly or ask for help coordinating.
models.caution: It isn't a technique for getting others to do what you want, and it doesn't require you to always be gentle, suppress your anger, or reveal private matters. A request leaves room for the other person to say no or negotiate; a threat dressed up in nicer phrasing is still a threat. In situations of ongoing harm or clear danger, protecting yourself, putting some distance in place, or seeking support matters more than getting through all four steps.
models.exercise: Write down one complaint you've really wanted to make lately. Circle the facts and the judgments separately, then add your feelings, the need you care about, and one small request that's open to discussion.
models.brief: Two stick figures talk on equal footing. A spiky speech bubble is set down, and a rounded bubble crosses a small bridge supported by icons for observation, feeling, need, and request; a thin arrow pointing back represents listening to the response.

models.title: Ladder of Inference
models.lead: Between "what I saw" and "what kind of person I've decided they are," you may have skipped several steps.
models.when: When you've quickly drawn conclusions about someone's attitude, keep failing to agree about the same issue, or want to find out at which step the two of you started understanding things differently.
models.body:
You message a coworker and don't hear back for ages. First you notice "no reply." Then you think, "Is he ignoring me on purpose?" Then you decide, "He doesn't care about working together at all," and finally you resolve not to offer him help next time. A single observation has turned, step by step, into a judgment about a person and an action of your own.

The Ladder of Inference is a framework for examining reasoning. It describes how people select from observable information, assign meaning, add assumptions, and then form conclusions and beliefs and take action.

The ladder slows down a process that usually happens very fast. At the bottom is the information you can observe. Moving up, there's which information we picked, how we interpreted it, and what assumptions we added; only above that come conclusions and actions. Different people seeing the same event can reach different conclusions because they picked and interpreted different things.

When you use it, the point isn't to accuse others of "making things up in your head." It's to check yourself first: "What do I actually know? Which step was a guess? What other explanations are there?" Saying these steps out loud gives the other person a chance to fill in what you didn't know.

It points in a different direction from second-order thinking. Second-order thinking looks forward at what an action will lead to; the Ladder of Inference looks back at how you got from the information to your current judgment. One examines what comes next, the other examines how you interpreted things, and you can use them together.

In a ladder diagram, observable information sits on the lower rungs, with interpretations, assumptions, and conclusions above. Climbing up, it's easy to mistake guesses for facts; checking back down helps you find the gaps. The rungs show how reasoning connects, not status or ability.
models.example:
In a meeting, you present a proposal, and a coworker frowns and glances at their phone. You decide they disagree and don't respect the work you put in, so your explanation gets more and more rushed. Back on the fact rung, all you can be sure of is that you saw a frown and a glance at a phone. You can't directly know what they're thinking.

You could ask first: "Is there anything about this plan that concerns you?" Maybe they really do disagree with the proposal, or maybe they were reading another urgent notification. Once you get an answer, discuss the specific issue. You don't need to assume in advance that you misread them; just let your conclusion be checked rather than taking a facial expression as proof of an attitude.
models.extra:
A client says, "Let me think about it," and the salesperson decides the price must be too high and immediately offers a big discount. But what the client is actually unsure about might be the delivery time, the terms of use, or whether they need the service at all.

First write the fact down as "the client hasn't decided yet," then ask: "What else would you like to confirm?" You might discover information you need to add, or you might confirm that price really is the obstacle. Checking your inferences isn't stalling. It keeps you from acting on a reason you haven't verified.
steps: Write down what you can directly observe and verify, and strip out judgments about motives, character, and intentions first.
Trace your interpretation back: which information did I pick, what assumptions did I add, and what other possibilities are there?
Gather more information with neutral questions and explain how you arrived at your understanding, then adjust your judgment and actions based on the response.
models.caution: It's a tool for reflection and conversation, not a precise map of a brain that must climb one rung at a time; real understanding can jump back and forth. Don't use it to demand that others keep proving their feelings, either. When there's clear evidence and repeated behavior, deal seriously with responsibility and boundaries instead of forever pushing the problem back to "maybe it's just a misunderstanding."
models.exercise: Pick a recent judgment that's been bothering you and draw three columns: "what I saw," "my interpretation," and "information still missing." Using only the first column, write one question that could check the situation.

models.title: Johari Window
models.lead: The me I picture and the me others see may not be the same picture.
models.when: When team members' assessments of each other differ widely, "I thought you knew" keeps coming up, or you want useful feedback or to explain what you need to work well together.
models.body:
You think you're an active participant in meetings, but your coworkers feel you often cut them off. You think people know you're not good at speaking on the spot, but you've never actually told them. Some gaps in communication come from the two sides having different information, not just from someone expressing themselves badly.

The Johari Window is a framework for understanding how people see themselves and each other. It sorts information by "Do I know it?" and "Do others know it?" into an open area, a blind spot, a hidden area, and an unknown area, as a way to talk about feedback and appropriate self-disclosure.

The Johari Window uses two questions to divide information into four boxes: Do I know it? Do others know it? What both sides know is the open area. What others see but I don't realize is the blind spot. What I know but haven't told others yet is the hidden area. What neither side knows yet is the unknown area. "Others" here should be understood within a specific relationship and setting.

Listening to specific feedback can turn part of a blind spot into something both sides know. Sharing a bit about your situation can likewise move part of the hidden area into the open. New tasks or experiences can also bring to light abilities and limits no one had noticed before.

A bigger open area isn't automatically better, and it certainly doesn't mean handing over all your privacy. Where it really helps is in letting you check: what do we need to know about each other for this collaboration, and which information gaps could be closed in a suitable way?

In the four-square grid, the columns can show whether you know something or not, and the rows whether others know it or not. Feedback can move things from the blind spot into the open area, and voluntary sharing can move things from the hidden area into the open area. The arrows show information shifting; they aren't a demand to empty every box.
models.example:
You think you're always good at chiming in with ideas during discussions. One day a coworker gives you feedback: "Twice just now, I hadn't finished talking and you jumped in. After that I didn't really feel like going on." That's different from "You're too pushy," because it describes a specific behavior and its effect, which makes it easier for you to look back on.

You could first check which two moments they mean, then ask them to use an agreed signal to remind you next time. After that, try pausing for two seconds and making sure the other person has finished before you speak, and see whether things improve. Feedback helps you discover a possible blind spot, but you still need to verify the situation rather than treat one observation as a final verdict on who you are.
models.extra:
On a new project, you're often called on without warning to give a demo. When you're underprepared, you get very nervous, but you've always acted as if it's no big deal, so everyone assumes the arrangement suits you fine. You can choose to share only the part that's relevant to working together: "If I could know the demo topic a day in advance, I'd be able to prepare more thoroughly."

This is sharing your work needs to a suitable degree; you don't have to explain all your personal reasons. Once the information each side has is closer, the arrangements are likely to fit better. You still get to decide what you'd rather keep private and whom you're willing to tell.
steps: Pick a specific relationship and setting, and sort out what relevant information you know and what the other person knows.
Invite the other person to describe specific behaviors and their effects, and share only information you're willing to share that's relevant to working together.
Check the feedback, agree on one small adjustment, then see whether later interactions improve, without rushing to label yourself or anyone else.
models.caution: It isn't a personality test, and it can't accurately measure how many blind spots someone has. Other people's feedback can also be one-sided or biased, so check it against facts and across different situations. A hidden area isn't the same as lying; keeping things private and declining inappropriate questions are normal boundaries. And the unknown area isn't a blank space for freely guessing at what's going on inside someone else.
models.exercise: Pick a collaborator you trust and ask: "In our most recent project together, what's one specific thing I did that helped you? What's one thing I could adjust?" Listen all the way through before checking anything, then try one small, fact-based suggestion.

models.title: Circle of Competence
models.lead: Know what you truly understand, and where you still need help.
models.when: When you're about to assess an unfamiliar proposal or take on a new task, or you notice that you can talk a lot about something but can't clearly explain the key reasons.
models.body:
A friend asks you to look over a proposal. You can follow the data analysis in it, but you don't know much about visual design. You'd love to give a complete answer, but "I can understand every sentence" and "I'm able to judge whether it holds up" aren't the same thing. The circle of competence reminds us to first sort out where our judgment reliably ends.

The circle of competence is a framework for the limits of your judgment. It emphasizes identifying the areas you can reliably understand and evaluate, and distinguishing what you're merely familiar with, what you've truly mastered, and what you don't yet understand.

Inside the circle isn't every topic you enjoy. It's where, through study, practice, and feedback, you can explain the key reasons, spot common problems, and also know what evidence might overturn your judgment. Having heard a lot of jargon or seen a few cases doesn't necessarily put you inside it.

Outside the circle isn't off-limits forever, either. You can start by checking with someone experienced, practice on lower-risk tasks, and notice whether you're increasingly able to judge on your own. Growth isn't drawing your boundary with more and more confidence; it's letting your understanding and your actual ability expand outward together.

A circle diagram can distinguish the parts where you can explain your reasoning, the edge that still needs checking, and the parts you don't understand yet. The distances are just a way of organizing; they aren't a score of your ability, and they don't mean things outside the circle can never be learned.
models.example:
You're good at organizing spreadsheets and checking data, and your team asks you to review a new product proposal. You can point out that the statistics use inconsistent definitions, and explain that a certain conclusion lacks data to back it up. But you've never done usability testing, and you're not sure whether users will understand the pages.

You can say plainly: "I can check the data side, but the user experience needs a trial with users or a look from someone experienced." Then join one round of testing and note how your original judgment differed from what actually happened. Dividing things up this way makes your input more reliable and gives you a way in to learn, without having to pass verdict on everything just to seem thorough.
models.extra:
You often recommend apps you've used for a long time to friends, but the first time you come across an unfamiliar tool, a nice-looking interface isn't enough to promise it'll work well. Try it on one or two real tasks first, check its limitations, and then separate "what I've actually tested" from "what I'm guessing for now."

Stating your limits doesn't make your advice less valuable. If anything, it makes it easier for others to know what they can rely on directly and what they need to verify themselves.
steps: Break the problem down, marking the parts you've done or verified yourself and the parts you've only heard about or are guessing at.
For unfamiliar parts with a big impact, first get more information, ask for advice, or hand them to the right person, rather than covering everything with a confident attitude.
Pick one small task to practice on, record your judgment beforehand and the feedback afterward, and use actual results to gradually adjust the boundary of your competence.
models.caution: The circle of competence isn't a way to label yourself "not good enough," and lack of interest isn't proof that you don't understand something. Experience goes out of date, so judgments inside the circle need checking too. It's about "Do I understand this well enough?" while the circle of control is about "What can I directly decide or influence?" Don't merge the two into one circle.
models.exercise: Pick something you'll soon need to give an opinion on and make three columns: "can explain why," "needs checking," and "needs help." For the last column, write down one person you could ask or one source you could check.
models.brief: A stick figure stands at the edge of a familiar mechanical-puzzle workspace, using a magnifying glass to inspect the parts they've mastered; outside the circle are dashed-line unfamiliar devices and entry points for asking for help and learning, emphasizing judgment ability rather than the scope of control.

models.title: Margin of Safety
models.lead: Don't plan things down to the last minute; leave a little room for surprises.
models.when: When your estimates might be off, things keep changing, or a single mistake would be hard to fix, and yet your plan has almost no slack.
models.body:
A meeting starts at ten. Your map app says the drive takes thirty minutes, so you leave at nine-thirty. Hit a few more red lights or struggle to find the entrance, and a plan that was "just enough" suddenly isn't. A margin of safety asks a simple question: if your estimates aren't quite right, does your plan still have room to adjust?

A margin of safety is a buffer kept between estimated demand and available resources, or between expected conditions and the maximum that can be handled, to reduce the impact of estimation errors and unexpected changes.

It can be extra time, a backup copy of a file, someone who can step in, or a system that isn't running at full capacity all the time. Keeping a buffer costs something, but it lowers the chance that a small change instantly becomes a big problem.

The point isn't to double everything. It's to look at how big the possible error is, how serious the consequences of a mistake would be, and whether you could fix things in time. A routine small task and an arrangement that can't be redone may need very different margins.

In the comparison diagram, the expected demand stays fixed while different limits for available resources are drawn. The gap between demand and the limit is the margin. It's preparation that comes at a cost, not proof that any arrangement is completely safe.
models.example:
You're giving an online presentation. You expect to talk for fifteen minutes, but you've only been given a fifteen-minute slot, and your slides exist only as an online file. If logging in takes a bit longer or someone asks a question, you'll easily run over. And if the connection is shaky, your materials might not even open.

Start with a practice run to see how long it really takes, then leave some time for questions and switching screens. Prepare an offline copy and a shorter version too. These buffers target specific risks; they're not endless extra time. Afterward, note where you actually used the margin and adjust next time, instead of always adding a fixed percentage by gut feeling.
models.extra:
Say a small team plans its week and fills every person's every day completely. One unexpected request for help will throw off the whole week. Leaving a few time slots for surprises, or making it clear who can take over key tasks, makes the plan more flexible.

If the margin runs out week after week, look at the workload and the process. Don't dress up long-term overload as an occasional surprise.
steps: List the key estimates your plan depends on, and find the ones most likely to be off and most costly if they are.
Add a reasonable margin or backup plan for those spots, and weigh it against the cost of keeping the buffer.
Afterward, check what you actually used and where the surprises came from, then adjust your margin; for problems that keep coming back, change the process itself.
models.caution: More buffer isn't always better: idle resources and waiting have costs too. A margin of safety can't replace necessary checks, and it can't guarantee there's no risk. For professional equipment, structures, or safety standards, follow the professional requirements; adding a bit of slack on your own is no substitute for the rules.
models.exercise: Pick one thing you have planned for tomorrow and write down: "Which estimate does it depend on most?" "What happens if that's a little off?" "What room can I leave?" Then choose one low-cost preparation that actually targets the risk.

models.title: Bayesian Updating
models.lead: When new evidence comes in, re-estimate instead of digging in your heels.
models.when: When you need to make a judgment under uncertainty and you run into new information, a test signal, or someone else's assessment, and want to know whether you should change your mind.
models.body:
Say you think it's unlikely a machine will break down today. When the alarm goes off, of course you check more carefully. But how often the alarm goes off by mistake, and how often it stays silent during a real fault, also affect how much that signal should count. A new piece of information can't instantly turn "unlikely" into "definitely."

Bayesian updating is the process of combining a prior probability judgment with the relative likelihood of new evidence to arrive at an updated probability according to Bayes' rule.

Bayesian updating puts several questions together: How common was this situation to begin with? If it's true, how normal would it be to see this evidence? If it's not true, how easily could the same evidence show up anyway? Together, these decide how much your judgment should shift.

In everyday life you can't always work out exact numbers, but you can build a habit: keep your starting point, check how strong the evidence is, and say what you adjusted. When better information arrives, you can keep revising.

The flowchart keeps both the original starting point and the new evidence, rather than drawing new information as a button that spits out a conclusion. The better the evidence tells possibilities apart, the more reason there is to adjust, and later information can still flow into the process.
models.example:
Let's use some made-up numbers for a machine alarm. Out of 100 uses, about 10 involve some kind of fault. The system raises an alarm in 9 of those 10, but it also raises a false alarm in 18 of the other 90 normal uses. So of the 27 alarms, about 9 are real faults, roughly one in three.

That doesn't mean the alarm is useless: the chance of a fault has risen from one in ten to about one in three, which is worth checking further. But hearing that "it catches 90% of faults" doesn't mean every alarm has a 90% chance of being a real problem. These numbers only illustrate how conditional probability works; they aren't the real performance of any device.
models.extra:
Suppose you're judging whether a new coworker knows a certain kind of work. One shaky answer might just be nerves. Explaining things clearly across several separate tasks and delivering steadily gives you information of a different weight.

Don't count the same rumor repeated by three people as three independent pieces of evidence. First look at where the information came from, then decide how much it should change your original judgment.
steps: Write down your original judgment and why, using the relevant overall picture as a starting point where you can.
Check how common the new evidence would be under different explanations, watching for false alarms, misses, and information that's just repeated.
Adjust your judgment accordingly while keeping the uncertainty; keep checking on important questions and let later evidence revise it again.
models.caution: If the probabilities you put in are unreliable, careful calculation won't make them accurate. Independence, how representative the sample is, and changing conditions can all affect the result. This isn't decoration for slapping a number on any personal opinion. When information is thin, honestly stating your range and assumptions is more useful than an answer precise to several decimal places.
models.exercise: Pick a judgment you recently changed and write down: "Why did I think that at first?" "Which new evidence changed my mind?" "Could that evidence have another explanation?"

models.title: Base Rate Thinking
models.lead: Before judging the case in front of you, look at how things usually go for similar cases.
models.when: When a success or failure story has won you over, you're estimating how long a project will take, or you feel very sure about something, but haven't yet looked at similar cases.
models.body:
You hear about someone who improved fast with a certain study method, and you immediately feel it'll work for you too. Before you jump in, it's worth asking: how many people have tried it, how long do they usually stick with it, and what share of them didn't get results? One great story only shows you one spot in the bigger picture.

Base rate thinking means that before judging an individual case, you first consider the overall proportion of an outcome in a relevant reference group and combine it with case-specific information, rather than relying only on a vivid story or a few local features.

A base rate gives your judgment a starting point. It doesn't ask you to treat everyone as the same. It asks you to learn the usual outcome for similar situations first, then think about what real differences this case has and whether they're enough to change your expectations.

Choosing the right comparison group matters too. Beginners and experienced people, or simple and complex tasks, may not belong in the same group. Data that looks precise but comes from different conditions isn't much more reliable than a story.

The tree diagram starts from a comparable whole, branches into different outcomes, and then locates the current case. Drawing the full denominator first makes it easier to spot missing information than just zooming in on the most eye-catching case.
models.example:
You're scheduling a new project and simply feel that "we're well prepared this time, so it shouldn't run late." Suppose your team has had 20 similar projects in the past and 14 of them ran late. Then you need to look seriously at the reasons behind that common pattern, rather than brushing it aside on this round's confidence alone.

Next, ask: Is the scope smaller this time? Are there fewer outside dependencies? Have past review bottlenecks been dealt with? If things really have changed, you can adjust your estimate. If the only difference is that everyone feels motivated, the track record is still worth keeping as a warning. These numbers are a teaching example and don't represent any real team.
models.extra:
You see a beautiful user showcase for a new tool and want to move your whole workflow over. Besides this one case, look for how it works for users with similar workloads and skills: completion rates, common obstacles, and why people stop using it.

If there's no comparable data, admit the uncertainty first and try it on a small scale. Base rate thinking helps you ask the missing questions; it doesn't require you to make up an overall rate when there's no information.
steps: Define a truly comparable group first, checking that the tasks, timing, experience, and conditions are close.
Find the overall results, paying special attention to the denominator, the cases that didn't succeed, and how the data was collected.
Then check what well-supported differences the current case has, and explain why you're keeping or adjusting your starting point.
models.caution: An overall rate isn't any one person's destiny, and changing circumstances can make old data obsolete. Unreasonable groupings, tiny samples, or keeping only the success stories can all mislead you. It works well with Bayesian updating: base rates remind you to find a starting point first, and Bayesian updating goes further into how new evidence changes the probability.
models.exercise: Pick a case that recently got you excited and ask three more questions: "How many people tried this in total?" "How do similar people usually do?" "What verifiable differences does this case have?"

models.title: Expected Value
models.lead: Look at how much you might get together with how likely it is.
models.when: When there are several possible outcomes and you can reasonably estimate how often they happen, or you want to compare average time, cost, and benefit across repeated choices.
models.body:
One route is usually fast but occasionally gets stuck in long traffic jams. Another is a bit slower but more predictable. Looking only at the best case makes you overly optimistic; looking only at the worst case can make you ignore how things normally go. Expected value gives you a way to compare possible outcomes together with how likely they are.

Expected value is the average of a random outcome weighted by the probabilities of its possible values; in the discrete case, you multiply each outcome by its probability and add the results.

It doesn't predict which number will show up next time. It describes the average level under given probabilities. An average may never actually happen even once: if a trip takes either ten minutes or thirty-five, the average could still be fifteen.

So expected value is one part of a judgment. It should be weighed alongside variability, the worst possible loss, whether the choice can be repeated, and your own limits. An arrangement that's good on average may not suit a situation where you can't be late or can't afford a single failure.

The branch diagram shows "likelihood" and "size of outcome" separately, then looks at each branch's weighted contribution. The length of a branch doesn't equal its probability, and the average isn't a promise of where the next result will land.
models.example:
Suppose Route A takes 10 minutes 80% of the time and 35 minutes 20% of the time. The average is 10 x 0.8 + 35 x 0.2 = 15 minutes. In this simplified example, Route B always takes 18 minutes. Comparing averages alone, A is shorter.

But if you must arrive within 20 minutes, A still has a 20% chance of going over, while B meets the requirement under these assumptions. Your choice depends not only on the average but also on whether being late is acceptable. The numbers are only for demonstrating the calculation and don't represent any real road.
models.extra:
When planning a task you do over and over, you can compare how long each method takes and how often it needs redoing. A method that's faster each time but often has to be redone may not have a lower average cost once you factor in the chance of rework.

If you can only roughly estimate the probabilities, try the calculation with a few reasonable ranges and see how sensitive the conclusion is to your assumptions, rather than pretending you know the odds down to the percentage point.
steps: List the main outcomes and their probabilities, making sure they cover the cases you need to consider and add up to 1.
Multiply each outcome by its probability and add them up, checking that the units match.
Then check variability, extreme consequences, and real-world limits, instead of deciding only by which average is bigger.
models.caution: An average isn't a guarantee, and it isn't necessarily the most common result. Bad estimates, outcomes that depend on each other, and conditions that change over time can all make the calculation less useful. A loss you can't bear can't simply be canceled out by average gains elsewhere. For one-time decisions with big consequences, also consider what you can tolerate and whether it can be undone.
models.exercise: Pick an everyday plan with some uncertainty and list two or three possible outcomes with rough probabilities. Calculate the average once, then write down one real-world limit that would make you not choose by the average.

models.title: Leverage Points
models.lead: Don't just keep cleaning up the consequences; look for what you could change so problems happen less.
models.when: When the same kind of problem keeps happening, the fixes keep getting busier, or you suspect people are being pushed along by certain rules or ways information is arranged.
models.body:
Your team chases the same kind of task every day. You send more reminders, which seems to help briefly, but a few days later things are back to how they were. Maybe the problem isn't too few reminders. Maybe it's unclear who owns the task, priorities that conflict, or nobody being able to see what the next step is waiting for.

A leverage point is a place to intervene in an interconnected system where a change can have a large effect on the system's overall behavior, such as its information flows, rules, feedback structures, or goals.

Leverage points remind us to shift our attention from a single consequence to the structure that produces it: who gets what information, how responsibility is assigned, what behavior the rules encourage, and what the whole system is actually pursuing. Adjusting these can change the course of things more than endless patching.

But "high impact" doesn't mean "easy to change." Some rules need many people to agree, and some adjustments have unexpected effects. Even after finding a cause that sounds fundamental, you still need to explain how the change would work, test it, and watch what happens.

The structure diagram connects the surface problem to information, rules, and feedback. Mark the relationship you plan to change, then draw the expected effects and possible side effects. These arrows are explanations to be tested, not a proven chain of cause and effect.
models.example:
Your team's shared documents are always out of date, and every week people ask, "Where's the latest version?" Reposting the file in the group chat over and over only solves the search problem for the moment.

Another approach is to set one fixed place to find things, name an owner and an update date for each document, and make old links point to the current version. These changes alter how information flows and who's responsible for keeping it up. Try it with one type of document first and see whether repeat questions, wrong versions, and upkeep effort go down before deciding whether to roll it out.
models.extra:
Meetings often run long, and the host keeps urging everyone to talk faster. Look deeper at the structure, and it might turn out that nobody said in advance which decision needs to be made or who should bring what materials, so time gets spent filling in background on the spot.

Try writing down the meeting's goal, the needed materials, and how the decision will be made ahead of time. It won't guarantee every meeting gets shorter, but it's more likely to uncover why meetings keep running over than blaming everything on how fast one person talks.
steps: Map out the people, information, rules, and feedback involved, and find how the problem keeps getting produced.
Propose one structural change that could shift behavior, and spell out which relationship it works through to affect the outcome.
Start in a small area that's negotiable and observable, check the overall effect and side effects, then decide whether to keep it or change it.
models.caution: This isn't a promise that one button will fix everything. Systems have delays, interactions, and outside changes, and a local improvement can shift the burden onto someone else. The theory of constraints focuses on the bottleneck limiting the system's current overall output, while leverage points look more broadly at where to intervene to change how a system behaves.
models.exercise: Pick a small problem that keeps coming back and write down two things: "What I keep patching up" and "What arrangement keeps bringing it back." Then propose one rule or information change you could test on a small scale.

models.title: Network Effects
models.lead: Some tools become more or less valuable as the right people join them.
models.when: When you're choosing a collaboration platform, running a community, or trying to understand why a service only works well once the relevant people are on it.
models.body:
A messaging app can have great features, but if the people you need to reach aren't on it, it can be pretty inconvenient. Once your coworkers, friends, and partners can all be reached in one place, its usefulness to you changes. That change doesn't come just from feature upgrades. It also comes from who's in the same network as you.

A network effect is when the value a product or service provides to a user depends on the number and makeup of other users who use it or something compatible with it.

What matters isn't just the total number of people, but whether new people bring useful connections. A huge group that has nothing to do with your work isn't necessarily worth more than ten well-matched partners. Some services also need different roles to be present together, such as people who provide something and people who use it.

Network effects can also hit limits: when too many people join, more noise, crowded resources, and lower quality can all hurt the experience. So check how new connections change real usefulness, rather than treating "more users" as automatically "better."

The network diagram shows participants as nodes and useful relationships as links. It can highlight the links a newcomer brings while distinguishing irrelevant, congested, or duplicate links. More nodes don't automatically mean everyone benefits.
models.example:
You and two partners are picking a project communication tool, and at first you only compare feature lists. Then you find that another tool, though it has fewer features, lets your collaborators join directly, so you don't have to copy messages back and forth every day, and it's easier to confirm materials in one place.

Now you can compare: Are the people you really need to work with willing to join? Are permissions and formats compatible? How high are the costs of switching and managing it? The convenience a network brings has to be weighed against these costs, and lots of people using something is no reason to ignore your specific needs.
models.extra:
Picture an item-swap community with only people posting items and nobody who needs them. There may be plenty of listings, but few swaps actually happen. Bringing in the right participants and improving search and matching is what can raise the value for existing members.

If adding more people only brings ads and irrelevant posts, adjust the rules and how things are organized. Numbers are a clue; whether the connections are useful is the question closer to the goal.
steps: First spell out which connections users actually get value from, and which roles need to take part.
Check whether new participants improve contact, matching, or available content, rather than just looking at the total headcount.
Also watch for noise, congestion, compatibility, and switching costs, and keep checking whether the network's growth improves the real experience.
models.caution: Not every product has a clear network effect, and "the more connections the better" is no substitute for analysis. Network effects, word of mouth, and economies of scale are different ideas: word of mouth is about how people hear of something, economies of scale are about how average cost changes, and network effects are about how other people's participation affects its value to me.
models.exercise: Pick a group or tool you use often and write down three kinds of connections that make it valuable to you. Then think: who could be added to make it more useful, and what kind of added information would only become a burden?

models.title: Incentives
models.lead: To understand why people act the way they do, look at what the rules are rewarding.
models.when: When what the rules say doesn't match how people actually behave, cooperation keeps relying on a few people carrying extra weight, or you're about to introduce rewards or performance reviews.
models.body:
A team says it values collaboration, but when it comes to praise and handing out opportunities, it only looks at how much each person gets done individually. If some people then don't want to spend time helping coworkers, it's not necessarily a lack of team spirit. They may simply be responding to the rules that actually count.

Incentives are the arrangements of rewards, costs, and rules that shape behavioral choices, including material gain, recognition, responsibility, relationships, and the consequences of actions.

Incentives aren't just bonuses. Being noticed, being trusted, avoiding hassle, protecting your reputation, and having room to choose can all shape behavior. The same arrangement can also affect different people differently, so you can't assume how people will respond based only on what the designer hopes.

The purpose of seeing incentives clearly is to bring the rules more in line with the behavior you really want to encourage, and to see who bears the costs and who gets the benefits. It's not about seeing everyone as only chasing their own interest, and it's certainly not about finding buttons to manipulate others.

The flowchart starts with the behavior you hope for, then the actual consequences, and then how people might choose next time. Marking who bears the costs and who gets the rewards makes it easier to see whether the rules are steering behavior toward the goal.
models.example:
A team wants members to share what they've learned in a timely way, but sharing takes preparation, presenting, and answering questions, and none of that time counts as part of the workload. People have to squeeze it into their free time, and over time the sessions become harder and harder to keep going.

First confirm that members actually need it, then make room for it during work hours, recognize specific contributions, and cut down on repeated prep. After a trial, see whether sharing really helps others and whether the presenters' load has grown. The change isn't just one more word of praise; it's making effort and reward, and responsibility and resources, line up better.
models.extra:
A family says it wants the kids to enjoy reading, but after every book the only question is what prize they'll get. Outside rewards can sometimes help kids get started, but they can also gradually shift attention to the reward.

You could talk together about what they like to read, let them choose for themselves, and share what they read, rather than turning every book into piecework. There's no fixed reward plan that works for everyone; you need to watch how they actually respond and how things change over time.
steps: Write down the specific behavior you want to encourage, and who has to spend time and bear the cost for it.
Check which current rules actually bring rewards or hassle, and whether they line up with the goal.
Make small adjustments in a transparent, negotiable way, and watch participation, quality, sense of fairness, and long-term side effects.
models.caution: People are also shaped by values, habits, abilities, and relationships, so not all behavior can be explained as calculation. Rewards can crowd out existing interest, and punishment can lead people to hide things. Goodhart's law focuses on how a measure can become distorted once people chase it; incentives cover a broader range, including consequences that aren't expressed as numerical targets.
models.exercise: Pick something you wish others were more willing to take part in and write down: "What do they have to give?" "What do they get?" "What do the current rules actually encourage?" Then find one place you could adjust fairly.
models.brief: Two stick figures complete a shared structure, and specific useful contributions are linked to star-shaped recognition; a magnifying glass checks the link between behavior and consequences, with hints of cooperation and inner motivation nearby.

models.title: Comparative Advantage
models.lead: Dividing up work isn't just about who's faster; it's also about what each person gives up to do it.
models.when: When a team or household needs to divide up work and one person seems faster at everything, or you want to understand why people with different abilities can still help each other.
models.body:
A coworker is fast at making reports and fast at making posters. Should you hand him both kinds of tasks? Not necessarily. Besides who's faster, you need to look at how much of the other kind of output he gives up by spending his time on one, and how the team can best be combined.

Comparative advantage is the relative advantage a person or organization has in carrying out an activity at a lower opportunity cost; it differs from absolute advantage, which means doing it faster or with fewer resources.

Comparative advantage uses opportunity cost to compare ways of dividing work. Even if someone is slower at both tasks, they may give up relatively less on one of them, which makes them a good partner for it. That word "relative" matters. It's not simply about finding the job each person likes most or feels most confident in.

Real teams also have to consider quality, learning, handoffs, deadlines, and fairness, so you can't lock everyone into roles based on a single timesheet. Comparative advantage offers one angle of analysis. It doesn't mean everyone should only ever do what they're best at right now.

In the matrix, rows are people and columns are tasks, with quality and units kept consistent first. Raw times only show who's faster in absolute terms; comparative advantage also compares the same person's two tasks to work out how much of the other output is given up.
models.example:
Here are some made-up times. Alex takes 1 hour for a report and 3 hours for a poster; Sam takes 4 hours for a report and 5 hours for a poster. Alex is faster at both, but a report costs Alex only one-third of a poster, while it costs Sam four-fifths of a poster. So Alex has the comparative advantage in reports. Flip it around, and Sam has the lower opportunity cost for posters.

If you need two reports and two posters, having each person do one of each takes 13 hours of work in total; having Alex do both reports and Sam do both posters takes 12. This is only a simplified comparison of total work hours. When things actually get finished also depends on whether work can happen in parallel, handoffs, and quality, so "fewer work hours" doesn't automatically mean "delivered sooner."
models.extra:
Two roommates splitting chores shouldn't just say, "You're better at everything than me, so you do it all." They can compare how much time and effort each of them spends on cooking, tidying, and shopping, then talk about how to divide and trade.

Even if one arrangement saves more time, both people should have a say, a chance to practice, and reasonable rest. If the efficiency gains only benefit one person, the arrangement may not last.
steps: With quality kept roughly equal, list the resources and time each person needs for each task.
Compare how much other output is given up for each task, separating relative opportunity cost from absolute speed.
Bring handoffs, deadlines, fairness, and learning needs into the discussion, then try the division of work and review it.
models.caution: This depends on tasks, resources, and opportunity costs that can be compared, so you can't apply fixed ratios to every kind of work. Professional quality, coordination costs, learning over time, and power differences can all change the arrangement. Comparative advantage isn't an inborn identity either, and it should never be used to justify making someone carry work they don't want to do over the long term.
models.exercise: Pick two people and two comparable tasks, and write down rough times and quality requirements. First see who's faster, then separately work out how much of one task is given up to do the other, and see whether the conclusions match.

models.title: Present Bias
models.lead: When planning, you're happy to wait; when the moment arrives, it's much harder to say no to feeling good right now.
models.when: When your plans for the future keep getting derailed by a bit of comfort in the moment, or you notice you're eager before it's time to act but keep changing your mind once the moment comes.
models.body:
On the weekend, as you plan next week, reading twenty minutes a day seems perfectly reasonable. Then one evening, the book is right there, but the phone is easier to pick up, and you think, "I'll start for real tomorrow." The plan hasn't become worthless. It's just that the ease of right now and the hassle of getting started suddenly weigh more than they did a few days ago.

Present bias is the tendency, compared with choosing between two points that are both in the future, to give disproportionate weight to immediate benefits or costs once one of the outcomes becomes available right away.

Present bias isn't just any choice to get something sooner. A key clue is that your preference changes as "now" gets closer: while both options are still in the future, you're willing to wait, but once one is available immediately, you change your mind.

Once you understand this, you can blame yourself a little less and plan ahead a little more. Put helpful actions within easy reach, cut down the steps to get started, and give yourself some quick feedback, so your plan doesn't depend only on willpower in the moment.

The comparison diagram separates two moments: "still planning" and "choosing right now." The focus is on whether attention and choices change once something becomes immediate, not on painting anyone who chooses enjoyment as doing something wrong.
models.example:
On Sunday you decide that on workdays you'll spend five minutes sorting your materials when you get home, then watch videos. Thinking about it Sunday night, it doesn't seem hard. On Monday you get home tired; a video offers instant relaxation, while the benefit of sorting feels like it'll only show up later, so the order keeps getting flipped.

The day before, put the materials to sort in a set spot, ask yourself to handle just one small batch first, and agree that you'll rest once it's done. Also notice whether the problem is really that the temptation in front of you is stronger, or that work has left you overly exhausted. Setting up your environment in advance can help, but a real need for rest deserves care too.
models.extra:
You promise to start next week on a small task you've put off for ages. While it's still far off, that seems fine, but when the day comes, you think, "Just give me one more day." If nothing has clearly changed, that habit of pushing things back again and again is worth noticing.

Shrink the goal to one specific first step, set up a cue in advance, and see a bit of progress once you're done. If the task itself is unclear, you lack the resources, or it's no longer worth doing, just change the plan. Not every delay needs to be blamed on one bias.
steps: Note what you care about when planning versus when it's time to act, and check whether your preference changed even though conditions didn't.
Lower the cost of getting started in advance by preparing the cues, items, and first step, so the behavior that serves your goal is easier to do.
Build in some quick feedback and rest and watch the results; if needed, change the task, resources, or goal instead of just demanding more of yourself.
models.caution: Choosing rest and enjoyment now isn't necessarily irrational, and future benefits may be uncertain too. Present bias isn't a complete explanation for all procrastination and changes of mind, and it's certainly not a label for judging other people's self-control. Any commitment you set up in advance should be moderate and understandable, and you should avoid harsh penalties that hurt yourself or others.
models.exercise: Write down one small task you often say you'll "do tomorrow." Compare what you think when planning with what you think in the moment, then pick one thing you can set up tonight to make tomorrow's first step a little lighter.
models.brief: The same stick figure first plans reading next to a future calendar, then, at the moment of choosing, gets pulled away by a phone right in front of them; a dashed line leads back to a reading spot prepared in advance, showing how preference shifts with immediacy.
